meeting_start = Int('meeting_start')    # Time meeting with Betty begins

opt.add(meeting_start + meeting_duration <= 765)

        suffix = "AM"

An “optimal” schedule (minimizing idle waiting and freeing you to meet additional friends) is the one that minimizes waiting at Pacific Heights and uses the minimum meeting duration (105 minutes). In this case, the best solution is to leave Bayview at exactly 172 minutes after 9:00AM (11:52AM) so that you arrive exactly at 195 minutes (12:15PM), meet Thomas for 105 minutes (until 2:00PM), and then travel back arriving at 2:22PM.

    """
    Converts the time given in minutes from midnight into a formatted string with AM/PM.
    """
    hour = minutes // 60
    minute = minutes % 60
    suffix = "AM"
    if hour == 0:
        hour = 12
    elif hour == 12:
        suffix = "PM"
    elif hour > 12:
        hour -= 12
        suffix = "PM"
    return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"

def main():
    # Fixed times (in minutes after midnight)
    start_time = 9 * 60               # 9:00AM = 540 minutes

In our case, we start at Marina District at 9:00AM (time zero) and want to meet Timothy at Haight‑Ashbury – but Timothy is available only from 5:00PM to 8:15PM. We also know the travel time from Marina District to Haight‑Ashbury is 16 minutes (and 17 minutes on the return). One decision we can make is what time to depart from Marina so that, after traveling those 16 minutes, our arrival time “matches” best with Timothy’s availability. In particular, if we arrive before 5:00PM (which is 480 minutes after 9:00AM) we must wait until 5:00PM to start the meeting. On the other hand, if we depart too late we may lose meeting time (since the meeting must be at least 60 minutes long and Timothy leaves at 8:15PM). 

Thus we introduce a decision variable d (in minutes from 9:00AM) for our departure time from Marina. Our arrival time is then d + 16. We define the meeting start time as:
  meeting_start = 480  if (d + 16) < 480 (i.e. you arrive early and must wait)
  meeting_start = d + 16  if (d + 16) ≥ 480.
The meeting must last at least 60 minutes and must finish before Timothy leaves (8:15PM, which is 675 minutes after 9:00AM). In addition, we can “optimize” the schedule by minimizing the idle waiting time (or, equivalently, by finishing the meeting as early as possible so you’re free to meet other friends later). 

For example, if you choose d = 464 (which is 4:44PM, because 9:00AM + 464 minutes is 4:44PM), then your arrival is 464 + 16 = 480 (exactly 5:00PM). In that case you have zero waiting time and can start meeting Timothy immediately at 5:00PM for the required 60 minutes (until 6:00PM). Then you can get back to Marina District in 17 minutes arriving at 6:17PM – a schedule that “optimizes” your day to potentially allow further meetings.

from z3 import *

# Our variable:
# d represents the departure time (in minutes since 9:00AM) from Marina District.
d = Int('d')

# Constants (times are in minutes from 9:00AM)
travel_to_Haight = 16
meeting_min = 60
timothy_start = 480   # 5:00PM (9:00AM + 480 minutes)
timothy_end   = 675   # 8:15PM (9:00AM + 675 minutes)
travel_back = 17

# Arrival time at Haight-Ashbury:
arrival = d + travel_to_Haight

# Meeting start:
# If arrival is before Timothy is available, you must wait until 5:00PM.
meeting_start = If(arrival < timothy_start, timothy_start, arrival)
# We decide to meet the minimum required time.
meeting_end = meeting_start + meeting_min

# Constraint: The meeting must finish by the time Timothy leaves.
# Also, we need to guarantee meeting duration of at least 60 minutes.
constraints = [
    d >= 0,          # cannot depart before 9:00AM
    d <= 599,        # if we depart too late, meeting time will be < 60 minutes
    meeting_end <= timothy_end  # meeting must finish before or when Timothy leaves
]

# Define waiting time.
# Waiting time, if any, is the time you have to wait for Timothy if you arrive early.
waiting_time = If(arrival < timothy_start, timothy_start - arrival, 0)

# Use z3 Optimize to choose the best schedule.
opt = Optimize()
for c in constraints:
    opt.add(c)

# Our goal is to minimize waiting time.
h1 = opt.minimize(waiting_time)
# As a secondary objective, minimize the meeting end time (so you’re free sooner).
h2 = opt.minimize(meeting_end)

if opt.check() == sat:
    model = opt.model()
    sol_d = model[d].as_long()
    arr = sol_d + travel_to_Haight
    # Meeting will start at 5:00PM if you arrive early.
    meeting_start_val = timothy_start if (arr < timothy_start) else arr
    meeting_end_val = meeting_start_val + meeting_min
    
    # Helper function: convert minutes from 9:00AM to a proper time string.
    def format_time(minutes):
        total_minutes = 9 * 60 + minutes
        hours = total_minutes // 60
        mins = total_minutes % 60
        period = "AM" if hours < 12 else "PM"
        # adjust the hour for 12-hour clock
        if hours > 12:
            hours -= 12
        return f"{hours}:{mins:02d}{period}"
    
    dep_str = format_time(sol_d)
    arr_str = format_time(arr)
    meet_start_str = format_time(meeting_start_val)
    meet_end_str = format_time(meeting_end_val)
    # If there was waiting, note it.
    schedule = []
    schedule.append("You start at Marina District at 9:00AM.")
    schedule.append(f"You depart from Marina District at {dep_str}.")
    schedule.append(f"You travel to Haight-Ashbury in {travel_to_Haight} minutes and arrive at {arr_str}.")
    if arr < timothy_start:
        schedule.append(f"You wait until {format_time(timothy_start)}.")
    schedule.append(f"You meet Timothy for 60 minutes from {meet_start_str} to {meet_end_str}.")
    schedule.append(f"You travel back to Marina District in {travel_back} minutes and arrive at {format_time(meeting_end_val + travel_back)}.")
    
```python
    print(schedule)
else:
    print("No solution found")
```

We can view the problem as one of scheduling under constraints. In our case the “variables” are the start times for each leg of our day‐plan (expressed in minutes after 9:00AM). For example, we define:
 • m_depart = the time we leave Mission District (our starting point at 9:00AM),
 • j_start = the time we begin meeting Joseph at the Financial District,
 • r_start = the time we begin meeting Robert at the Embarcadero.

The “domains” of these integer variables are determined by our available time window and travel durations. In particular, note that:
 – We leave Mission District at or after 9:00AM (time ≥ 0).
 – The travel time from Mission to the Financial District is 17 minutes so our arrival there is m_depart + 17.
 – Joseph is available in the Financial District from 1:30PM (270 minutes) to 6:00PM (540 minutes) and you require at least 105 minutes with him. Thus we must have j_start ≥ 270 and j_start + 105 ≤ 540.
 – We can only meet Joseph after arriving; hence j_start ≥ m_depart + 17.
 – After finishing with Joseph, you travel 4 minutes from the Financial District to the Embarcadero. That is, if Joseph’s meeting ends at j_start + 105, you arrive at Embarcadero at j_start + 105 + 4.
 – Robert is available at the Embarcadero from 5:15PM (495 minutes) until 9:00PM (720 minutes) and you need at least 30 minutes with him. Therefore, r_start must be at least 495 and r_start must be no earlier than your arrival time (i.e. r_start ≥ j_start + 105 + 4) while also r_start + 30 ≤ 720.

We interpret “optimizing your goals” as meeting both friends (thus “maximizing the number of friends”) and—in our case—minimizing any unnecessary waiting time. For instance, if you leave too early from Mission you must wait at the Financial District until Joseph begins his visit, and if you finish with Joseph too early you must wait at the Embarcadero until Robert appears. We can capture these waiting times as:
  wait1 = j_start – (m_depart + 17)
  wait2 = r_start – (j_start + 105 + 4)
and then set the objective to minimize wait1 + wait2. In an optimal plan the travel “connects” exactly with the meeting times; one very good solution is:

# Create an optimization instance
opt = Optimize()

# Decision variables (all times in minutes after 9:00AM)
m_depart = Int('m_depart')  # time to leave Mission District
j_start  = Int('j_start')   # start time meeting Joseph (Financial District)
r_start  = Int('r_start')   # start time meeting Robert (Embarcadero)

# Add constraints:
# 1. You start at or after 9:00AM.
opt.add(m_depart >= 0)

# 2. Travel from Mission District to Financial District takes 17 minutes.
#    Thus, arrival at Financial District is m_depart + 17
#    You can only start meeting after arrival and when Joseph is available.
opt.add(j_start >= m_depart + 17)
opt.add(j_start >= 270)      # Joseph available from 1:30PM (270 min after 9:00AM)
opt.add(j_start <= 540 - 105)  # Meeting 105 mins must finish by 6:00PM (540 min)

# 3. Meeting with Joseph lasts at least 105 minutes.
opt.add(j_start + 105 <= 540)  # Ensure meeting ends by 6:00PM

# 4. After meeting Joseph, travel to Embarcadero takes 4 minutes.
#    So arrival at Embarcadero is (j_start + 105) + 4.
#    Robert is available from 5:15PM (495 min after 9:00AM).
opt.add(r_start >= j_start + 105 + 4)
opt.add(r_start >= 495)

# 5. Meeting Robert lasts at least 30 minutes and must finish by 9:00PM (720 min).
opt.add(r_start + 30 <= 720)

# For a “best” schedule we can minimize the total waiting time.
# Waiting time at the Financial District: if you arrive before Joseph arrives.
wait1 = j_start - (m_depart + 17)
# Waiting time at the Embarcadero: if you arrive before Robert is available.
wait2 = r_start - (j_start + 105 + 4)
opt.minimize(wait1 + wait2)

    m_depart_val = model[m_depart].as_long()

        hour = total // 60
        minute = total % 60
        # Determine AM/PM and convert to 12-hour format.
        suffix = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
        hour_mod = hour if hour <= 12 else hour - 12
        if hour_mod == 0:
            hour_mod = 12
        return f"{hour_mod}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"

    j_end = j_start_val + 105          # end of Joseph meeting
    arrival_E = j_end + 4              # arrival at Embarcadero
    r_end = r_start_val + 30           # end of Robert meeting

    schedule.append(f"You travel to Embarcadero in 4 minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival_E)}.")
    schedule.append(f"You meet Robert for 30 minutes from {format_time(r_start_val)} to {format_time(r_end)}.")

    # Output schedule (format similar to the provided example)
    print(schedule)
else:

Let’s look at the problem as a scheduling (constraint‐satisfaction) task. We have several “activities” with fixed travel times and friends’ availability windows. You begin at the Sunset District at 9:00AM, and you want to “meet” two friends:
 • Kevin is in the Financial District from 11:30AM to 1:45PM and you need to spend at least 75 minutes with him.
 • Rebecca is in Pacific Heights from 2:15PM to 9:30PM and you need to spend at least 15 minutes with her.

In our scheduling model the “activities” include:

 1. Departing from your starting location (Sunset District) at 9:00AM.
 2. Traveling from Sunset District to the friend’s location. (Travel times are given – for example, Sunset→Financial takes 30 minutes, and Financial→Pacific takes 13 minutes.)
 3. Waiting if you arrive before the friend’s availability.
 4. Meeting the friend for at least the required duration (75 minutes for Kevin; 15 minutes for Rebecca).

The constraints can be written in “minutes‐after–9:00AM”. For example:
 – You arrive at the Financial District (FD) at 9:00AM+30=9:30AM.
 – Kevin is available from 150 minutes (11:30AM) to 285 minutes (1:45PM); his meeting interval must be at least 75 minutes and fully lie within that window.
 – After finishing with Kevin, you travel from FD to Pacific Heights (PH) (taking 13 minutes) and then must wait until Rebecca becomes available at 315 minutes (2:15PM) before starting a meeting that lasts at least 15 minutes.
 – In addition, the “travel‐to” constraint means that the start of the Rebecca meeting can’t occur earlier than your FD meeting finish plus 13 minutes.

In other words, we want to assign start and end times to the two meetings (with Kevin and Rebecca) subject to:
  • t_K_start ≥ max(arrival_at_FD, 150) (with arrival_at_FD fixed as 30 since you depart at 9:00, though you might wait at FD if you arrive early)
  • t_K_end ≤ 285 and t_K_end − t_K_start ≥ 75
  • Your arrival at PH is t_K_end + 13 minutes.
  • t_R_start ≥ max(315, t_K_end + 13) (with 315=2:15PM)
  • t_R_end ≤ 750 and t_R_end − t_R_start ≥ 15

One “good” schedule is to simply leave immediately from Sunset at 9:00AM – travel to FD, wait there until Kevin’s availability begins at 11:30AM, meet him exactly for 75 minutes from 11:30AM to 12:45PM, then travel to PH (arriving about 12:58PM) and wait until Rebecca becomes available at 2:15PM to meet her for the minimum 15 minutes. (There are alternatives – for example, you could delay leaving Sunset so that waiting at FD is lower – but this schedule meets all constraints while “maximizing” the number of friends met.)

```python
t_k_end   = Int('t_k_end')

t_r_end   = Int('t_r_end')

s.add(t_k_start >= arrival_fd)      # Must be after arrival (9:30AM)
s.add(t_k_end <= 285)               # Must finish by 1:45PM
s.add(t_k_end - t_k_start >= 75)    # At least 75 minutes with Kevin

# Set arrival time at Pacific Heights after finishing with Kevin:
arrival_ph = t_k_end + travel_fd_ph  # leaving immediately from FD to PH

# Add constraints for Rebecca's meeting (must occur during her availability window)
s.add(t_r_start >= 315)             # Rebecca is available from 2:15PM
s.add(t_r_start >= arrival_ph)      # You cannot start meeting her before arriving at PH
s.add(t_r_end <= 750)               # Must finish by 9:30PM (if needed)

    kevin_end   = m[t_k_end].as_long()

    rebecca_end   = m[t_r_end].as_long()

    ph_arrival = kevin_end + travel_fd_ph

    schedule = []
    schedule.append(f"You start at Sunset District at 9:00AM.")
    schedule.append(f"You travel to Financial District in {travel_sd_fd} minutes and arrive at {format_time(fd_arrival)}.")

    schedule.append(f"You meet Kevin for {kevin_end - kevin_start} minutes from {format_time(kevin_start)} to {format_time(kevin_end)}.")
    
    schedule.append(f"You travel to Pacific Heights in {travel_fd_ph} minutes and arrive at {format_time(ph_arrival)}.")
    
    # Wait until Rebecca is available if necessary:

    # Print the schedule list
    print(schedule)
```

 2. Traveling from Sunset District to the friend’s location. (Travel times are given – for example, Sunset→Financial takes 30 minutes, and Financial→Pacific takes 13 minutes.)
 3. Waiting if you arrive before the friend’s availability.
 4. Meeting the friend for at least the required duration (75 minutes for Kevin; 15 minutes for Rebecca).

SOLUTION:
Below is one way to view and solve the problem. We have three “meeting‐tasks” (one for each friend) that must be scheduled during their available intervals. For each friend we introduce two key integer decision variables:
  • a meeting start time (measured in minutes after 9:00AM) and
  • a visit “order” (an integer 1, 2, or 3 indicating which friend is visited first, second, or third).

Each friend’s meeting must satisfy:
  – Its meeting start plus its minimum duration falls inside that friend’s availability window.
  – If that friend is the first visited, its meeting start cannot be before the travel time from Bayview.
Furthermore, when one friend is scheduled before another we add a constraint enforcing that the first friend’s meeting finish time plus the travel time from that friend’s location to the next friend’s location is not later than the next friend’s meeting start time. In other words, if friend A’s order is less than friend B’s, then

  A_start + A_duration + travel_time(A → B) ≤ B_start

An overall “finish” time variable is then constrained to be at least the finish time of every friend and we choose to minimize this variable. This casts our scheduling problem as a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) with an optimization objective.

The revised Python/Z3 script below implements these ideas. (Note that one common pitfall is to compare the result of check() to the string "sat"—instead we compare to the constant sat provided by Z3.) 

Below is the complete code:

------------------------------------------------------------
```python
from z3 import *

# Helper function to convert minutes (after 9:00AM) to a time string.
def minutes_to_time(m):
    total = 9 * 60 + m
    hour = total // 60
    minute = total % 60
    suffix = "AM"
    if hour >= 12:
        if hour > 12:
            hour -= 12
        suffix = "PM"
    return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"

# Data: travel times between locations.
travel_times = {
    ("Bayview", "Alamo Square"): 16,
    ("Bayview", "Union Square"): 17,
    ("Bayview", "Golden Gate Park"): 22,
    ("Alamo Square", "Bayview"): 16,
    ("Alamo Square", "Union Square"): 14,
    ("Alamo Square", "Golden Gate Park"): 9,
    ("Union Square", "Bayview"): 15,
    ("Union Square", "Alamo Square"): 15,
    ("Union Square", "Golden Gate Park"): 22,
    ("Golden Gate Park", "Bayview"): 23,
    ("Golden Gate Park", "Alamo Square"): 10,
    ("Golden Gate Park", "Union Square"): 22,
}

# Meeting durations (in minutes).
duration = {
    "Ronald": 90,   # meeting at Alamo Square
    "Richard": 30,  # meeting at Union Square
    "Kenneth": 60   # meeting at Golden Gate Park
}

# Availability windows [start, end] (minutes after 9:00AM).
# Ronald: available from 8:30AM but we start at 9:00AM so we use 0, until 7:45PM (645 minutes).
# Richard: available 2:30PM to 9:45PM --> [330, 765]
# Kenneth: available 10:00AM to 3:15PM --> [60, 375]
availability = {
    "Ronald": (0, 645),
    "Richard": (330, 765),
    "Kenneth": (60, 375)
}

# Fixed locations for each friend.
location = {
    "Ronald": "Alamo Square",
    "Richard": "Union Square",
    "Kenneth": "Golden Gate Park"
}

# Create an optimization model.
opt = Optimize()

# Decision variables: meeting start times (in minutes after 9:00AM)
r_start = Int("r_start")         # Ronald's meeting start time
richard_start = Int("richard_start")  # Richard's meeting start time
kenneth_start = Int("kenneth_start")  # Kenneth's meeting start time

# Meeting finish times.
finish_r = r_start + duration["Ronald"]
finish_richard = richard_start + duration["Richard"]
finish_kenneth = kenneth_start + duration["Kenneth"]

# A variable for the overall finish time.
finish = Int("finish")
opt.add(finish >= finish_r, finish >= finish_richard, finish >= finish_kenneth)

# Decision variables for ordering (each friend gets an order 1, 2, or 3, all distinct).
r_order = Int("r_order")
richard_order = Int("richard_order")
kenneth_order = Int("kenneth_order")

opt.add(And(r_order >= 1, r_order <= 3))
opt.add(And(richard_order >= 1, richard_order <= 3))
opt.add(And(kenneth_order >= 1, kenneth_order <= 3))
opt.add(Distinct(r_order, richard_order, kenneth_order))

# Each meeting must occur within the friend's availability.
opt.add(r_start >= availability["Ronald"][0], r_start + duration["Ronald"] <= availability["Ronald"][1])
opt.add(richard_start >= availability["Richard"][0], richard_start + duration["Richard"] <= availability["Richard"][1])
opt.add(kenneth_start >= availability["Kenneth"][0], kenneth_start + duration["Kenneth"] <= availability["Kenneth"][1])

# For the first visited friend, ensure enough travel time from Bayview.
opt.add(Implies(r_order == 1, r_start >= travel_times[("Bayview", location["Ronald"])]))
opt.add(Implies(richard_order == 1, richard_start >= travel_times[("Bayview", location["Richard"])]))
opt.add(Implies(kenneth_order == 1, kenneth_start >= travel_times[("Bayview", location["Kenneth"])]))

# Ordering constraints.
# If friend A is visited before friend B then A's finish plus travel time from A to B must be <= B's start.
# Ronald and Richard:
opt.add(Implies(r_order < richard_order, r_start + duration["Ronald"] + travel_times[(location["Ronald"], location["Richard"])] <= richard_start))
opt.add(Implies(richard_order < r_order, richard_start + duration["Richard"] + travel_times[(location["Richard"], location["Ronald"])] <= r_start))

# Ronald and Kenneth:
opt.add(Implies(r_order < kenneth_order, r_start + duration["Ronald"] + travel_times[(location["Ronald"], location["Kenneth"])] <= kenneth_start))
opt.add(Implies(kenneth_order < r_order, kenneth_start + duration["Kenneth"] + travel_times[(location["Kenneth"], location["Ronald"])] <= r_start))

# Richard and Kenneth:
opt.add(Implies(richard_order < kenneth_order, richard_start + duration["Richard"] + travel_times[(location["Richard"], location["Kenneth"])] <= kenneth_start))
opt.add(Implies(kenneth_order < richard_order, kenneth_start + duration["Kenneth"] + travel_times[(location["Kenneth"], location["Richard"])] <= richard_start))

# Objective: minimize the overall finish time.
opt.minimize(finish)

# Check for a solution and extract the schedule.
if opt.check() == sat:
    m = opt.model()
    # Get order and start times.
    r_order_val = m[r_order].as_long()
    richard_order_val = m[richard_order].as_long()
    kenneth_order_val = m[kenneth_order].as_long()
    r_start_val = m[r_start].as_long()
    richard_start_val = m[richard_start].as_long()
    kenneth_start_val = m[kenneth_start].as_long()
    
    # Build a dictionary mapping order position to friend details.
    # Each entry: (Name, location, meeting start, meeting end, travel time from Bayview)
    details = {
        r_order_val: ("Ronald", location["Ronald"], r_start_val, r_start_val + duration["Ronald"],
                       travel_times[("Bayview", location["Ronald"])]),
        richard_order_val: ("Richard", location["Richard"], richard_start_val, richard_start_val + duration["Richard"],
                             travel_times[("Bayview", location["Richard"])]),
        kenneth_order_val: ("Kenneth", location["Kenneth"], kenneth_start_val, kenneth_start_val + duration["Kenneth"],
                             travel_times[("Bayview", location["Kenneth"])]),
    }
    
    # Assemble the schedule in the order of visits.
    schedule = []
    schedule.append("You start at Bayview at 9:00AM.")
    current_time = 0  # minutes after 9:00AM
    current_loc = "Bayview"
    
    # Process the meetings in sorted order (1st, 2nd, 3rd).
    for order in sorted(details.keys()):
        name, loc, meet_start, meet_end, bay_travel = details[order]
        # Determine travel time from current location to this meeting's location.
        if current_loc == "Bayview":
            travel_time = bay_travel
        else:
            travel_time = travel_times[(current_loc, loc)]
        arrival = current_time + travel_time
        schedule.append(f"You travel to {loc} in {travel_time} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival)}.")
        # Wait if arriving earlier than the scheduled meeting start.
        if arrival < meet_start:
            schedule.append(f"You wait until {minutes_to_time(meet_start)}.")
        meeting_duration = duration[name]
        schedule.append(f"You meet {name} for {meeting_duration} minutes from {minutes_to_time(meet_start)} to {minutes_to_time(meet_end)}.")
        # Update current time and location (depart immediately after meeting ends).
        current_time = meet_end
        current_loc = loc

    # Print the schedule.
    print(schedule)
else:
    print("No solution found.")
```

 • The meeting “start time” (expressed in minutes after 9:00AM) at each location. (The “end time” is given by the start time plus the minimum meeting duration—in our case 90 minutes for Ronald, 30 minutes for Richard and 60 minutes for Kenneth.)
 • An overall “finish time” (the latest finishing time of the meetings) that we want to minimize so that you meet all friends as early as possible (or, equivalently, you “maximize the number of friends met” with as little idle time as possible).

The constraints come from several sources:
 1. Availability windows. For example, Ronald is available from 8:30AM until 7:45PM – but since you only start at 9:00AM the meeting with him must happen after that and finish by 7:45PM. In minutes after 9:00AM, his meeting must finish by 645 minutes (i.e. 7:45PM). Below is one way to view and solve the problem. We have three “meeting‐tasks” (one for each friend) that must be scheduled during their available intervals. For each friend we introduce two key integer decision variables:
  • a meeting start time (measured in minutes after 9:00AM) and
  • a visit “order” (an integer 1, 2, or 3 indicating which friend is visited first, second, or third).

Each friend’s meeting must satisfy:
  – Its meeting start plus its minimum duration falls inside that friend’s availability window.
  – If that friend is the first visited, its meeting start cannot be before the travel time from Bayview.
Furthermore, when one friend is scheduled before another we add a constraint enforcing that the first friend’s meeting finish time plus the travel time from that friend’s location to the next friend’s location is not later than the next friend’s meeting start time. In other words, if friend A’s order is less than friend B’s, then

  A_start + A_duration + travel_time(A → B) ≤ B_start

An overall “finish” time variable is then constrained to be at least the finish time of every friend and we choose to minimize this variable. This casts our scheduling problem as a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) with an optimization objective.

 • leave your starting location (Alamo Square),
 • begin and end your meeting with Steven at Russian Hill,
 • begin and end your meeting with Joshua at The Castro, and
 • begin and end your meeting with Richard at Fisherman’s Wharf.

Each friend is available only during a fixed window and you want to spend a minimum amount of time with each:
 – Steven is available from 1:15PM to 2:15PM (i.e. from minute 255 to 315); you need at least 60 minutes – so the only feasible option is to meet him exactly from 1:15 to 2:15.
 – Joshua is available from 2:45PM to 9:30PM (i.e. from minute 345 to 750) and you need at least 90 minutes. However, since you must catch Richard later, you will “stretch” your meeting with Joshua as long as possible while still leaving enough time for travel.
 – Richard is at Fisherman’s Wharf from 9:15PM to 10:15PM (i.e. from minute 735 to 795) and needs 60 minutes.
 
Additionally, the travel time between locations is given:
 • From Alamo Square to Russian Hill: 13 minutes.
 • From Russian Hill to The Castro: 21 minutes.
 • From The Castro to Fisherman’s Wharf: 24 minutes.
 
The chain of constraints then is:
1. You must leave Alamo Square at some time (t) so that if you travel 13 minutes you arrive by 1:15PM. In an “optimal” schedule (minimizing waiting time at the destination) you would leave at 9:00 + 242 minutes = 1:02PM so that you arrive at Russian Hill exactly at 1:15.
2. At Russian Hill the meeting with Steven must occur exactly from minute 255 to 315.
3. After finishing with Steven (at 2:15PM, minute 315) you then need 21 minutes of travel to The Castro. This gives an arrival time of 336 minutes. Since Joshua isn’t available until minute 345, you wait until then.
4. For Joshua’s meeting, you want to maximize his meeting duration (meeting as long as possible while still catching Richard). If you start at 2:45PM (minute 345) then, in order to catch Richard you must leave The Castro by 735 – 24 = 711. That gives Joshua a meeting duration of 711 – 345 = 366 minutes which is well above the minimum of 90 minutes.
5. You then travel 24 minutes from The Castro so that you are at Fisherman’s Wharf at exactly 9:15PM (735 minutes) to meet Richard from 9:15PM to 10:15PM.
 
In summary, the “optimal” schedule is:
 • Wait at Alamo Square until 1:02PM, leave and take 13 minutes to arrive at Russian Hill at 1:15PM.
 • Meet Steven exactly from 1:15PM to 2:15PM.
 • Immediately leave and travel 21 minutes to The Castro. Arriving at 2:36PM, wait until 2:45PM and begin meeting Joshua.
 • Meet Joshua from 2:45PM to 8:51PM (366 minutes).
 • Leave promptly and travel 24 minutes to arrive at Fisherman’s Wharf at 9:15PM and meet Richard from 9:15PM to 10:15PM.
 
We now “encode” this scheduling problem with Z3. Variables represent the departure and meeting start/end times with the following constraints:
 – S_start = departure_time_AS + 13, and must be at least 255.
 – Steven’s meeting must last at least 60 minutes and finish by 315.
 – Joshua’s meeting must start no earlier than max(345, S_end + 21) and last at least 90 minutes.

 – Richard’s meeting must be 60 minutes within the window [735,795].
We then use Z3’s Optimize module to “maximize” Joshua’s meeting time (thus stretching his meeting as long as possible while still obeying the constraints).

SOLUTION:
Below is one way of “thinking out loud” about the problem. We can view the day’s schedule as a constraint‐satisfaction problem with decision variables that capture the start and end times (measured in minutes after 9:00AM) of each meeting event. In our case we have three friends with fixed availability windows and minimum meeting‐durations:

• Paul is at Presidio between 9:00AM (time 0) and 1:00PM (time 240). He needs at least 120 minutes of meeting time. In addition, you start at Sunset District at 9:00AM and it takes 16 minutes to travel from Sunset to Presidio. Thus we introduce a variable Paul_start (with domain ≥16) and set the duration constraint  
  Paul_end − Paul_start ≥ 120  
and also enforce that Paul_end ≤ 240.

• John is available at Embarcadero from 1:15PM (time 255) to 4:00PM (time 420) and you need to talk for at least 90 minutes. After finishing with Paul, you must travel from Presidio to Embarcadero (20 minutes). Hence John’s meeting cannot start until after Paul_end + 20 and also not before 255. We therefore set  
  John_start ≥ max(Paul_end + 20, 255)  
with the meeting lasting at least 90 minutes (John_end − John_start ≥ 90) and John_end ≤ 420.

• Daniel is at Mission District from 3:45PM (time 405) to 6:00PM (time 540) and a 90‐minute meeting is required. After finishing with John, you travel from Embarcadero to Mission District (20 minutes), so Daniel_start must satisfy  
  Daniel_start ≥ max(John_end + 20, 405)  
and Daniel_end − Daniel_start ≥ 90 with Daniel_end ≤ 540.

Because our “goal” is to meet as many friends as possible (and if all three can be met then that is best) we can also add an objective to minimize the finish time of the day (Daniel_end) so that we are not “waiting unnecessarily”. In an “optimal” solution the meetings are scheduled at their minimum required durations and the waiting times (if you arrive early to an availability window you must wait) are “as short as possible.”

Below is an implementation of the above ideas in a Python script that uses the Z3 solver. (When run the script prints a list describing your full day’s schedule in the style of the sample output.)

------------------------------------------------------------

```python
from z3 import *

# Start time = 9:00AM. We use minutes past 9:00.
# Availability (in minutes after 9:00):
#   Paul: [0, 240] (9:00AM to 1:00PM)
#   John: [255, 420] (1:15PM to 4:00PM)
#   Daniel: [405, 540] (3:45PM to 6:00PM)
#
# Travel times (in minutes) between districts:
#   Sunset -> Presidio = 16
#   Presidio -> Embarcadero = 20
#   Embarcadero -> Mission District = 20

# Create solver and optimization object (we wish to minimize end time)
opt = Optimize()

# Create integer variables representing meeting start and end times (minutes from 9:00AM)
P_start = Int('P_start')  # Paul meeting start at Presidio
P_end   = Int('P_end')    # Paul meeting end
J_start = Int('J_start')  # John meeting start at Embarcadero
J_end   = Int('J_end')    # John meeting end
D_start = Int('D_start')  # Daniel meeting start at Mission District
D_end   = Int('D_end')    # Daniel meeting end

# We assume the meetings are held at exactly the minimum durations (optimal for finishing early)
# so we enforce equality with the minimum requirement.
opt.add(P_end - P_start == 120)  # Paul: at least 120 minutes
opt.add(J_end - J_start == 90)   # John: at least 90 minutes
opt.add(D_end - D_start == 90)   # Daniel: at least 90 minutes

# Constraint: Our day begins at Sunset District at 9:00. We travel to Presidio in 16 minutes.
# So the meeting with Paul cannot start before 16.
opt.add(P_start >= 16)
# Also, Paul is only available until 1:00 (240 minutes after 9:00)
opt.add(P_end <= 240)

# After finishing with Paul, travel from Presidio to Embarcadero takes 20 minutes.
# John's meeting can only start after that and not before his window opens (255).
opt.add(J_start >= P_end + 20)
opt.add(J_start >= 255)
# John's meeting must finish by 4:00PM (420 minutes after 9:00)
opt.add(J_end <= 420)

# After finishing with John, travel from Embarcadero to Mission District takes 20 minutes.
# Daniel’s meeting can only start after that and not before his window opens (405).
opt.add(D_start >= J_end + 20)
opt.add(D_start >= 405)
# Daniel's meeting must finish by 6:00PM (540 minutes after 9:00)
opt.add(D_end <= 540)

# (Optional optimization: We wish to minimize the final finish time, so that our waiting is minimized.)
opt.minimize(D_end)

# Solve the constraints
if opt.check() == sat:
    mod = opt.model()
    # Retrieve solution values (they are integers: minutes after 9:00AM)
    p_start = mod.evaluate(P_start).as_long()
    p_end   = mod.evaluate(P_end).as_long()
    j_start = mod.evaluate(J_start).as_long()
    j_end   = mod.evaluate(J_end).as_long()
    d_start = mod.evaluate(D_start).as_long()
    d_end   = mod.evaluate(D_end).as_long()
    
    # Calculate travel arrival times:
    #  1. Arrival at Presidio:
    arr_presidio = 16  # always fixed: Sunset -> Presidio = 16 minutes after 9:00
    #  2. Arrival at Embarcadero: after Paul meeting then 20-minute travel
    arr_embarcadero = p_end + 20
    #  3. Arrival at Mission District: after John meeting then 20-minute travel
    arr_mission = j_end + 20

    # A helper function to convert minutes-from-9:00 into "H:MMAM/PM" time
    def minutes_to_time(mins):
        # 9:00AM is our zero point; add 9 hours (540 minutes) to get minutes from midnight.
        total = 540 + mins
        hours = total // 60
        minutes = total % 60
        suffix = "AM"
        if hours >= 12:
            suffix = "PM"
            if hours > 12:
                hours -= 12
        return f"{hours}:{minutes:02d}{suffix}"

    # Build the schedule (as a list of strings) similar to the sample output format.
    schedule = []
    schedule.append(f"You start at Sunset District at 9:00AM.")
    schedule.append(f"You travel to Presidio in 16 minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arr_presidio)}.")
    schedule.append(f"You meet Paul for 120 minutes from {minutes_to_time(p_start)} to {minutes_to_time(p_end)}.")
    schedule.append(f"You travel to Embarcadero in 20 minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arr_embarcadero)}.")
    # If you arrive earlier than John's availability, you must wait.
    if arr_embarcadero < j_start:
        schedule.append(f"You wait until {minutes_to_time(j_start)}.")
    schedule.append(f"You meet John for 90 minutes from {minutes_to_time(j_start)} to {minutes_to_time(j_end)}.")
    schedule.append(f"You travel to Mission District in 20 minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arr_mission)}.")
    if arr_mission < d_start:
        schedule.append(f"You wait until {minutes_to_time(d_start)}.")
    schedule.append(f"You meet Daniel for 90 minutes from {minutes_to_time(d_start)} to {minutes_to_time(d_end)}.")
    
    # Print the schedule as a list
    print(schedule)
else:
    print("No solution found.")
```

Explanation:
1. We define six decision variables: the start and end times for Paul’s, John’s and Daniel’s meetings (minutes after 9:00AM).
2. We add the “minimum duration” constraints (120 minutes for Paul; 90 minutes for John and Daniel) and force that the meeting ends do not exceed the friend’s availability (Paul’s meeting ends by 1:00PM, John by 4:00PM, and Daniel by 6:00PM).
3. We account for travel times along the fixed route: starting at Sunset, then going to Presidio (16 minutes), then after Paul’s meeting travel 20 minutes to Embarcadero, then after John’s meeting travel 20 minutes to Mission District.
4. We add “availability” constraints for John and Daniel so that their meeting cannot start before the posted times.
5. Finally, we use Optimize to “minimize” the final finish time (Daniel_end), thereby “optimizing” our overall schedule.

Below is an explanation of how the “meet‐friends” problem can be seen as a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) along with a complete Python script that uses Z3 to “choose” among different schedules and finally output the best (feasible) route.

──────────────────────────────
1. REASONING AS A CONSTRAINT SATISFACTION PROBLEM

We are given three visits (to meet Sandra, Margaret and George) that must be “scheduled” during the day. The “tasks” (friend meetings) come with time‐windows and minimum durations. In addition, there are travel times between locations and from the starting point (Fisherman’s Wharf); these force relationships between the finish time of one meeting and the start time of the next scheduled meeting.

We can model the problem by defining:

• Variables for each friend meeting:
  – For friend i we define s[i] (meeting start time) and e[i] (meeting end time). All times are measured in minutes after midnight.
  – We add the constraint that e[i] – s[i] must be at least the friend’s required meeting duration.
  – We add “availability” constraints. For example, Sandra (at Embarcadero) is available from 5:15PM (1035 minutes) until 10:00PM (1320 minutes) so we require s[Sandra] ≥ 1035 and e[Sandra] ≤ 1320 (and the meeting lasts at least 90 minutes). Similarly for Margaret (Presidio, available 3:30PM–6:15PM; at least 30 minutes) and George (Bayview, available 8:45PM–9:45PM; at least 45 minutes).

• Ordering decisions:
  – We have three possible visits but the friend‑availability windows “force” an order. For example, Margaret’s available period is earlier than Sandra’s so to “catch” Margaret you must visit her before Sandra.
  – We introduce three integer decision variables order0, order1 and order2 that represent a permutation (with values 0,1,2 indexing the set of friends) expressing in which sequence to visit the friends. (For our mapping we let friend 0 = Sandra, friend 1 = Margaret and friend 2 = George.)
  
• Travel time constraints:
  – From the start (Fisherman’s Wharf) the travel times to each friend’s location are given (e.g. 8 minutes to Embarcadero, 17 to Presidio and 26 to Bayview).
  – There is also a travel time between any two friend locations (for instance, from Presidio to Embarcadero it takes 20 minutes, from Embarcadero to Bayview 21 minutes, etc.).
  – For the friend visited in the first position (order0) we require that the meeting start s[i] is not before “arrival time” computed as (9:00AM + travel time). Then, for every consecutive pair – say the first friend i (in position order0) and the second friend j (in position order1) – we require that s[j] is at least e[i] plus the travel time from the location of friend i to friend j. A similar constraint is added for the transition from the second meeting (order1) to the third meeting (order2).

• In summary, we impose the following types of constraints:
  • Time‐window and minimum meeting duration constraints for each friend.
  • “Precedence” constraints: if friend i is visited immediately before friend j then
        s[j] ≥ e[i] + (travel time from i to j)
  • The decision variables order0, order1, order2 are forced to be all different.
  
Since the overall “goal” is to “meet as many friends as possible” (and if more than one combination were possible one might choose one that minimizes overall finishing time or waiting time), we can introduce an objective (for example, minimize the finish time of the last meeting). In our case it turns out that the only order that meets all the windows is Margaret → Sandra → George.

1. REASONING AS A CONSTRAINT SATISFACTION PROBLEM

We are given three visits (to meet Sandra, Margaret and George) that must be “scheduled” during the day. The “tasks” (friend meetings) come with time‐windows and minimum durations. In addition, there are travel times between locations and from the starting point (Fisherman’s Wharf); these force relationships between the finish time of one meeting and the start time of the next scheduled meeting.

• Variables for each friend meeting:
  – For friend i we define s[i] (meeting start time) and e[i] (meeting end time). All times are measured in minutes after midnight.
  – We add the constraint that e[i] – s[i] must be at least the friend’s required meeting duration.
  – We add “availability” constraints. Similarly for Margaret (Presidio, available 3:30PM–6:15PM; at least 30 minutes) and George (Bayview, available 8:45PM–9:45PM; at least 45 minutes).

• Ordering decisions:
  – We have three possible visits but the friend‑availability windows “force” an order. For example, Margaret’s available period is earlier than Sandra’s so to “catch” Margaret you must visit her before Sandra.
  – We introduce three integer decision variables order0, order1 and order2 that represent a permutation (with values 0,1,2 indexing the set of friends) expressing in which sequence to visit the friends. (For our mapping we let friend 0 = Sandra, friend 1 = Margaret and friend 2 = George.)

SOLUTION:
We can “model” our day as a scheduling (constraint‐satisfaction) problem. In our problem the “jobs” are the meetings with our friends. For each friend we know:
 • Their meeting location and available time window (for example, Mary is available at Embarcadero from 4:45PM to 6:15PM, and you need at least 90 minutes with her – which in her case means you must be there for the entire fixed interval).
 • The minimum meeting duration.
 • The “setup” or travel time needed to get from one location to the next (for example, going from Embarcadero to North Beach takes 5 minutes).
 • You start the day at Mission District at 9:00AM.

We introduce three decision “slots” (one per friend) together with Boolean variables (to decide whether or not to “schedule” a meeting with that friend) and start–time variables (in minutes after 9:00AM). For instance, if you choose to meet Mary then her meeting must occur during her availability. (Her availability and 90‐minute “minimum” forces her meeting to be exactly 4:45PM–6:15PM.) Similarly, Steven’s meeting (at Alamo Square) can only start between 7:00PM and 7:30PM (so that 45 minutes finish by 8:15PM) and Margaret’s meeting (at North Beach) must be scheduled sometime in her window (with at least 105 minutes duration, it is possible to start as late as 6:00PM). 

Because you cannot “be in two places at once,” if two meetings are chosen then their time intervals (plus added travel time from one location to the next) must not overlap. (For example, if you meet Mary at Embarcadero, then to later meet Steven at Alamo Square you must allow the travel time of 19 minutes from Embarcadero to Alamo Square – that forces Steven’s meeting to happen after Mary’s meeting.) 

Finally, our overall “goal” is to maximize the number of friends you meet (and if several schedules yield the same count you might also maximize the total meeting time). (It turns out that meeting all three friends is impossible because Mary’s fixed earlier meeting combined with the travel times forces the schedule to “choose” only two friends; among the possible pairs, the pair Mary plus Margaret gives you 90+105 = 195 minutes of friend–time, which is best.) 

Below is a complete Python script (using Z3’s Optimize functionality) that encodes these constraints and “searches” for an optimal schedule. (This code is now fixed so that no invalid literal appears.)

```python
from z3 import *

# Create an optimization object.
opt = Optimize()

# Decision booleans: whether to meet each friend.
meet_steven   = Bool('meet_steven')
meet_margaret = Bool('meet_margaret')
meet_mary     = Bool('meet_mary')

# Start time (in minutes after 9:00AM) for each meeting.
s_steven   = Int('s_steven')
s_margaret = Int('s_margaret')
s_mary     = Int('s_mary')

# Meeting durations (in minutes)
d_steven   = 45
d_margaret = 105
d_mary     = 90

# Available time windows (relative to 9:00AM):
# Steven: available from 7:00PM to 8:15PM, so start must be between 600 and 630 minutes.
opt.add(Implies(meet_steven, And(s_steven >= 600, s_steven <= 630)))
# Margaret: available from 4:00PM to 8:45PM, so start ∈ [420, 600] (since s_margaret + 105 <= 705).
opt.add(Implies(meet_margaret, And(s_margaret >= 420, s_margaret <= 600)))
# Mary: available from 4:45PM to 6:15PM; with a 90–minute meeting this forces s_mary = 465.
opt.add(Implies(meet_mary, s_mary == 465))

# Define travel times (in minutes) between locations.
# (The keys are (start_location, destination).)
travel = {
    ("Mission District", "Alamo Square"): 11,
    ("Mission District", "North Beach"): 17,
    ("Mission District", "Embarcadero"): 19,
    ("Alamo Square", "Mission District"): 10,
    ("Alamo Square", "North Beach"): 15,
    ("Alamo Square", "Embarcadero"): 17,
    ("North Beach", "Mission District"): 18,
    ("North Beach", "Alamo Square"): 16,
    ("North Beach", "Embarcadero"): 6,
    ("Embarcadero", "Mission District"): 20,
    ("Embarcadero", "Alamo Square"): 19,
    ("Embarcadero", "North Beach"): 5
}

# Define each meeting’s location.
loc_steven   = "Alamo Square"
loc_margaret = "North Beach"
loc_mary     = "Embarcadero"

# Add constraints ensuring that you can get from your start (Mission District) to the meeting.
opt.add(Implies(meet_steven, s_steven >= travel[("Mission District", loc_steven)]))
opt.add(Implies(meet_margaret, s_margaret >= travel[("Mission District", loc_margaret)]))
opt.add(Implies(meet_mary,     s_mary   >= travel[("Mission District", loc_mary)]))

# The ordering constraints: if you choose two meetings then one must finish (plus travel time) before the other starts.
# Note: Because Mary’s meeting has a fixed start (465) and duration (90), that fixes her interval.
#
# (1) For Steven and Mary: Only possible ordering is Mary then Steven.
#     Mary finishes at 465+90; plus travel from Embarcadero to Alamo Square takes 19 minutes.
opt.add(Implies(And(meet_steven, meet_mary),
                s_steven >= s_mary + d_mary + travel[("Embarcadero", "Alamo Square")]))
                
# (2) For Margaret and Mary: Only possible ordering is Mary then Margaret.
#     Mary finishes at 465+90; travel from Embarcadero to North Beach is 5 minutes.
opt.add(Implies(And(meet_margaret, meet_mary),
                s_margaret >= s_mary + d_mary + travel[("Embarcadero", "North Beach")]))
                
# (3) For Margaret and Steven (when Mary is not involved, this pair can be scheduled in one order only).
#     The only viable ordering is Margaret then Steven.
#     That is, Steven can only start after Margaret’s meeting ends plus travel time from North Beach to Alamo Square.
opt.add(Implies(And(meet_margaret, meet_steven),
                s_steven >= s_margaret + d_margaret + travel[("North Beach", "Alamo Square")]))

# Our objective is to maximize the number of friends met.
num_meetings = If(meet_steven, 1, 0) + If(meet_margaret, 1, 0) + If(meet_mary, 1, 0)
h1 = opt.maximize(num_meetings)
# As a tie-breaker, we maximize the total meeting time (in minutes).
total_meeting_time = d_steven*If(meet_steven, 1, 0) + d_margaret*If(meet_margaret, 1, 0) + d_mary*If(meet_mary, 1, 0)
h2 = opt.maximize(total_meeting_time)

# Find an optimal solution.
if opt.check() == sat:
    model = opt.model()
    # Build a schedule (a list of strings) based on the chosen meetings.
    schedule = []
    schedule.append("You start at Mission District at 9:00AM.")
    
    # Gather chosen meetings as tuples: (FriendName, meeting start, location, duration)
    chosen = []
    if model.evaluate(meet_mary):
        chosen.append(("Mary", model.evaluate(s_mary).as_long(), loc_mary, d_mary))
    if model.evaluate(meet_margaret):
        chosen.append(("Margaret", model.evaluate(s_margaret).as_long(), loc_margaret, d_margaret))
    if model.evaluate(meet_steven):
        chosen.append(("Steven", model.evaluate(s_steven).as_long(), loc_steven, d_steven))
    
    # Sort the meetings in order of their start times.
    chosen.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
    
    # A helper function to convert minutes after 9:00AM into a time string.
    def format_time(minutes):
        total_minutes = 9 * 60 + minutes  # since 9:00AM is our zero
        hour = total_minutes // 60
        minute = total_minutes % 60
        suffix = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
        # Convert to 12-hour format.
        if hour > 12:
            hour -= 12
        return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"
    
    # For the first meeting, add travel from Mission District.
    if chosen:
        first_friend = chosen[0]
        t_travel = travel[("Mission District", first_friend[2])]
        arrival = t_travel
        schedule.append(f"You travel to {first_friend[2]} in {t_travel} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival)}.")
        if arrival < first_friend[1]:
            schedule.append(f"You wait until {format_time(first_friend[1])}.")
        meeting_end = first_friend[1] + first_friend[3]
        schedule.append(f"You meet {first_friend[0]} for {first_friend[3]} minutes from {format_time(first_friend[1])} to {format_time(meeting_end)}.")
    
        # For subsequent meetings, add travel steps and meeting intervals.
        for i in range(1, len(chosen)):
            prev = chosen[i - 1]
            curr = chosen[i]
            t_travel = travel[(prev[2], curr[2])]
            arrival = (prev[1] + prev[3] + t_travel)
            schedule.append(f"You travel from {prev[2]} to {curr[2]} in {t_travel} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival)}.")
            if arrival < curr[1]:
                schedule.append(f"You wait until {format_time(curr[1])}.")
            meeting_end = curr[1] + curr[3]
            schedule.append(f"You meet {curr[0]} for {curr[3]} minutes from {format_time(curr[1])} to {format_time(meeting_end)}.")
    else:
        schedule.append("No meetings scheduled.")
    
    print(schedule)
else:
    print("No solution found")
```

We can “model” the day using a set of decision variables that represent which friend meetings are “taken” and at what times (using minutes past 9:00AM as our time‐scale). In our problem we have three potential meetings:
 • Mary will be at Embarcadero from 4:45PM to 6:15PM – a 90‐minute block (in minutes, that is [465,555]). Since her entire available interval exactly equals the minimum meeting time, if you choose to meet Mary the meeting time is fixed.
 • Steven is available at Alamo Square from 7:00PM to 8:15PM – a window in which you must secure a 45‐minute meeting. (For example, you could start at any time s between 600 and 630 minutes so that s+45 ≤ 675.)
 • Margaret is available at North Beach from 4:00PM to 8:45PM. To meet her you must schedule a continuous 105–minute block. This meeting can start as early as 420 minutes and as late as 600 minutes (so that m+105 ≤ 705).

Travel times (in minutes) between the locations (Mission District = starting point):
 • From Mission District to Embarcadero, North Beach or Alamo Square are 19, 17 and 11 minutes respectively.
 • When switching between meeting locations the travel times are also given. For example, going from Embarcadero (Mary’s meeting) to North Beach (Margaret’s meeting) takes 5 minutes; from Embarcadero to Alamo Square is 19 minutes; and from North Beach to Alamo Square is 16 minutes.

Notice that because the meeting windows partly overlap but the travel times “force” a sequential order, you cannot “chain” all three meetings.
For example, suppose you try to meet Mary (fixed 4:45–6:15) and then Margaret. If you finish Mary at 6:15 and travel (5 minutes from Embarcadero to North Beach), you arrive at 6:20. Then you can meet Margaret for 105 minutes up to 8:05 – which is acceptable since her window finishes at 8:45.
On the other hand, if you tried to “insert” Steven (whose meeting would have to occur at Alamo Square between 7:00 and 8:15) in addition to the other two, you would run into an impossible ordering. A brief check shows:
 – Mary’s meeting is fixed 4:45–6:15.
 – If Mary comes first then Margaret second then Steven third you’d have
  6:15 + 5 (travel from Embarcadero to North Beach) = 6:20 start for Margaret; then Margaret ends at 6:20+105 = 8:05 and it takes 16 minutes from North Beach to Alamo Square so Steven would not be reached until about 8:21 – too late.
Thus, a decision–variable formulation is natural. In our Z3 formulation we define Boolean variables (meetMary, meetMargaret, meetSteven) and meeting‐start time variables (for Margaret and Steven, since Mary’s meeting time is “fixed”). We add constraints for:
 1. The meeting window (for example, s must lie between 600 and 630 when meeting Steven is chosen).
 2. Travel “ordering” constraints. For instance, if Mary and Margaret are both chosen then because you finish Mary at 555 and need 5 minutes to go from Embarcadero to North Beach, you must have m ≥ 560.
 3. (Similarly, the pair Margaret+Steven forces m + 105 + 16 ≤ s.)
Finally, we “optimize” the schedule by maximizing the number of friends met (our primary goal) and—for any ties—a secondary objective of maximizing total meeting time.

A quick analysis shows that although there are three potential meetings, all three together lead to a conflict in travel sequencing. In fact the maximum number that you can “squeeze in” is 2.
Among the three possible pairs, one can compare:
 • Mary + Steven gives 90+45 = 135 minutes.
 • Margaret + Steven gives 105+45 = 150 minutes.
 • Mary + Margaret gives 90+105 = 195 minutes.
Therefore the “best” schedule is to meet Mary and Margaret.
One such schedule is:
 1. You start at Mission District at 9:00AM and (since you are free until your first meeting) wait until 4:26PM – the time you must leave in order to travel 19 minutes from Mission District to Embarcadero and arrive exactly at 4:45PM.
 2. At 4:45PM you meet Mary at Embarcadero until 6:15PM.
 3. You then travel from Embarcadero to North Beach (a 5–minute trip) arriving at 6:20PM.
 4. Immediately you meet Margaret for 105 minutes until 8:05PM (well within her window ending at 8:45PM).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
from z3 import Optimize, Int, Bool, If, And, Or

# Helper: convert minutes past 9:00AM to a string time in 12-hour format.
def minutes_to_time(minutes):
    # Base time is 9:00AM, which is 9*60 = 540 minutes since midnight.
    total = 540 + minutes  
    hour = total // 60
    minute = total % 60
    period = "AM"
    if hour >= 12:
        period = "PM"
        if hour > 12:
            hour = hour - 12
    return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{period}"

opt = Optimize()

# Decision variables: whether to meet each friend.
meetMary     = Bool("meetMary")
meetMargaret = Bool("meetMargaret")
meetSteven   = Bool("meetSteven")

# For Mary, her meeting time is fixed: available from 4:45PM to 6:15PM.
# In minutes after 9:00AM: start = 465, end = 555.
mary_start = 465
mary_end   = 555
mary_duration = 90  # fixed

# For Margaret, meeting start is a variable if the meeting is taken.
# Her available window is from 4:00PM to 8:45PM -> [420, 705] with duration 105 minutes.
m_start = Int("m_start")
m_duration = 105
# If meeting Margaret is chosen, m_start must be between 420 and 600 (so that end m_start+105 <= 705).
opt.add(If(meetMargaret, And(m_start >= 420, m_start <= 600), True))

# For Steven, meeting start is a variable.
# His window is from 7:00PM to 8:15PM -> [600, 675] with duration 45 minutes.
s_start = Int("s_start")
s_duration = 45
# s_start must be between 600 and 630 (since s_start+45 <=675) when chosen.
opt.add(If(meetSteven, And(s_start >= 600, s_start <= 630), True))

# Now add ordering/travel constraints.
# Our locations:
# Mary meeting is at Embarcadero.
# Margaret meeting is at North Beach.
# Steven meeting is at Alamo Square.
# Travel times from the table:
# From Mission District (starting point) to:
#   Embarcadero: 19 minutes, North Beach: 17 minutes, Alamo Square: 11 minutes.
# Between meetings:
#   Embarcadero->North Beach: 5 minutes
#   Embarcadero->Alamo Square: 19 minutes
#   North Beach->Alamo Square: 16 minutes
# (Other directions are defined but our schedule will follow the order imposed by time windows.)

# If Mary is chosen, we assume we plan to be at Embarcadero by her start time 465.
# This is achievable since 465 >= 19.
opt.add(If(meetMary, 465 >= 19, True))  # trivial

# Now, if both Mary and Margaret are met then Mary (at Embarcadero) must come before Margaret.
# So after Mary ends (555) plus travel time Embarcadero -> North Beach (5 minutes), we need:
opt.add(If(And(meetMary, meetMargaret), mary_end + 5 <= m_start, True))
# That is: 555+5 <= m_start, so m_start must be at least 560.

# If both Mary and Steven are met then Mary comes first.
# So from Embarcadero to Alamo Square travel is 19 minutes: 555 + 19 <= s_start.
opt.add(If(And(meetMary, meetSteven), mary_end + 19 <= s_start, True))
# (555+19 = 574; note s_start must be at least 600 anyway)

# If both Margaret and Steven are met then the only viable order is Margaret then Steven.
# From North Beach (Margaret) to Alamo Square (Steven) travel: m_start + 105 + 16 <= s_start.
opt.add(If(And(meetMargaret, meetSteven), m_start + m_duration + 16 <= s_start, True))

# For travel from the starting point (Mission District) to the first meeting,
# the constraints are automatically satisfied because the meeting windows start much later.
# (e.g. for Mary: 465 >= 19, for Margaret: 420 >= 17, for Steven: 600 >= 11)

# Now, note that if we try to take all three meetings, the constraints become unsatisfiable.
# (For instance, if meetMary, meetMargaret, and meetSteven are all True,
#  the constraints force: 555+5 <= m_start and m_start+105+16 <= s_start.
#  With the least possible m_start = 560, we get s_start >= 560+121 = 681, which contradicts s_start <=630.)
#
# Our objective is to maximize the number of meetings (friends met) and, secondarily, to maximize the total meeting time.
# (Mary: 90 min, Margaret: 105 min, Steven: 45 min)
objective = 1000*(If(meetMary,1,0) + If(meetMargaret,1,0) + If(meetSteven,1,0)) \
            + (90*If(meetMary,1,0) + 105*If(meetMargaret,1,0) + 45*If(meetSteven,1,0))
opt.maximize(objective)

# For Mary, we want to depart from Mission District at (mary_start - travel_M_to_E).

        # Travel from Embarcadero to Alamo Square takes 19 minutes.

 • The minimum meeting duration.
 • The “setup” or travel time needed to get from one location to the next (for example, going from Embarcadero to North Beach takes 5 minutes).
 • You start the day at Mission District at 9:00AM.

We introduce three decision “slots” (one per friend) together with Boolean variables (to decide whether or not to “schedule” a meeting with that friend) and start–time variables (in minutes after 9:00AM). For instance, if you choose to meet Mary then her meeting must occur during her availability. (Her availability and 90‐minute “minimum” forces her meeting to be exactly 4:45PM–6:15PM.) Similarly, Steven’s meeting (at Alamo Square) can only start between 7:00PM and 7:30PM (so that 45 minutes finish by 8:15PM) and Margaret’s meeting (at North Beach) must be scheduled sometime in her window (with at least 105 minutes duration, it is possible to start as late as 6:00PM). 

Because you cannot “be in two places at once,” if two meetings are chosen then their time intervals (plus added travel time from one location to the next) must not overlap. (For example, if you meet Mary at Embarcadero, then to later meet Steven at Alamo Square you must allow the travel time of 19 minutes from Embarcadero to Alamo Square – that forces Steven’s meeting to happen after Mary’s meeting.) 

Finally, our overall “goal” is to maximize the number of friends you meet (and if several schedules yield the same count you might also maximize the total meeting time). (It turns out that meeting all three friends is impossible because Mary’s fixed earlier meeting combined with the travel times forces the schedule to “choose” only two friends; among the possible pairs, the pair Mary plus Margaret gives you 90+105 = 195 minutes of friend–time, which is best.)

```python
from z3 import *

# Create an optimization object.
opt = Optimize()

# Decision booleans: whether to meet each friend.
meet_steven   = Bool('meet_steven')
meet_margaret = Bool('meet_margaret')
meet_mary     = Bool('meet_mary')

# Start time (in minutes after 9:00AM) for each meeting.
s_steven   = Int('s_steven')
s_margaret = Int('s_margaret')
s_mary     = Int('s_mary')

# Meeting durations (in minutes)
d_steven   = 45
d_margaret = 105
d_mary     = 90

# Available time windows (relative to 9:00AM):
# Steven: available from 7:00PM to 8:15PM, so start must be between 600 and 630 minutes.
opt.add(Implies(meet_steven, And(s_steven >= 600, s_steven <= 630)))
# Margaret: available from 4:00PM to 8:45PM, so start ∈ [420, 600] (since s_margaret + 105 <= 705).
opt.add(Implies(meet_margaret, And(s_margaret >= 420, s_margaret <= 600)))
# Mary: available from 4:45PM to 6:15PM; with a 90–minute meeting this forces s_mary = 465.
opt.add(Implies(meet_mary, s_mary == 465))

# Define travel times (in minutes) between locations.
# (The keys are (start_location, destination).)
travel = {
    ("Mission District", "Alamo Square"): 11,
    ("Mission District", "North Beach"): 17,
    ("Mission District", "Embarcadero"): 19,
    ("Alamo Square", "Mission District"): 10,
    ("Alamo Square", "North Beach"): 15,
    ("Alamo Square", "Embarcadero"): 17,
    ("North Beach", "Mission District"): 18,
    ("North Beach", "Alamo Square"): 16,
    ("North Beach", "Embarcadero"): 6,
    ("Embarcadero", "Mission District"): 20,
    ("Embarcadero", "Alamo Square"): 19,
    ("Embarcadero", "North Beach"): 5
}

# Define each meeting’s location.
loc_steven   = "Alamo Square"
loc_margaret = "North Beach"
loc_mary     = "Embarcadero"

# Add constraints ensuring that you can get from your start (Mission District) to the meeting.
opt.add(Implies(meet_steven, s_steven >= travel[("Mission District", loc_steven)]))
opt.add(Implies(meet_margaret, s_margaret >= travel[("Mission District", loc_margaret)]))
opt.add(Implies(meet_mary,     s_mary   >= travel[("Mission District", loc_mary)]))

# The ordering constraints: if you choose two meetings then one must finish (plus travel time) before the other starts.
# Note: Because Mary’s meeting has a fixed start (465) and duration (90), that fixes her interval.
#
# (1) For Steven and Mary: Only possible ordering is Mary then Steven.
#     Mary finishes at 465+90; plus travel from Embarcadero to Alamo Square takes 19 minutes.
opt.add(Implies(And(meet_steven, meet_mary),
                s_steven >= s_mary + d_mary + travel[("Embarcadero", "Alamo Square")]))
                
# (2) For Margaret and Mary: Only possible ordering is Mary then Margaret.
#     Mary finishes at 465+90; travel from Embarcadero to North Beach is 5 minutes.
opt.add(Implies(And(meet_margaret, meet_mary),
                s_margaret >= s_mary + d_mary + travel[("Embarcadero", "North Beach")]))
                
# (3) For Margaret and Steven (when Mary is not involved, this pair can be scheduled in one order only).
#     The only viable ordering is Margaret then Steven.
#     That is, Steven can only start after Margaret’s meeting ends plus travel time from North Beach to Alamo Square.
opt.add(Implies(And(meet_margaret, meet_steven),
                s_steven >= s_margaret + d_margaret + travel[("North Beach", "Alamo Square")]))

# Our objective is to maximize the number of friends met.
num_meetings = If(meet_steven, 1, 0) + If(meet_margaret, 1, 0) + If(meet_mary, 1, 0)
h1 = opt.maximize(num_meetings)
# As a tie-breaker, we maximize the total meeting time (in minutes).
total_meeting_time = d_steven*If(meet_steven, 1, 0) + d_margaret*If(meet_margaret, 1, 0) + d_mary*If(meet_mary, 1, 0)
h2 = opt.maximize(total_meeting_time)

# Find an optimal solution.
if opt.check() == sat:
    model = opt.model()
    # Build a schedule (a list of strings) based on the chosen meetings.
    schedule = []
    schedule.append("You start at Mission District at 9:00AM.")
    
    # Gather chosen meetings as tuples: (FriendName, meeting start, location, duration)
    chosen = []
    if model.evaluate(meet_mary):
        chosen.append(("Mary", model.evaluate(s_mary).as_long(), loc_mary, d_mary))
    if model.evaluate(meet_margaret):
        chosen.append(("Margaret", model.evaluate(s_margaret).as_long(), loc_margaret, d_margaret))
    if model.evaluate(meet_steven):
        chosen.append(("Steven", model.evaluate(s_steven).as_long(), loc_steven, d_steven))
    
    # Sort the meetings in order of their start times.
    chosen.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
    
    # A helper function to convert minutes after 9:00AM into a time string.
    def format_time(minutes):
        total_minutes = 9 * 60 + minutes  # since 9:00AM is our zero
        hour = total_minutes // 60
        minute = total_minutes % 60
        suffix = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
        # Convert to 12-hour format.
        if hour > 12:
            hour -= 12
        return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"
    
    # For the first meeting, add travel from Mission District.
    if chosen:
        first_friend = chosen[0]
        t_travel = travel[("Mission District", first_friend[2])]
        arrival = t_travel
        schedule.append(f"You travel to {first_friend[2]} in {t_travel} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival)}.")
        if arrival < first_friend[1]:
            schedule.append(f"You wait until {format_time(first_friend[1])}.")
        meeting_end = first_friend[1] + first_friend[3]
        schedule.append(f"You meet {first_friend[0]} for {first_friend[3]} minutes from {format_time(first_friend[1])} to {format_time(meeting_end)}.")
    
        # For subsequent meetings, add travel steps and meeting intervals.
        for i in range(1, len(chosen)):
            prev = chosen[i - 1]
            curr = chosen[i]
            t_travel = travel[(prev[2], curr[2])]
            arrival = (prev[1] + prev[3] + t_travel)
            schedule.append(f"You travel from {prev[2]} to {curr[2]} in {t_travel} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival)}.")
            if arrival < curr[1]:
                schedule.append(f"You wait until {format_time(curr[1])}.")
            meeting_end = curr[1] + curr[3]
            schedule.append(f"You meet {curr[0]} for {curr[3]} minutes from {format_time(curr[1])} to {format_time(meeting_end)}.")
    else:
        schedule.append("No meetings scheduled.")
    
    print(schedule)
else:
    print("No solution found")
```

```python
        hour = 12
    elif hour > 12:
        hour -= 12
    return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{ampm}"

B = Int('B')  # Start time for meeting Barbara in Sunset District

L_avail_end   = 17 * 60 + 15   # 5:15PM = 1035

# From Marina District to Pacific Heights:

# From Pacific Heights to Sunset District:

solver.add(L >= L_avail_start)  # Must wait until 9:30AM even if arriving at 9:10AM.
solver.add(L + meeting_duration <= L_avail_end)

solver.add(E >= arrival_pacific)
solver.add(E >= E_avail_start)
solver.add(E + meeting_duration <= E_avail_end)

# Constraints for meeting with Barbara:

solver.add(B >= arrival_sunset)
solver.add(B >= B_avail_start)
solver.add(B + meeting_duration <= B_avail_end)
```

The overall goal is to “optimize” the schedule – here we choose to minimize the finish time of the last meeting (Sarah) while satisfying all temporal, travel‐time, and meeting–duration constraints. 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have a number of “tasks” – meeting our four friends – each at a fixed location with its own available time window and a minimum meeting duration. In addition, there are travel times between locations. We start at Richmond District at 9:00AM (our time zero). For each friend we must “schedule” a meeting by choosing:

 • A meeting duration (which must be at least the required minimum).
 • A finish time (which is the sum of the start time and duration and must not be later than the friend’s available end time).

Travel between meetings is modeled by adding fixed travel‐time “lags” between the finish of one meeting and the arrival at the next location. For example, if we decide to visit Sandra at The Castro first, we set:
  arrival_at_Castro = departure_from_Richmond + 16.
Then we constrain the meeting start at The Castro to be at least the later of arrival_at_Castro and Sandra’s window start (12:30PM, or 210 minutes from 9:00AM). Similar constraints hold for the other meetings (Kenneth at Fisherman’s Wharf, Emily at Golden Gate Park, Sarah at Nob Hill), with the following travel times:
  Richmond → The Castro: 16 minutes
  The Castro → Fisherman’s Wharf: 24 minutes
  Fisherman’s Wharf → Golden Gate Park: 25 minutes
  Golden Gate Park → Nob Hill: 20 minutes

A natural “objective” is to choose the departure and meeting start times so that we finish the day as soon as possible (i.e. minimize the final finish time of Sarah’s meeting). Our decision variables then are times (in minutes from 9:00AM) for:
  – When we leave Richmond (thus “waiting” in Richmond if we depart later than 9:00AM)
  – The meeting start times and durations for each friend.
We add constraints requiring that each meeting lie inside the friend’s available window and that the travel time between successive meeting locations is respected. In an optimal solution the solver “chooses” to set the meeting times exactly at the earliest allowed values so that waiting is minimized.

SOLUTION:
Our goal is to “meet as many friends as possible” by finding a day‐schedule that obeys all time–window and meeting–duration requirements while “paying” the travel time needed to get from one neighborhood to the next. This naturally can be modeled as a constraint satisfaction (and optimization) problem. In our formulation we have:

1. Decision variables for each friend:
 • When do you start meeting that friend (start_time) and finish (finish_time). We force the meeting to last at least the minimum required time. In our optimized solution we “minimize waiting time” so the solver will choose the meeting time to be as early as possible (and we can even force finish_time = start_time + required_duration).
 • An ordering variable (an integer in {1, 2, 3, 4}) that tells in which sequence you visit Mary (at Pacific Heights), Lisa (at Mission District), Betty (at Haight-Ashbury) and Charles (at Financial District). The order constraints guarantee that the meetings do not overlap and that if friend A comes immediately before friend B in the schedule then friend B’s meeting cannot start until after friend A finishes and after you travel from A’s location to B’s location.
 
2. Additional (global) constraints:
 • You start at Bayview at 9:00AM (540 minutes after midnight) so the very first meeting must be scheduled to begin only after you travel from Bayview to that friend’s location.
 • Each friend is only “available” inside his/her time window. For example, Mary is available from 10:00AM (600 minutes) to 7:00PM (1140 minutes), so the meeting with Mary must be scheduled in that window.
 • When you move from one friend to the next (i.e. from friend A to friend B that are consecutive in the schedule), the start time for meeting B must be at least the finish time for meeting A plus the travel time (given in the problem) between A’s neighborhood and B’s neighborhood.
 
3. Optimization objective:
 • Since waiting (time arriving early to a location before the scheduled meeting) is “waste”, we add an objective to minimize the sum of “waiting times” – that is, the gap after arriving (using the appropriate travel time) and before the scheduled start of a meeting.
 
In our Z3 implementation we set up integer variables for each friend’s meeting start time, finish time (which we “pin” to start_time + minimum duration) and order (an integer 1–4, with all four orders required to be different). Then we add constraints for:
 – the available time windows,
 – the “travel–based” ordering constraints between consecutive meetings, and
 – the initial travel from Bayview.
An Optimize() object minimizes the total “waiting time.” In a possible optimal solution the solver finds, for instance, the following schedule (one among several possible):

 • Depart Bayview at 9:00AM, travel (in 19 minutes) to Haight-Ashbury and arrive 9:19AM. (Betty is available – her window is 7:15AM to 5:15PM – and you meet her for 90 minutes from 9:19AM to 10:49AM.)
 • Next, travel from Haight-Ashbury to Pacific Heights (12 minutes) so that you can meet Mary (available 10:00AM–7:00PM) for at least 45 minutes.
 • Then travel from Pacific Heights (13 minutes) to Financial District to meet Charles (available 11:15AM–3:00PM) for 120 minutes.
 • Finally, travel to Mission District (17 minutes) where Lisa is available only from 8:30PM until 10:00PM; you wait (if needed) and meet her for 75 minutes.
 
The complete Python script below uses the Z3 solver to define these variables, add the constraints and “minimize” waiting time. (The printed output is a list of sentences that describe the travel and meeting events.)
