from z3 import *

def solve_schedule():
    # --- Data definitions ---
    # Define the friends, their locations, availability windows (in minutes after midnight),
    # and required meeting durations.
    friends = ["Mary", "Lisa", "Betty", "Charles"]
    locations = {
        "Mary": "Pacific Heights",
        "Lisa": "Mission District",
        "Betty": "Haight-Ashbury",
        "Charles": "Financial District"
    }
    # Availability windows:
    avail_start = {
        "Mary": 600,      # 10:00AM
        "Lisa": 1230,     # 8:30PM
        "Betty": 435,     # 7:15AM
        "Charles": 675    # 11:15AM
    }
    avail_end = {
        "Mary": 1140,     # 7:00PM
        "Lisa": 1320,     # 10:00PM
        "Betty": 1035,    # 5:15PM
        "Charles": 900    # 3:00PM
    }
    meeting_min = {
        "Mary": 45,
        "Lisa": 75,
        "Betty": 90,
        "Charles": 120
    }
    
    # Travel times (in minutes) between locations.
    # We assume these are directional so we list them as provided:
    travel = {}
    travel[("Bayview", "Pacific Heights")] = 23
    travel[("Bayview", "Mission District")] = 13
    travel[("Bayview", "Haight-Ashbury")] = 19
    travel[("Bayview", "Financial District")] = 19
    travel[("Pacific Heights", "Bayview")] = 22
    travel[("Pacific Heights", "Mission District")] = 15
    travel[("Pacific Heights", "Haight-Ashbury")] = 11
    travel[("Pacific Heights", "Financial District")] = 13
    travel[("Mission District", "Bayview")] = 15
    travel[("Mission District", "Pacific Heights")] = 16
    travel[("Mission District", "Haight-Ashbury")] = 12
    travel[("Mission District", "Financial District")] = 17
    travel[("Haight-Ashbury", "Bayview")] = 18
    travel[("Haight-Ashbury", "Pacific Heights")] = 12
    travel[("Haight-Ashbury", "Mission District")] = 11
    travel[("Haight-Ashbury", "Financial District")] = 21
    travel[("Financial District", "Bayview")] = 19
    travel[("Financial District", "Pacific Heights")] = 13
    travel[("Financial District", "Mission District")] = 17
    travel[("Financial District", "Haight-Ashbury")] = 19

    initial_loc = "Bayview"
    initial_time = 540  # 9:00AM in minutes
    
    # --- Set up Z3 optimization problem ---
    opt = Optimize()

    # For each friend, create integer variables:
    #   start_times: when the meeting with friend begins (in minutes)
    #   finish_times: when the meeting ends (we will set finish = start + minimum duration)
    #   order: an integer (1..4) representing the order in which the friend is visited.
    start_times = {f: Int(f + "_start") for f in friends}
    finish_times = {f: Int(f + "_finish") for f in friends}
    order = {f: Int(f + "_order") for f in friends}
    
    # Meeting time constraints:
    for f in friends:
        # The meeting cannot start before the friend’s available time.
        opt.add(start_times[f] >= avail_start[f])
        # Meeting must finish by the available end.
        opt.add(finish_times[f] <= avail_end[f])
        # Meeting duration must be at least as long as required.
        opt.add(finish_times[f] - start_times[f] >= meeting_min[f])
        # For an optimal schedule, we set the meeting to last exactly the minimum time.
        opt.add(finish_times[f] == start_times[f] + meeting_min[f])
    
    # Order variables must take a value 1,2,3,4.
    for f in friends:
        opt.add(order[f] >= 1, order[f] <= len(friends))
    
    # All order values must be distinct.
    for i in range(len(friends)):
        for j in range(i+1, len(friends)):
            f1 = friends[i]
            f2 = friends[j]
            opt.add(order[f1] != order[f2])
    
    # Add travel-time constraints for consecutive meetings.
    # If friend f is immediately before friend g (i.e. order[f] + 1 == order[g]),
    # then the meeting with g cannot start until after f finishes plus the travel time from f to g.
    for f in friends:
        for g in friends:
            if f != g:
                opt.add(Implies(order[f] + 1 == order[g],
                                start_times[g] >= finish_times[f] + travel[(locations[f], locations[g])]))
    
    # For the very first meeting (order == 1), you must travel from Bayview.
    for f in friends:
        opt.add(Implies(order[f] == 1,
                        start_times[f] >= initial_time + travel[(initial_loc, locations[f])]))
    
    # Additionally, if a friend f is scheduled before friend g in the day, enforce that f’s finish time is before g’s start.
    for f in friends:
        for g in friends:
            if f != g:
                opt.add(Implies(order[f] < order[g], finish_times[f] <= start_times[g]))
    
    # Define “waiting time” to capture time spent waiting after arrival, before a meeting starts.
    wait_times = []
    # For the first meeting, waiting = start_time - (initial_time + travel_time from Bayview)
    for f in friends:
        wait_times.append(If(order[f] == 1,
                             start_times[f] - (initial_time + travel[(initial_loc, locations[f])]),
                             0))
    # For every consecutive pair, waiting = start_time(next) - (finish_time(prev) + travel_time)
    for f in friends:
        for g in friends:
            if f != g:
                wait_times.append(If(order[f] + 1 == order[g],
                                     start_times[g] - (finish_times[f] + travel[(locations[f], locations[g])]),
                                     0))
    
    total_wait = Sum(wait_times)
    opt.minimize(total_wait)

    # --- Solve and print the schedule ---
    if opt.check() == sat:
        model = opt.model()
        # Sort friends in order of their scheduled visit (order value 1 ... 4).
        ordered_friends = sorted(friends, key=lambda f: model[order[f]].as_long())
        schedule_msgs = []
        schedule_msgs.append("You arrive at Bayview at 9:00AM.")
        current_time = initial_time
        current_loc = initial_loc
        for f in ordered_friends:
            # Compute travel details:
            t_travel = travel[(current_loc, locations[f])]
            depart_time = current_time
            arrival_time = depart_time + t_travel
            # Fetch scheduled meeting times from the model.
            meeting_start = model[start_times[f]].as_long()
            meeting_finish = model[finish_times[f]].as_long()
            schedule_msgs.append("You travel to " + locations[f] + " in " +
                                 str(t_travel) + " minutes and arrive at " +
                                 convert_time(arrival_time) + ".")
            if arrival_time < meeting_start:
                schedule_msgs.append("You wait until " + convert_time(meeting_start) + ".")
            duration = meeting_finish - meeting_start
            schedule_msgs.append("You meet " + f + " for " + str(duration) +
                                 " minutes from " + convert_time(meeting_start) +
                                 " to " + convert_time(meeting_finish) + ".")
            # Update current position and time.
            current_time = meeting_finish
            current_loc = locations[f]
        print(schedule_msgs)
    else:
        print("No solution found")

def convert_time(total_minutes):
    # Converts minutes after midnight into a formatted time string HH:MMAM/PM.
    hours = total_minutes // 60
    mins = total_minutes % 60
    period = "AM"
    if hours >= 12:
        period = "PM"
        if hours > 12:
            hours -= 12
    if hours == 0:
        hours = 12
    return f"{hours}:{mins:02d}{period}"

if __name__ == '__main__':
    solve_schedule()

SOLUTION:
Below is one way to “think‐through” the problem as a constraint satisfaction problem. In our formulation we have a set of “meeting” tasks (one for each friend at a specific location with a fixed availability window and a minimum duration requirement). The decision variables include a Boolean “attend” flag for each friend (for example, x_lisa, x_deborah, x_joseph, and x_jeffrey) and a meeting‐start time (s_i) when you meet friend i. (In our case the Jeffrey meeting turns out to be “infeasible” because his available window [7:00–7:45AM] lies before your fixed start at 9:00AM.) 

For each friend i the constraints enforce that if you “choose” to meet friend i then:
 • the meeting start time s_i must lie in the friend’s available window (after adjusting for the minimum meeting duration) 
 • the meeting lasts at least the required number of minutes 
 • if i is not chosen, its meeting time can be set to 0. 

In addition we have “travel/time‐ordering” constraints. For any two friends i and j that are scheduled (that is, if both x_i and x_j are true) the model must decide which meeting comes first. For example, if you decide to visit Lisa (at The Castro) and Deborah (at Union Square) then one natural ordering is that you meet Lisa first and, after finishing her “slot,” you travel (in 19 minutes from The Castro to Union Square) and start meeting Deborah. (A similar constraint is added for Lisa–Joseph; meanwhile, when it comes to Deborah and Joseph the constraints simply force you not to choose both visits since their windows and travel times make it impossible to get a 90‐minute Deborah meeting and a 120‐minute Joseph meeting in separate blocks.) 

We then add an objective: “meet as many friends as possible” – that is, maximize the sum of the Boolean choices – and a secondary objective to maximize the total meeting time (which will favor, for instance, meeting Joseph’s 120‐minute window over Deborah’s 90‐minute one when coupled with Lisa’s 30‐minute meeting).

The python script below uses z3’s Optimize object to set up and solve the problem. One expected “optimal” schedule is to skip Jeffrey (and, because Deborah and Joseph cannot both be met under the constraints, choose the pair that gives the greatest total meeting time) – namely, meet Lisa at The Castro (available 1:45PM–4:00PM, minimum 30 minutes) and then meet Joseph at Golden Gate Park (available 5:30PM–9:15PM, minimum 120 minutes). The resulting schedule (after accounting for the travel times from your starting location Embarcadero at 9:00AM and between locations) is rendered as a list of messages.

    if hour > 12:
        h_display = hour - 12
    else:
        h_display = hour
    return f"{h_display}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"

# Information for each meeting friend.
# avail_start and avail_end given in minutes from 9:00AM:
#   (e.g., 1:45PM = 285 minutes, 4:00PM = 420)
meeting_info = {
    "Lisa": {
        "location": "The Castro",
        "avail_start": 285,   # 1:45PM
        "avail_end": 420,     # 4:00PM
        "duration": 30
    },

        "duration": 120
    },

        "location": "Chinatown",
        "avail_start": -120,  # 7:00AM (i.e. -120 min from 9:00AM)
        "avail_end": -75,     # 7:45AM
        "duration": 30
    }
}

# Travel times between locations (in minutes)
# Locations: Embarcadero, Union Square, Golden Gate Park, Chinatown, The Castro
travel_times = {
    ("Embarcadero", "Union Square"): 10,
    ("Embarcadero", "Golden Gate Park"): 25,

    ("The Castro", "Union Square"): 19,
    ("The Castro", "Golden Gate Park"): 11,
    ("The Castro", "Chinatown"): 20
}

# -----------------------
# Setting up the z3 optimization problem

opt = Optimize()

# Create Boolean decision variables for each meeting
x_lisa    = Bool("x_lisa")
x_deborah = Bool("x_deborah")
x_joseph  = Bool("x_joseph")
x_jeffrey = Bool("x_jeffrey")   # will not be scheduled due to time conflict

s_deborah = Int("s_deborah")

# (so that meeting start plus required duration does not exceed the end)
# If not scheduled, we force the start time to be 0.
def add_meeting_constraints(friend, x, s):

    d = info["duration"]
    avail_start = info["avail_start"]

add_meeting_constraints("Deborah", x_deborah, s_deborah)
add_meeting_constraints("Joseph",  x_joseph,  s_joseph)
add_meeting_constraints("Jeffrey", x_jeffrey, s_jeffrey)

# Also, from the start location (Embarcadero) the meeting must be reachable.
# (In our case each availability window starts much later than the minimal travel time so these constraints hold automatically.)
def add_from_start_constraint(friend, x, s):
    info = meeting_info[friend]
    loc = info["location"]
    travel = travel_times.get(("Embarcadero", loc), 0)
    opt.add(If(x, s >= travel, True))

add_from_start_constraint("Deborah", x_deborah, s_deborah)
add_from_start_constraint("Joseph",  x_joseph, s_joseph)
add_from_start_constraint("Jeffrey", x_jeffrey, s_jeffrey)

# Ordering (if both meetings are scheduled, then the travel time between locations must be taken into account)
# For Lisa and Deborah: Likely (and only) order is Lisa then Deborah.
opt.add(Implies(And(x_lisa, x_deborah), 
                s_lisa + meeting_info["Lisa"]["duration"] + travel_times[("The Castro", "Union Square")] <= s_deborah))
# For Lisa and Joseph: order is Lisa then Joseph.
opt.add(Implies(And(x_lisa, x_joseph), 
                s_lisa + meeting_info["Lisa"]["duration"] + travel_times[("The Castro", "Golden Gate Park")] <= s_joseph))
# For Deborah and Joseph: they cannot both be scheduled due to time/travel conflicts.
opt.add(Not(And(x_deborah, x_joseph)))
# (No ordering constraints needed for Jeffrey because his times are before 9:00AM.)
opt.add(Not(x_jeffrey))  # Jeffrey cannot be met

# -----------------------
# Objectives
# Primary objective: maximize the number of meetings (friends met).
num_meetings = If(x_lisa, 1, 0) + If(x_deborah, 1, 0) + If(x_joseph, 1, 0) + If(x_jeffrey, 1, 0)
opt.maximize(num_meetings)

# Secondary objective: maximize total meeting time
total_meeting_time = (meeting_info["Lisa"]["duration"]    * If(x_lisa, 1, 0) +
                      meeting_info["Deborah"]["duration"] * If(x_deborah, 1, 0) +
                      meeting_info["Joseph"]["duration"]  * If(x_joseph, 1, 0) +
                      meeting_info["Jeffrey"]["duration"] * If(x_jeffrey, 1, 0))
opt.maximize(total_meeting_time)

# -----------------------
# Solve the constraints and extract the model
if opt.check() == sat:
    model = opt.model()
    
    # Create a list of scheduled meetings with (friend, start_time, end_time, location, duration)
    scheduled = []
    for friend, x, s in [("Lisa",    x_lisa,    s_lisa),
                         ("Deborah", x_deborah, s_deborah),
                         ("Joseph",  x_joseph,  s_joseph),
                         ("Jeffrey", x_jeffrey, s_jeffrey)]:
        if is_true(model.evaluate(x)):
            start_val = model.evaluate(s).as_long()
            d = meeting_info[friend]["duration"]
            scheduled.append((friend, start_val, start_val + d, meeting_info[friend]["location"], d))
    
    # Sort scheduled meetings by their start time.
    scheduled.sort(key=lambda tup: tup[1])
    
    # Construct a schedule script.
    steps = []
    # Start at Embarcadero at 9:00AM.
    steps.append("You start at Embarcadero at 9:00AM.")
    
    current_location = "Embarcadero"
    current_time = 0  # in minutes from 9:00AM
    
    for friend, start_time, end_time, location, dur in scheduled:
        # Travel from current_location to the meeting location.
        travel = travel_times.get((current_location, location), 0)
        arrival = current_time + travel
        steps.append(f"You travel from {current_location} to {location} in {travel} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time_str(arrival)}.")
        # If you arrive before the meeting start time, you wait.
        if arrival < start_time:
            steps.append(f"You wait until {minutes_to_time_str(start_time)}.")
        # Meeting step.
        steps.append(f"You meet {friend} for {dur} minutes from {minutes_to_time_str(start_time)} to {minutes_to_time_str(end_time)}.")
        # Update current location and time.
        current_location = location
        current_time = end_time

    # Print the resulting schedule.
    print(steps)
else:
    print("No solution found.")

SOLUTION:
Below is one way to “reason‐through” the problem and then solve it with z3. One may view the task as a constraint satisfaction/scheduling problem. In our formulation we decide for each friend (Ashley, Jessica, Joseph and Stephanie) whether to “visit” that friend – and if so, we must choose a start‐time (in minutes after 9:00AM) for the meeting and an “order” (position in the schedule). The following constraints must be met:

1. Each friend is available only over a given time window. For example, Ashley is available from 10:00AM (= 60 minutes after 9:00AM) until 2:30PM (= 330 minutes after 9:00AM) and you must “meet” her for at least 120 minutes within that window (so the meeting must start no later than 330–120 = 210). Similarly the other friends have their own “start–finish” limits.
2. Travel times are given between all locations (including starting at Richmond District at 9:00AM). If friend F is scheduled before friend G then the meeting with F (which lasts its minimum duration) and the travel time (from F’s location to G’s location) must “fit” into the schedule so that you get to G’s meeting on time (i.e. before or at the start time that you choose for G’s meeting).
3. An ordering (ranking) variable is assigned to each meeting. If a friend is “visited,” its order is between 1 and 4 (and all such orders are distinct). If a friend is skipped then we set the order to 0 and ignore that friend.
4. Finally, the goal is to “meet as many friends as possible”. In our optimization we maximize the number of friends scheduled.

When you write the full set of constraints – availability (start ≥ friend’s available‐time and meeting finishing before the friend’s end time), travel‐time between consecutive meetings, and the ordering conditions – you soon discover that because of the very tight time windows (notably Jessica’s 11:00–12:30 slot and the long meeting required with Ashley) it is impossible to schedule all four meetings. In fact, one must “drop” one friend. (For instance, one valid optimal solution meets three friends – say, Ashley, Joseph and Stephanie. One good schedule in that case is to start by going directly to Embarcadero to meet Ashley right when she becomes available at 10:00AM, then later travel a short distance to North Beach to meet Joseph and finally finish at Nob Hill to meet Stephanie.) 

The python script below uses the z3 Optimize module. It declares for each friend a Boolean decision variable (visit or not), an integer “start time” variable T (minutes after 9:00AM) and an integer “order” variable. It then adds the constraints described above – including the travel–time constraints (if friend f is before friend g then T_f + (meeting duration of f) + (travel time from f’s location to g’s location) ≤ T_g). Finally it tells z3 to maximize the number of friends visited and, if a feasible optimum is found, prints a schedule in a list-of-strings format. (See the “Example output format” in the problem statement.)

Below is the complete code.

```python
from z3 import *

# ---------------------
# Data definitions
# ---------------------
# Locations:
#   Richmond District (starting point)
#   Embarcadero, Presidio, North Beach, Nob Hill are friend locations.
# Travel times in minutes – note they are not symmetric.
travel = {
    "Richmond District": {"Embarcadero": 19, "Presidio": 7, "North Beach": 17, "Nob Hill": 17},
    "Embarcadero": {"Richmond District": 21, "Presidio": 20, "North Beach": 5, "Nob Hill": 10},
    "Presidio": {"Richmond District": 7, "Embarcadero": 20, "North Beach": 18, "Nob Hill": 18},
    "North Beach": {"Richmond District": 18, "Embarcadero": 6, "Presidio": 17, "Nob Hill": 7},
    "Nob Hill": {"Richmond District": 14, "Embarcadero": 9, "Presidio": 17, "North Beach": 8},
}

# Friend info in minutes after 9:00AM.
# (E.g., 10:00AM is 60 minutes after 9:00AM)
friend_info = {
    "Ashley":   {"location": "Embarcadero", "avail_start": 60,  "avail_end": 330, "duration": 120},
    "Jessica":  {"location": "Presidio",    "avail_start": 120, "avail_end": 150, "duration": 30},
    "Joseph":   {"location": "North Beach", "avail_start": 135, "avail_end": 285, "duration": 45},
    "Stephanie":{"location": "Nob Hill",    "avail_start": 180, "avail_end": 720, "duration": 75}
}

friends = list(friend_info.keys())
N = len(friends)

# ---------------------
# Z3 Variables
# ---------------------
opt = Optimize()

# For each friend f, we create:
#   b[f]   : Bool, True if we decide to meet with f.
#   T[f]   : Int, meeting start time (minutes after 9:00AM)
#   pos[f] : Int, ordering (if visited, pos in {1,..,N}, otherwise 0)
b = {}
T = {}
pos = {}
for f in friends:
    b[f] = Bool(f+"_visit")
    T[f] = Int(f+"_start")
    pos[f] = Int(f+"_order")
    # Bound the start time from 0 to, say, 10000 (a safe upper bound).
    opt.add(T[f] >= 0, T[f] < 10000)
    # If not visited, set T to 0 and pos to 0.
    # If visited then order must be between 1 and N.
    opt.add( If(b[f], And(pos[f] >= 1, pos[f] <= N), pos[f] == 0) )
    
    # If visited: meeting must lie in friend’s available window.
    info = friend_info[f]
    opt.add(If(b[f],
               And(T[f] >= info["avail_start"],
                   T[f] + info["duration"] <= info["avail_end"]),
               T[f] == 0))
    
    # Also, if friend is visited and is the first meeting (order==1),
    # then you must have enough time from the starting point in Richmond District.
    opt.add(If(And(b[f], pos[f] == 1),
               T[f] >= travel["Richmond District"][ info["location"] ],
               True))

# For every pair of distinct friends, if both are scheduled then their order must be different.
for i in range(N):
    for j in range(i+1, N):
        fi = friends[i]
        fj = friends[j]
        opt.add(If(And(b[fi], b[fj]),
                   pos[fi] != pos[fj],
                   True))
        # Now add travel/time-between-meetings constraints.
        # If fi is scheduled before fj then meeting fi must finish
        # and you must allow travel from fi's location to fj's.
        info_i = friend_info[fi]
        info_j = friend_info[fj]
        # Two possible orders: either fi comes before fj or vice‐versa.
        opt.add(If(And(b[fi], b[fj], pos[fi] < pos[fj]),
                   T[fi] + info_i["duration"] + travel[ info_i["location"] ][ info_j["location"] ] <= T[fj],
                   True))
        opt.add(If(And(b[fi], b[fj], pos[fj] < pos[fi]),
                   T[fj] + info_j["duration"] + travel[ info_j["location"] ][ info_i["location"] ] <= T[fi],
                   True))

# ---------------------
# Objective: maximize the number of friends visited.
total_visits = Sum([If(b[f], 1, 0) for f in friends])
opt.maximize(total_visits)

# ---------------------
# Solve and extract solution
# ---------------------
if opt.check() == sat:
    model = opt.model()
    
    # Get a list of scheduled friends with their order.
    scheduled = []
    for f in friends:
        if is_true(model[b[f]]):
            scheduled.append((model.evaluate(pos[f]).as_long(), f))
    scheduled.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    
    # Helper: convert minutes (after 9:00) to time string.
    def format_time(m):
        total = 9*60 + m  # total minutes after midnight
        hour = total // 60
        minute = total % 60
        suffix = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
        # convert to 12-hour format:
        if hour == 0:
            hour = 12
        elif hour > 12:
            hour = hour - 12
        return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"
    
    # Build the schedule messages.
    schedule_msgs = []
    schedule_msgs.append("You start at Richmond District at 9:00AM.")
    
    current_location = "Richmond District"
    current_time = 0  # 9:00AM
    for order_val, f in scheduled:
        info = friend_info[f]
        # Travel from current_location to friend f's location.
        travel_time = travel[current_location][ info["location"] ]
        arrival_time = current_time + travel_time
        msg = f"You travel from {current_location} to {info['location']} in {travel_time} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival_time)}."
        schedule_msgs.append(msg)
        # Wait, if arrival time is before meeting start.
        meeting_start = model[T[f]].as_long()
        if arrival_time < meeting_start:
            wait_msg = f"You wait until {format_time(meeting_start)}."
            schedule_msgs.append(wait_msg)
        # Meeting message.
        meeting_end = meeting_start + info["duration"]
        meet_msg = f"You meet {f} for {info['duration']} minutes from {format_time(meeting_start)} to {format_time(meeting_end)}."
        schedule_msgs.append(meet_msg)
        # Update current location and time: assume you depart right after the meeting.
        current_location = info["location"]
        current_time = meeting_end
        
    # Print the schedule (as a list, per the example format).
    print(schedule_msgs)
else:
    print("No solution found.")

In our formulation we decide for each friend (Ashley, Jessica, Joseph and Stephanie) whether to “visit” that friend – and if so, we must choose a start‐time (in minutes after 9:00AM) for the meeting and an “order” (position in the schedule). The following constraints must be met:

For example, Ashley is available from 10:00AM (= 60 minutes after 9:00AM) until 2:30PM (= 330 minutes after 9:00AM) and you must “meet” her for at least 120 minutes within that window (so the meeting must start no later than 330–120 = 210). Similarly the other friends have their own “start–finish” limits.
2. Travel times are given between all locations (including starting at Richmond District at 9:00AM). If friend F is scheduled before friend G then the meeting with F (which lasts its minimum duration) and the travel time (from F’s location to G’s location) must “fit” into the schedule so that you get to G’s meeting on time (i.e. before or at the start time that you choose for G’s meeting).
3. An ordering (ranking) variable is assigned to each meeting. If a friend is “visited,” its order is between 1 and 4 (and all such orders are distinct). If a friend is skipped then we set the order to 0 and ignore that friend.
4. Finally, the goal is to “meet as many friends as possible”. In our optimization we maximize the number of friends scheduled.

We have a set of “friend‐meeting” events – one for each friend (Timothy, Linda, Joseph, Barbara, Emily). For each event we must decide a meeting start time (and hence an end time given the minimum required duration) so that:

Step 1. Constraint Satisfaction Reasoning

SOLUTION:
Below is our approach. We first “model” the problem as a constraint–satisfaction (and scheduling) problem. In our view the following items must be decided for each friend meeting:

1. A meeting start time (s[i]) – an integer representing the number of minutes past 9:00AM when you begin the meeting. (Because you “arrive” at Nob Hill at 9:00AM, we use that as our zero‐time reference.)
2. The order in which you visit the friends. We introduce an order variable for each friend (order[i] taking a value from 1 to 5); the friend with order value 1 is visited first and so on.

For each meeting we must enforce:
 • The meeting occurs during the friend’s available window. (For example, Jeffrey is available from 3:00PM to 4:00PM – which, measured as minutes from 9:00AM, is [360,420].)
 • The meeting lasts at least its minimum required duration.
 • If a friend is not the first appointment, then the travel time from the previous friend’s location to this friend’s location must be taken into account. (For instance, if you meet Timothy at Embarcadero and then next go to Nancy at Union Square, you must allow at least 10 extra minutes to travel from Embarcadero to Union Square.)
 • For the very first meeting you start at Nob Hill at 9:00AM so the travel time from Nob Hill to that friend’s location must be included.

Thus, for two friends i and j, whenever friend i is scheduled immediately before friend j (i.e. order[j] equals order[i]+1) we impose the constraint

   s[i] + (meeting duration for friend i) + (travel time from i to j) ≤ s[j].

We also require that the ordering variables be distinct. (The “permutation” of friends then defines the complete route.) An extra (optional) goal is to “optimize” the overall finish time so that waiting/travel time is minimized – in our model we introduce a variable for the final finishing time and minimize it.

Below is the complete Python script that uses z3 to set up these constraints and then extract a “day‐plan” in a sequence of human–readable messages. (Notice that the printed schedule is in an example format similar to:
 ["You start at Nob Hill at 9:00AM.", "You travel to Embarcadero in 9 minutes and arrive at 9:09AM.", … ]
)

from z3 import *

# FRIEND INFORMATION (times in minutes relative to 9:00AM):
# We use 9:00AM as time 0.
# For friends with a start time earlier than 9:00AM (like Timothy, available from 7:15AM),
# we use the effective start time of 0.
friends = {
    0: {"name": "Timothy", "location": "Embarcadero",     "duration": 45,  "window_start": 0,    "window_end": 690},  # 8:30PM => 690 minutes from 9:00
    1: {"name": "Jeffrey", "location": "Financial District", "duration": 45,  "window_start": 360,  "window_end": 420},  # 3:00PM-4:00PM
    2: {"name": "Daniel",  "location": "Mission District",   "duration": 105, "window_start": 300,  "window_end": 600},  # 2:00PM-7:00PM
    3: {"name": "Nancy",   "location": "Union Square",       "duration": 60,  "window_start": 195,  "window_end": 465},  # 12:15PM-4:45PM
    4: {"name": "Patricia","location": "Russian Hill",       "duration": 15,  "window_start": 360,  "window_end": 510}   # 3:00PM-5:30PM
}

# TRAVEL TIMES (in minutes)
# Matrix for travel times between friends’ locations.
# The indices refer to the friend’s location:
# 0: Embarcadero, 1: Financial District, 2: Mission District, 
# 3: Union Square, 4: Russian Hill.
travel = [
    [0,  5, 20, 10, 8],   # from Embarcadero
    [4,  0, 17, 9,  10],  # from Financial District
    [19, 17, 0, 15, 15],  # from Mission District
    [11, 9, 14, 0, 13],   # from Union Square
    [8,  11, 16, 11, 0]   # from Russian Hill
]

# Travel times from the starting location Nob Hill to each friend location
# Nob Hill -> Embarcadero: 9, -> Financial District:9, -> Mission District:13, -> Union Square:7, -> Russian Hill:5.
travel_from_nobhill = [9, 9, 13, 7, 5]

# Create an optimizer to also minimize overall finishing time.
opt = Optimize()

# For each friend we create two decision variables:
# s[i]: the meeting start time (minutes after 9:00AM)
# order[i]: an integer in {1,...,5} that represents this friend’s position in the schedule.
s_vars = [Int('s_%d' % i) for i in range(5)]
order_vars = [Int('order_%d' % i) for i in range(5)]

# Add constraints related to each friend’s time window and ordering:
for i in range(5):
    friend = friends[i]
    # Meeting must start no earlier than the friend’s available start, and finish by window_end.
    opt.add(s_vars[i] >= friend["window_start"])
    opt.add(s_vars[i] + friend["duration"] <= friend["window_end"])
    # If friend i is the first meeting (order == 1), then the earliest you can start is after traveling from Nob Hill.
    opt.add(Implies(order_vars[i] == 1, s_vars[i] >= travel_from_nobhill[i]))
    # Order must be between 1 and 5.
    opt.add(order_vars[i] >= 1, order_vars[i] <= 5)

# Ensure the order numbers are all different.
opt.add(Distinct(order_vars))

# For any two different friends, if one is scheduled immediately before the other, include the travel time constraint.
for i in range(5):
    for j in range(5):
        if i != j:
            # If friend j immediately follows friend i, then finish meeting i plus travel time from friend i's location to j's must be no later than s[j].
            opt.add(Implies(order_vars[j] == order_vars[i] + 1,
                            s_vars[i] + friends[i]["duration"] + travel[i][j] <= s_vars[j]))

# (Optional) To ensure consistency, if friend i is scheduled before friend j then s[i] should be no later than s[j].
for i in range(5):
    for j in range(5):

Also, the very first appointment has the extra constraint that you start in the Presidio at 9:00AM (i.e. 540 minutes after midnight) and you must travel from Presidio to the first friend’s location.

Thus, the decision variables are:
 • an ordering: an array “order” of five integers (each from 0 to 4, all distinct) so that order[0] is the friend seen first, order[1] second, etc.
 • a start time s[i] (in minutes from midnight) for the meeting in schedule “slot” i.

Then, for each slot we add the following constraints:
 – If friend j is scheduled in slot i (i.e. order[i]==j) then the meeting must start no earlier than friend j’s available‐start time and must end (start + required duration) no later than friend j’s available‐end time.

   s[i] ≥ s[i–1] + (duration required for friend j) + (travel time from location of friend j to location of friend k).

One way to think about the problem is to view it as a constraint satisfaction (or scheduling) problem where the “tasks” are meeting our friends. For each friend we have:
 • A time window (availability) in which the meeting can occur.
 • A required duration that the meeting must last.
 • A fixed location.
We also have travel times between locations (including from our starting location, the Presidio). In our model we introduce two sets of decision variables:
 1. A permutation (ordering) variable called “route” that indicates in what order we meet the friends.
 2. For each friend we have a “start time” variable (measured in minutes after 9:00AM) that indicates when the meeting begins.
The constraints are then as follows:
 – For each friend, the start time must be no earlier than her avail_start and must finish (start + duration) no later than avail_end.
 – For the very first friend in the route, the meeting start must be no earlier than our travel time from Presidio.
 – For every consecutive pair of friends f then g in our route, we require that g’s meeting start is at least (f’s meeting start + f’s duration + travel time from f’s location to g’s location).
 – All friends appear exactly once in the route.
A solution (if one exists) assigns an ordering and appropriate meeting start times so that (even if we arrive early and must wait) each meeting occurs during the friend’s availability window and all inter–meeting travel durations are respected. (In our “best–case” schedule our goal is to meet all the friends.)

Below is one way to think about the problem and a complete Python script that uses the Z3 solver.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Explanation – Modeling as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have five friends, each “located” at a different San Francisco district. For each friend we know:
 • Their location (for example, Stephanie is at Pacific Heights).
 • Their availability window (for example, Stephanie is available from 7:15AM until 6:45PM).
 • A minimum meeting duration required.

We start our day at Golden Gate Park at 9:00AM. In addition, we have travel times (which are not necessarily symmetric) between every pair of locations (and from Golden Gate Park to each friend’s location).

Our decision variables are as follows:
1. For each friend we introduce a meeting “start time” variable (in minutes after midnight) and, by adding the fixed meeting duration, we know the meeting “end time.”
2. We also decide the order in which we visit the friends. We introduce an integer variable (order index) for each friend (for example, 0 means the first friend we visit, 1 the second, and so on). The order variables are required to be all different.
3. We add “ordering constraints”: If friend f is scheduled before friend g (i.e. order[f] < order[g]) then the meeting with g cannot begin until after f has finished AND after you’ve traveled from f’s location to g’s location.
4. For the very first friend (i.e. whose order equals 0) we require that the meeting start time is at least the start time (9:00AM, i.e. 540 minutes) plus the travel time from Golden Gate Park to that friend’s district.
5. For each friend we also require that the meeting start and end times lie within the friend’s availability window.
6. Finally an “objective” can be used to optimize the day by, for instance, minimizing the overall finishing time of the last meeting. (Since our goal is to “meet as many friends as possible,” we assume it is best if all meetings are scheduled as early as can be without “wasting” time.)

The travel/waiting times are “implicitly” modeled when we require that the meeting start time for friend g is at least
  (f meeting start + meeting duration of f + travel time from f’s location to g’s location)
if friend f comes before friend g. (If you arrive earlier than the friend’s available start time, you will “wait” until their window opens.)

This problem can be modeled as a constraint satisfaction (and optimization) problem. We have five “tasks” (meeting each friend) that must be scheduled during the day. For each friend we know:
• The fixed location (e.g. Financial District for Betty, North Beach for Steven, etc.)
• Their time‐availability window (for example, Betty is available from 8:00PM to 10:00PM)
• A minimum meeting duration (e.g. 90 minutes for Betty).

We start at a fixed location (“Richmond District”) at 9:00AM. In our model the “time” will be represented as the number of minutes from 9:00AM (so 9:00AM is time 0). In addition, travel times between districts are given (and note they are not necessarily symmetric).

The decision variables are:
1. For each friend, a meeting start time (in minutes after 9:00) that must lie in an interval defined by the friend’s availability (adjusted so that there is time to meet the minimum required duration).
2. For each friend, an “order” (an integer between 0 and 4) representing the sequence in which the meetings are visited. The order is a permutation of the five meetings.

The constraints are then:
• For each friend f:
 – meeting_start[f] ≥ friend_f_avail_start.
 – meeting_start[f] ≤ friend_f_avail_end – friend_f_min_duration.
• For the friend that is visited first (order = 0) the meeting cannot start until after you travel from Richmond District to that friend’s location.
• For any two different friends f and g, if friend f is visited before friend g (i.e. order[f] < order[g]) then the meeting with g must start only after f is finished and you have traveled from f’s location to g’s location. In other words,
  meeting_start[g] ≥ meeting_start[f] + (f’s min meeting duration) + (travel_time from f’s location to g’s location).
• The order variables are required to be distinct.

Optionally – and as used here – we also add an optimization objective: minimize the finishing time (the maximum over all meeting “end times”) so that we “pack” the day as efficiently as possible while still meeting everyone for at least their required duration.

The Python script below uses Z3 to solve this CSP. It then “simulates” the schedule by computing the arrival times (taking into account any waiting time due to early arrival or friend’s window) and prints a list of schedule steps (using a similar format as the provided example).

SOLUTION:
Below is one way to “think‐out” and solve the problem. In our formulation we have six potential “meet‐ings” (one per friend) – each friend i has a fixed location, an available time window and a minimum meeting duration. Also, travel times between locations (and from the starting point “The Castro”) must be honored. In our constraint–satisfaction formulation we introduce, for each friend i:

 • a Boolean decision variable B[i] that “chooses” whether to meet friend i or not,
 • an integer variable s[i] giving the (absolute) meeting start time (measured in minutes past 9:00AM). (For example, s₀ for Margaret is only “active” if we decide to meet her.)

Each friend i has a “time‐window” (its earliest possible start and a latest start so that meeting plus its minimum duration still falls within the friend’s availability). (For example, Margaret is available from 9:00AM to 7:00PM – that is 0 to 600 minutes after 9:00AM – and her meeting (75 minutes) forces s₀ to be between 20 (because you also must allow travel from “The Castro” to her North Beach location – 20 minutes) and 525 minutes.) 
Also, if two meetings i and j are both “activated” (B[i] and B[j] are true), then one must come before the other. We enforce this by “disjunctive” ordering constraints:
  Either meeting i is done (i’s start plus its duration plus the travel time from i’s location to j’s location) before j starts,
   or meeting j (plus duration and travel time from j to i) is finished before i begins.
This – along with the availabilities and the “from the Castro” constraints – ensures that any pair of scheduled visits have enough “gap” to allow travel and (if needed) waiting until the friend’s appointment begins.

Finally the optimizer is told to “maximize” the sum of the B[i] – that is, to choose a schedule (and order) that meets as many friends as possible.

The code below uses the z3 Optimize() module. (After solving the constraints the model “picks” values for the meeting start times; we then sort the scheduled meetings by s[i] so as to “simulate” the day: starting at The Castro at 9:00AM, we show travel, any waiting time, and then the meeting at the friend’s location.)

Below is the complete Python script.

# Friend indices and names:
#   0: Margaret at North Beach
#   1: Michelle at Golden Gate Park
#   2: George at Sunset District
#   3: Carol at Embarcadero
#   4: Melissa at Union Square
#   5: Joshua at Alamo Square

names = ["Margaret", "Michelle", "George", "Carol", "Melissa", "Joshua"]
# Each friend i has:
#   available window: [avail_start, avail_end] but note: meeting must finish by avail_end.
#   We work in “minutes after 9:00AM”. (9:00AM = 0.)
# Given availabilities (converted):
# Margaret: 9:00AM-7:00PM -> [0, 600] but meeting lasts 75 so latest start is 600 - 75 = 525.
# Michelle: 1:30PM-8:30PM -> 1:30PM is 270; 8:30PM is 690; latest start 690 - 15 = 675.
# George: 6:30PM-7:15PM -> 6:30PM is 570; 7:15PM is 615; latest start 615 - 15 = 600.
# Carol: 6:15PM-9:00PM -> 6:15PM is 555; 9:00PM is 720; latest start 720 - 75 = 645.
# Melissa: 8:00PM-9:00PM -> 8:00PM is 660; 9:00PM is 720; latest start 720 - 30 = 690.
# Joshua: 9:00PM-10:00PM -> 9:00PM is 720; 10:00PM is 780; latest start 780 - 60 = 720.
avail_lower = [0, 270, 570, 555, 660, 720]
max_start   = [525, 675, 600, 645, 690, 720]
durations   = [75, 15, 15, 75, 30, 60]

# In addition, you cannot arrive before leaving "The Castro".
# Travel times from The Castro (in minutes):
# North Beach:20, Golden Gate Park:11, Sunset District:17, Embarcadero:22, Union Square:19, Alamo Square:8.
travel_from_castro = [20, 11, 17, 22, 19, 8]

# To combine the friend availability with the travel condition you must be able to get there:
# So the effective lower bound L[i] is:
L = [ max(avail_lower[i], travel_from_castro[i]) for i in range(6) ]

# Travel times between friends.
# We use the provided directed minutes (from friend i's location to friend j's location),
# where friend indices correspond to:
# 0: North Beach
# 1: Golden Gate Park
# 2: Sunset District
# 3: Embarcadero
# 4: Union Square
# 5: Alamo Square
T = [[0,    22,   27,    6,    7,   16],    # from 0 (North Beach) 
     [24,    0,   10,   25,   22,   10],    # from 1 (Golden Gate Park)
     [29,   11,    0,   31,   30,   17],    # from 2 (Sunset District)
     [5,    25,   30,    0,   10,   19],    # from 3 (Embarcadero)
     [10,   22,   26,   11,    0,   15],    # from 4 (Union Square)
     [15,    9,   16,   17,   14,    0]]    # from 5 (Alamo Square)

# -------------------- Z3 Model --------------------
opt = Optimize()

# For each friend i, decide whether to meet them (B[i]) and, if so, at what start time s[i] (minutes from 9:00AM)
B = [Bool(f"B{i}") for i in range(6)]
s = [Int(f"s{i}") for i in range(6)]

# Add availability/travel-from-Castro constraints when meeting is chosen.
for i in range(6):
    # If the friend is met then s[i] is between L[i] and max_start[i]
    opt.add(Implies(B[i], s[i] >= L[i]))
    opt.add(Implies(B[i], s[i] <= max_start[i]))
    # (If not chosen, s[i] is “don’t care”)

# For every pair of friends i,j that are both scheduled, enforce that one meeting is finished 
# (including travel time between locations) before the other begins.
for i in range(6):
    for j in range(i+1, 6):
        # Only if both meetings occur do we have to order them.
        constraint = Implies(And(B[i], B[j]),
                             Or( s[i] + durations[i] + T[i][j] <= s[j],
                                 s[j] + durations[j] + T[j][i] <= s[i] ))
        opt.add(constraint)

# We want to maximize the total number of friends met:
total = sum([If(B[i], 1, 0) for i in range(6)])
opt.maximize(total)

# Solve!
if opt.check() == sat:
    m = opt.model()
    num_meetings = sum([1 for i in range(6) if m.evaluate(B[i])])
    # Retrieve scheduled meeting start times (only for those scheduled)
    schedule = []
    for i in range(6):
        if m.evaluate(B[i]):
            start_time = m.evaluate(s[i]).as_long()
            schedule.append( (start_time, i) )
    # Sort by meeting start time (the earlier meeting first)
    schedule.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    
    # ----------------- Helper function: convert minutes (offset from 9:00AM) to time string ------------------
    def minutes_to_time(min_offset):
        # Our reference: 9:00AM is 9*60 = 540 minutes after midnight.
        total = 540 + min_offset
        hour = total // 60
        minute = total % 60
        # Determine AM/PM format.
        suffix = "AM"
        if hour >= 12:
            suffix = "PM"
        display_hour = hour if hour <= 12 else hour - 12
        if display_hour == 0:
            display_hour = 12
        return f"{display_hour}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"
    
    # ----------------- Build the schedule of messages  ------------------
    output = []
    output.append("You start at The Castro at 9:00AM.")
    
    # We simulate traveling and meeting in order.
    current_time = 0    # 0 means 9:00AM (our time origin)
    current_location = "The Castro"
    # For our purposes, we also need to remember the “friend index” of the previous meeting (if any)
    prev_friend = None

    # For each meeting in the sorted schedule:
    for (mstart, friend) in schedule:
        # Determine travel time from previous location:
        if prev_friend is None:
            # travel from The Castro to friend's location:
            travel_time = travel_from_castro[friend]
        else:
            # travel from friend's location (prev_friend) to current friend:
            travel_time = T[prev_friend][friend]
        arrival = current_time + travel_time
        travel_msg = f"You travel to {names[friend]}'s location in {travel_time} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival)}."
        output.append(travel_msg)
        # If we arrive before the planned meeting start time, add a waiting message.
        if arrival < mstart:
            wait_msg = f"You wait until {minutes_to_time(mstart)}."
            output.append(wait_msg)
        meet_end = mstart + durations[friend]
        meet_msg = f"You meet {names[friend]} for {durations[friend]} minutes from {minutes_to_time(mstart)} to {minutes_to_time(meet_end)}."
        output.append(meet_msg)
        # Update current time (we finish the meeting at meet_end)
        current_time = meet_end
        # Update previous meeting location (use friend index as proxy)

    # Print the schedule messages as a list.
    print(output)
else:
    print("No solution found.")

1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We want to pick a subset of friends to meet (each with a “meeting‐decision” Boolean variable) and assign to each meeting a start time (s) and an end time (e) defined in minutes after 9:00AM. Each friend i has:

or
  s[j] + (duration[j]) + travel_time(j → i) ≤ s[i].

1. A set of friends (Mark, David, Michelle, Jeffrey, George, Kevin) with fixed locations. For each friend we know:
 – Their available time window (start and end times, expressed here in minutes after midnight—for example, 9:00AM is 540).
 – The minimum duration that you must “meet” them.

2. The “travel” part is modeled via a travel time matrix that gives the time needed to go from one location (Fisherman’s Wharf, North Beach, Richmond District, Bayview, Presidio, Financial District, Alamo Square) to another.

3. For each friend we introduce decision variables:
 • A Boolean variable (visited) that indicates whether you are going to meet that friend.
 • A meeting start time (S) variable. If you choose to meet a friend then S must be no earlier than:
  – The friend’s “available‐from” time,
  – The earliest possible “arrival” time coming directly from your starting point (Fisherman’s Wharf at 9:00AM) for a first meeting.
 • An “order” variable (an integer) that represents the relative order in which the meetings occur. In this way the “chain” of visits is built by requiring that the first friend (order = 1) is reached “from” Fisherman’s Wharf, and any meeting with order >1 must start not before the previous friend’s meeting finish time (which is its meeting start S plus its required duration) plus the travel time from that previous friend’s location.

4. In addition we enforce:

1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We want to pick a subset of friends to meet (each with a “meeting‐decision” Boolean variable) and assign to each meeting a start time (s) and an end time (e) defined in minutes after 9:00AM. Each friend i has:
 • An availability window [avail_start, avail_end] (already given in minutes from 9:00AM).
 • A required minimum meeting duration.
 • A fixed location.
 
For a meeting with friend i to occur, we require:
 – The meeting to start no earlier than avail_start and finish no later than avail_end.
 – The meeting duration to be at least the required minimum. In order to “use time efficiently” (so that later meetings can also be fit in) we will force the meeting duration to be exactly the minimum.
 – If friend i is to be met then the meeting’s scheduled start must also be at least as late as the travel time from our starting point (Fisherman’s Wharf) to friend i’s location.
 
Moreover, if two meetings are both scheduled then the travel time between the two locations must be “inserted” between the meetings. That is, for any two friends i and j that you meet, either
  s[i] + (duration[i]) + travel_time(i → j) ≤ s[j]
or
  s[j] + (duration[j]) + travel_time(j → i) ≤ s[i].
This “disjunctive” constraint makes sure the appointments do not overlap (even when travel time is needed).
 
Finally, the objective is to maximize the total number of friends met.
We then encode all these rules using Z3’s Optimize solver.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have a set of “meetings” with friends at different locations. For each meeting we know:
 • The friend’s location and available time window (for example, Sandra is at Richmond District from 9:45AM to 11:45AM).
 • A minimum meeting duration (e.g. 90 minutes for Sandra).
 • Also, travel times are given between landmarks, and our day begins at a fixed starting place (Alamo Square at 9:00AM).

Our decision variables include the meeting start‐times (expressed in minutes from 9:00AM) for each friend. (We choose to “use” the minimum meeting duration for each friend so that if the meeting starts as early as possible the subsequent travel and meeting windows can be feasibly aligned.) In addition, the “route” (or order) is decided by our planning; here we assume a fixed candidate order that turns out to be optimal for meeting as many friends as possible:
  • Morning: Go from Alamo Square to Richmond District to meet Sandra.
  • Mid–day: Travel next to Haight-Ashbury to meet Ashley.
  • Evening: Then visit Embarcadero (to meet Emily), then Union Square (to meet Joseph) and finally Golden Gate Park (to meet Ronald).

For each meeting “i” we impose the following constraints:
 1. The meeting must occur entirely within the friend’s available window. For example, if s_Sandra is the start time for Sandra’s meeting (in minutes after 9:00AM), we add:
       s_Sandra ≥ (start of Sandra’s availability)

       s_Sandra + 90 + 10 ≤ s_Ashley

Below is our reasoning and a complete Python script that uses Z3 to “choose” an ordering and appointment‐times that satisfy all the travel and meeting‐window constraints.

Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We model the day as a sequence of six meetings – one for each friend – with the following ingredients:
• Variables for each friend “F”:
  – s_F: the start time (in minutes after 9:00AM) at which you begin the meeting.
  – order_F: an integer (0–5) representing F’s position in your schedule.
• Fixed “meeting‐length” constants (the minimum required meeting time), plus each friend’s availability window (translated into minutes from 9:00AM). (For instance, Robert is available from 10:45AM (105 minutes) to 12:30PM (210 minutes) and his required meeting duration is 75 minutes.)
• Travel times are given both from your starting spot (Bayview) to each friend’s location and between friends’ locations. For any two friends “F” and “G”, if F immediately follows G in the schedule then 
   s_G + (meeting duration for G) + (travel time from G’s location to F’s location)
must be ≤ s_F.
• For the very first meeting (i.e. order = 0) the departure time is fixed – you start at Bayview at 9:00AM – so you must allow at least the travel time from Bayview to that friend’s location.
• In addition each meeting “F” must occur within F’s available time window (that is, s_F must be at or after F’s earliest available time and s_F + meeting duration no later than F’s “end‐time”).
• In the case of Linda the availability window forces her meeting to start at exactly 705 minutes (8:45PM) so that a 75–minute meeting finishes exactly at 10:00PM.
The constraints together form a “scheduling/ordering” problem that must choose (a) the permutation (ordering) of friends and (b) appropriate meeting start times subject to travel–time gaps and waiting (if you arrive early). Our goal is to “meet as many friends as possible” – that is, to include all meetings in a consistent schedule. (In a more elaborate model an objective function might minimize total idle time.)

        suffix = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
        hour12 = hour if hour <= 12 else hour - 12

        # Determine travel time from current_location to this meeting's location.

Below is an explanation of how the “meet‐friends” problem can be cast as a constraint satisfaction problem, followed by a complete Python script (enclosed in triple-backticks with “python”) that uses the Z3 solver to decide on an ordering (route) and meeting start times that satisfy all travel and availability constraints while “optimizing” the schedule (in this case, finishing as early as possible while meeting everyone).

──────────────────────────────
1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We start at Bayview at 9:00AM and want to visit six friends located in different neighborhoods. Each friend is available only during a given time window and you must meet them for at least a prescribed “minimum meeting duration.” In addition, travel times (in minutes) between any two locations (including from Bayview to a friend’s location) must be factored in.

The decision variables are:
 • An ordering of the visits. In our model we use an array order[0…5] where each slot is assigned one friend (indexed 0–5). We add a “distinct” constraint so that each friend is visited exactly once.
 • For each meeting slot i we introduce a variable t[i] representing the meeting’s starting time (measured in minutes after 9:00AM).

The constraints are:
 • If a friend f is scheduled in slot i then the meeting must be completely inside that friend’s available window. That is, 
   t[i] ≥ available_start(f) and t[i] + meeting_duration(f) ≤ available_end(f).
 • The meeting cannot start “too early.” For the very first slot the meeting start must be at least the travel time from Bayview to the friend’s location.
 • For every two consecutive visits – say friend g in slot i–1 and friend f in slot i – we require that
   t[i] ≥ t[i–1] + meeting_duration(g) + travel_time(g’s location, f’s location).
 • The travel times between every pair of locations (including from the starting Bayview location) are provided.
 
Finally, as an “optimization” goal we want to meet as many friends as possible. In our formulation all six meetings are included. (We also add an objective to “minimize” the finish time — that is, to choose among different schedules the one that ends as early as possible.)

──────────────────────────────
2. Python Script Using the Z3 Solver

Below is the complete Python script. (Copy the code including the ```python markers and run it with Z3 installed.)

------------------------------------------------------------
```python
from z3 import *

def main():
    # ------------------------
    # Data and travel times
    # ------------------------
    # Friend data: each friend is defined by a name, location,
    # available time window (in minutes after 9:00AM) and minimum meeting duration.
    # Times have been converted so that 9:00AM corresponds to time 0.
    # For example, 10:45AM is 105 minutes (since 9:00 + 1h45 = 105).
    friend_data = [
      {"name": "Rebecca", "location": "Nob Hill",          "avail_start": 390, "avail_end": 750, "duration": 45},
      {"name": "David",   "location": "Mission District",  "avail_start": 285, "avail_end": 750, "duration": 120},
      {"name": "Nancy",   "location": "Presidio",          "avail_start": 90,  "avail_end": 495, "duration": 45},
      {"name": "Robert",  "location": "Union Square",      "avail_start": 105, "avail_end": 210, "duration": 75},
      {"name": "Linda",   "location": "Fisherman's Wharf", "avail_start": 705, "avail_end": 780, "duration": 75},
      {"name": "John",    "location": "Alamo Square",      "avail_start": 210, "avail_end": 555, "duration": 90},
    ]
    num_friends = len(friend_data)

    # Travel distances (minutes) between locations – note that directions may differ.
    travel = {
      ("Bayview", "Nob Hill"): 20,
      ("Bayview", "Mission District"): 13,
      ("Bayview", "Presidio"): 31,
      ("Bayview", "Union Square"): 17,
      ("Bayview", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 25,
      ("Bayview", "Alamo Square"): 16,
      
      ("Nob Hill", "Bayview"): 19,
      ("Nob Hill", "Mission District"): 13,
      ("Nob Hill", "Presidio"): 17,
      ("Nob Hill", "Union Square"): 7,
      ("Nob Hill", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 11,
      ("Nob Hill", "Alamo Square"): 11,
      
      ("Mission District", "Bayview"): 15,
      ("Mission District", "Nob Hill"): 12,
      ("Mission District", "Presidio"): 25,
      ("Mission District", "Union Square"): 15,
      ("Mission District", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 22,
      ("Mission District", "Alamo Square"): 11,
      
      ("Presidio", "Bayview"): 31,
      ("Presidio", "Nob Hill"): 18,
      ("Presidio", "Mission District"): 26,
      ("Presidio", "Union Square"): 24,
      ("Presidio", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 19,
      ("Presidio", "Alamo Square"): 18,
      
      ("Union Square", "Bayview"): 15,
      ("Union Square", "Nob Hill"): 9,
      ("Union Square", "Mission District"): 14,
      ("Union Square", "Presidio"): 24,
      ("Union Square", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 15,
      ("Union Square", "Alamo Square"): 15,
      
      ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Bayview"): 26,
      ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Nob Hill"): 11,
      ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Mission District"): 22,
      ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Presidio"): 17,
      ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Union Square"): 13,
      ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Alamo Square"): 20,
      
      ("Alamo Square", "Bayview"): 16,
      ("Alamo Square", "Nob Hill"): 11,
      ("Alamo Square", "Mission District"): 10,
      ("Alamo Square", "Presidio"): 18,
      ("Alamo Square", "Union Square"): 14,
      ("Alamo Square", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 19,
    }
    
    # Precompute travel time from the starting location (Bayview) for each friend.
    travel_from_start = []
    for i in range(num_friends):
        loc = friend_data[i]["location"]
        travel_from_start.append(travel[("Bayview", loc)])
    
    # Build a matrix for travel times between friends’ locations.
    travel_between = [[None]*num_friends for _ in range(num_friends)]
    for i in range(num_friends):
        for j in range(num_friends):
            loc_i = friend_data[i]["location"]
            loc_j = friend_data[j]["location"]
            travel_between[i][j] = travel[(loc_i, loc_j)]
            
    # -----------------------------------------
    # Z3 Model: decision variables and constraints
    # -----------------------------------------
    opt = Optimize()

    # Decision variables:
    # 'order[i]' is an integer in 0..num_friends-1 indicating which friend is visited in slot i.
    # 't[i]' is the meeting start time (minutes after 9:00AM) for the meeting scheduled in slot i.
    order = [ Int(f"order_{i}") for i in range(num_friends) ]
    t = [ Int(f"t_{i}") for i in range(num_friends) ]
    
    # Order variables must be within range and all be different (a permutation).
    for i in range(num_friends):
        opt.add(order[i] >= 0, order[i] < num_friends)
    opt.add(Distinct(order))
    
    # For each meeting slot, add constraints on availability and travel.
    for i in range(num_friends):
        for f in range(num_friends):
            friend = friend_data[f]
            # When friend f is scheduled in slot i, the meeting must start no earlier
            # than f’s available start time and end by the available end time.
            opt.add(Implies(order[i] == f, t[i] >= friend["avail_start"]))
            opt.add(Implies(order[i] == f, t[i] + friend["duration"] <= friend["avail_end"]))
            # For the first slot, also enforce that you cannot start before arriving from Bayview.
            if i == 0:
                opt.add(Implies(order[i] == f, t[i] >= travel_from_start[f]))
            else:
                # For subsequent slots, if the previous slot has friend g and the current slot has friend f,
                # then meeting start time must be at least the previous meeting’s finish time plus travel time.
                for g in range(num_friends):
                    opt.add(Implies(And(order[i-1] == g, order[i] == f),
                                    t[i] >= t[i-1] + friend_data[g]["duration"] + travel_between[g][f]))
    
    # For an optimization objective, we choose to minimize the overall finish time.
    finish_time_with_meeting = Int("finish_time_with_meeting")
    finish_expr = []
    for f in range(num_friends):
        finish_expr.append(If(order[num_friends-1] == f, t[num_friends-1] + friend_data[f]["duration"], 0))
    opt.add(finish_time_with_meeting == Sum(finish_expr))
    opt.minimize(finish_time_with_meeting)
    
    # ------------------------
    # Solve the scheduling problem.
    # ------------------------
    if opt.check() == sat:
        model = opt.model()
        # Retrieve the order and meeting start times from the model.
        order_sol = [ model.evaluate(order[i]).as_long() for i in range(num_friends) ]
        t_sol = [ model.evaluate(t[i]).as_long() for i in range(num_friends) ]
        
        # ------------------------
        # Build a schedule narrative following this format:
        # ["You start at Bayview at 9:00AM.",
        #  "You travel to <location> in X minutes and arrive at <time>.",
        #  "You wait until <meeting start>." (if needed),
        #  "You meet <name> for Y minutes from <start> to <end>."]
        # ------------------------
        schedule = []
        
        # Helper function to convert minutes after 9:00AM into a clock time string.
        def convert_time(offset):
            # offset in minutes after 9:00AM
            total = 9 * 60 + offset
            hour = total // 60
            minute = total % 60
            period = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
            hour_mod = hour if hour <= 12 else hour - 12
            if hour_mod == 0:
                hour_mod = 12
            return f"{hour_mod}:{minute:02d}{period}"
        
        # Start at Bayview at 9:00AM
        schedule.append("You start at Bayview at 9:00AM.")
        current_time = 0
        current_location = "Bayview"
        
        for i in range(num_friends):
            f_idx = order_sol[i]
            friend = friend_data[f_idx]
            # Compute travel time from current location to the friend location.
            travel_time = travel[(current_location, friend["location"])]
            arrival_time = current_time + travel_time
            schedule.append(f"You travel to {friend['location']} in {travel_time} minutes and arrive at {convert_time(arrival_time)}.")
            # If you arrive before the scheduled meeting time, add a waiting message.
            if arrival_time < t_sol[i]:
                schedule.append(f"You wait until {convert_time(t_sol[i])}.")
            meeting_end = t_sol[i] + friend["duration"]
            schedule.append(f"You meet {friend['name']} for {friend['duration']} minutes from {convert_time(t_sol[i])} to {convert_time(meeting_end)}.")
            current_time = meeting_end
            current_location = friend["location"]
        
        print(schedule)
    else:
        print("No solution found.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation of the Script:

• The script first defines the data – the friends (with names, locations, availability windows, and required meeting durations) and the travel times between all pairs of locations including the starting Bayview.

• Decision variables are then created:
  – order[i] for i = 0…5 is a variable whose value (from 0 to 5) indicates which friend is visited in the i‑th slot.
  – t[i] is the meeting start time (in minutes after 9:00AM) for the meeting in slot i.

• Using a nested series of If/Implies constraints, the code ensures that if a friend f is assigned to slot i, then the meeting is scheduled within the friend’s time window and not before you are able to travel to that location. For consecutive slots the meeting start time of slot i is forced to be at least the finish time of the previous meeting (including its minimum meeting duration) plus the travel time from the previous friend’s location.

• An optimization objective is added (minimizing the overall finish time) so that among the viable schedules the “best” one (finishing as early as possible) is selected.

• The script then “reads” the model solution, translates minutes back into clock times (using a helper conversion function) and outputs a schedule as a list of strings – similar to the provided example output format.

You can run this script (with Z3 and its Python API installed) in order to see the step‐by‐step itinerary that meets all constraints.

This complete solution meets the goals of “meeting as many friends as possible” while obeying travel distances, friend availabilities and minimum meeting durations.

SOLUTION:

Below is our reasoning and a complete Python script that uses Z3 to “choose” an ordering and appointment‐times that satisfy all the travel and meeting‐window constraints.

Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We model the day as a sequence of six meetings – one for each friend – with the following ingredients:
• Variables for each friend “F”:
  – s_F: the start time (in minutes after 9:00AM) at which you begin the meeting.
  – order_F: an integer (0–5) representing F’s position in your schedule.
• Fixed “meeting‐length” constants (the minimum required meeting time), plus each friend’s availability window (translated into minutes from 9:00AM). (For instance, Robert is available from 10:45AM (105 minutes) to 12:30PM (210 minutes) and his required meeting duration is 75 minutes.)
• Travel times are given both from your starting spot (Bayview) to each friend’s location and between friends’ locations. For any two friends “F” and “G”, if F immediately follows G in the schedule then 
   s_G + (meeting duration for G) + (travel time from G’s location to F’s location)
must be ≤ s_F.
• For the very first meeting (i.e. order = 0) the departure time is fixed – you start at Bayview at 9:00AM – so you must allow at least the travel time from Bayview to that friend’s location.
• In addition each meeting “F” must occur within F’s available time window (that is, s_F must be at or after F’s earliest available time and s_F + meeting duration no later than F’s “end‐time”).
• In the case of Linda the availability window forces her meeting to start at exactly 705 minutes (8:45PM) so that a 75–minute meeting finishes exactly at 10:00PM.
The constraints together form a “scheduling/ordering” problem that must choose (a) the permutation (ordering) of friends and (b) appropriate meeting start times subject to travel–time gaps and waiting (if you arrive early). Our goal is to “meet as many friends as possible” – that is, to include all meetings in a consistent schedule. (In a more elaborate model an objective function might minimize total idle time.) 

Step 2. Python Script Using Z3

Below is the full code. (Please be sure that z3 is installed on your system – e.g. via pip install z3-solver.)

------------------------------------------------------------
```python
from z3 import *

# --- Data definition ---

# Our six friends with availability windows (in minutes after 9:00AM) and required meeting durations.
# For example: Robert: available from 10:45AM (105) to 12:30PM (210) and meeting duration 75.
friend_data = {
    "Robert":   {"location": "Union Square",    "avail_start": 105, "avail_end": 210, "duration": 75},
    "Nancy":    {"location": "Presidio",        "avail_start": 90,  "avail_end": 495, "duration": 45},
    "John":     {"location": "Alamo Square",    "avail_start": 210, "avail_end": 555, "duration": 90},
    "David":    {"location": "Mission District","avail_start": 285, "avail_end": 750, "duration": 120},
    "Rebecca":  {"location": "Nob Hill",        "avail_start": 390, "avail_end": 750, "duration": 45},
    "Linda":    {"location": "Fisherman's Wharf","avail_start": 705, "avail_end": 780, "duration": 75}
}

friends = list(friend_data.keys())

# Travel times FROM Bayview (the starting point) to each friend’s location:
fromBayview = {
    "Union Square": 17,
    "Presidio": 31,
    "Alamo Square": 16,
    "Mission District": 13,
    "Nob Hill": 20,
    "Fisherman's Wharf": 25
}

# Travel times between locations. 
# These values are taken from the provided travel distances.
# (Key: (src, dst))
inter_travel = {
    ("Nob Hill", "Mission District"): 13,
    ("Nob Hill", "Presidio"): 17,
    ("Nob Hill", "Union Square"): 7,
    ("Nob Hill", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 11,
    ("Nob Hill", "Alamo Square"): 11,
    
    ("Mission District", "Nob Hill"): 12,
    ("Mission District", "Presidio"): 25,
    ("Mission District", "Union Square"): 14,
    ("Mission District", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 22,
    ("Mission District", "Alamo Square"): 11,
    
    ("Presidio", "Nob Hill"): 18,
    ("Presidio", "Mission District"): 26,
    ("Presidio", "Union Square"): 24,
    ("Presidio", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 19,
    ("Presidio", "Alamo Square"): 18,
    
    ("Union Square", "Nob Hill"): 9,
    ("Union Square", "Mission District"): 15,
    ("Union Square", "Presidio"): 24,
    ("Union Square", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 15,
    ("Union Square", "Alamo Square"): 15,
    
    ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Nob Hill"): 11,
    ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Mission District"): 22,
    ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Presidio"): 17,
    ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Union Square"): 13,
    ("Fisherman's Wharf", "Alamo Square"): 20,
    
    ("Alamo Square", "Nob Hill"): 11,
    ("Alamo Square", "Mission District"): 10,
    ("Alamo Square", "Presidio"): 18,
    ("Alamo Square", "Union Square"): 14,
    ("Alamo Square", "Fisherman's Wharf"): 19
}

# --- Setup Z3 solver and decision variables ---

s = {}      # meeting start times for each friend (in minutes after 9:00 AM)
order = {}  # ordering index for each friend (0 means first meeting)

solver = Solver()

for f in friends:
    s[f] = Int("s_" + f)
    order[f] = Int("order_" + f)
    # Each friend’s meeting must be within the available time window.
    solver.add(s[f] >= friend_data[f]["avail_start"])
    solver.add(s[f] + friend_data[f]["duration"] <= friend_data[f]["avail_end"])
    # Order indices must lie between 0 and len(friends)-1.
    solver.add(order[f] >= 0, order[f] < len(friends))

# Linda’s available window forces her meeting to start exactly at 705 minutes.
solver.add(s["Linda"] == 705)

# The order variables must be all different.
solver.add(Distinct([order[f] for f in friends]))

# For whichever friend is scheduled first (order == 0), the meeting must start 
# no earlier than the travel time from Bayview.
for f in friends:
    loc = friend_data[f]["location"]
    solver.add(Implies(order[f] == 0, s[f] >= fromBayview[loc]))

# For any pair of friends f and g, if f immediately follows g then:
#   (s[g] + duration[g] + travel_time(g->f)) <= s[f]
for f in friends:
    for g in friends:
        if f != g:
            loc_g = friend_data[g]["location"]
            loc_f = friend_data[f]["location"]
            travel_time = inter_travel.get((loc_g, loc_f))
            # Make sure a travel time exists between these locations.
            if travel_time is not None:
                solver.add(Implies(order[f] == order[g] + 1, s[g] + friend_data[g]["duration"] + travel_time <= s[f]))

# --- Solve the constraints ---

if solver.check() == sat:
    model = solver.model()
    # Get the order (sorting friends by their order integer value)
    ordered_friends = sorted(friends, key=lambda f: model[order[f]].as_long())
    
    # Extract scheduled start times (and compute finish times)
    schedule = {}
    for f in friends:
        start = model[s[f]].as_long()
        finish = start + friend_data[f]["duration"]
        schedule[f] = (start, finish)
    
    # Helper function: convert minutes offset from 9:00AM into a time string.
    def format_time(offset):
        total = 540 + offset  # 9:00AM is 540 minutes after midnight
        hour = total // 60
        minute = total % 60
        suffix = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
        hour12 = hour if hour <= 12 else hour - 12
        return f"{hour12}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"
        
    # Build the schedule “story” step‐by‐step.
    actions = []
    actions.append(f"You start at Bayview at 9:00AM.")
    
    current_time = 0
    current_location = "Bayview"
    # For each meeting in order:
    for idx, f in enumerate(ordered_friends):
        loc = friend_data[f]["location"]
        # Determine travel time from current_location to this meeting's location.
        if current_location == "Bayview":
            travel_time = fromBayview[loc]
        else:
            travel_time = inter_travel.get((current_location, loc))
            if travel_time is None:
                travel_time = 0
        arrival_time = current_time + travel_time
        # Record travel only if travel time is positive.
        if travel_time > 0:
            actions.append(f"You travel from {current_location} to {loc} in {travel_time} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival_time)}.")
        # If you arrive earlier than the scheduled meeting start time, wait.
        meeting_start, meeting_finish = schedule[f]
        if arrival_time < meeting_start:
            actions.append(f"You wait until {format_time(meeting_start)}.")
        actions.append(f"You meet {f} for {friend_data[f]['duration']} minutes from {format_time(meeting_start)} to {format_time(meeting_finish)}.")
        # Update current time and location.
        current_time = meeting_finish
        current_location = loc
    # (No requirement to return home at end.)
    
    # Print the schedule as a list of strings.
    print(actions)
else:
    print("No valid schedule found.")

We want to “chain” together a series of visits to friends while respecting each friend’s time‐window and the minimum meeting duration required. In our problem the “resources” are time and the travel segments between different locations in San Francisco. We start at a fixed point (Alamo Square) at 9:00AM and we have a list of friends with fixed meeting locations, available time windows, and minimum meeting durations. In addition, the travel time between locations (which is not necessarily symmetric) must be added between consecutive meetings.

We can model the problem by making the following decisions and constraints:
 • For each friend we introduce integer variables for the meeting start time and end time (expressed as minutes from midnight). The domains of those variables are constrained by the friend’s availability (for example, Deborah is available from 7:00AM [420 minutes] to 11:00AM [660 minutes]). We also add the constraint that the meeting lasts at least the minimum required (e.g. at least 15 minutes for Deborah).
 • We also impose “travel constraints.” The very first meeting must not start before the time it takes to leave Alamo Square at 9:00AM and travel to the friend’s neighborhood. Then for each consecutive pair in our schedule the start time of the next meeting must be at least the previous meeting’s end time plus the travel time between those friend locations.
