Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem
────────────────────────────────────────────
We have six potential “meeting‐tasks” (one for each friend) that can be scheduled during the day. Each friend “f” has:
 • a fixed location (for example, Melissa is at Nob Hill),
 • a fixed time window during which the meeting can occur (e.g. Melissa is available from 9:15AM to 1:30PM, which we convert into minutes after 9:00AM as [15, 270]),
 • a minimum meeting duration (e.g. 60 minutes for Melissa), and
 • an “arrival‐from‐start” constraint given that you begin at Alamo Square at 9:00AM (so you must at least allow the travel time from Alamo Square to the friend’s district).

Moreover, there is a travel-time matrix between the different locations (for example, from Nob Hill to Presidio takes 17 minutes). When scheduling two meetings back–to–back, you must account not only for the meeting duration but also for the travel time from one friend’s location to the next.

Because meeting all six friends might not be mutually compatible (in our case the three “evening friends” – George, Daniel and Jessica – have overlapping windows such that only two can be scheduled), we introduce a binary (Boolean) decision variable for each friend indicating if you meet them. For each friend f that is “attended” (i.e. the Boolean is true), we introduce an integer variable s_f for the meeting start time (measured in minutes after 9:00AM) with the constraints:
  • s_f must be at least the friend’s availability start time and also no earlier than the travel time required from Alamo Square.
  • The meeting must finish within the friend’s available window (s_f + duration ≤ availability end).

For every pair of meetings that are both “attended” the ordering must be consistent with travel:
 Either meeting f finishes (s_f + duration_f) and then, after the travel time from f’s location to g’s location, meeting g starts or vice‐versa. This gives a disjunctive ordering constraint.

Finally, the “objective” is to maximize the number of friends met (in other words, maximize the sum of the Boolean attend–variables). Once the optimal solution is found we “simulate” the day by ordering the attended tasks by their start time. We then output a detailed schedule showing:
 – the initial departure from Alamo Square (at 9:00AM),
 – each travel segment (with travel time and arrival time),
 – any waiting time until the friend’s available meeting window starts,
 – and the meeting (with its fixed duration and its start and finish times).

 • a fixed time window during which the meeting can occur (e.g. Melissa is available from 9:15AM to 1:30PM, which we convert into minutes after 9:00AM as [15, 270]),
 • a minimum meeting duration (e.g. 60 minutes for Melissa), and
 • an “arrival‐from‐start” constraint given that you begin at Alamo Square at 9:00AM (so you must at least allow the travel time from Alamo Square to the friend’s district).

Moreover, there is a travel-time matrix between the different locations (for example, from Nob Hill to Presidio takes 17 minutes). When scheduling two meetings back–to–back, you must account not only for the meeting duration but also for the travel time from one friend’s location to the next.

Because meeting all six friends might not be mutually compatible (in our case the three “evening friends” – George, Daniel and Jessica – have overlapping windows such that only two can be scheduled), we introduce a binary (Boolean) decision variable for each friend indicating if you meet them. This problem can be formulated as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) in the following way. You have a set of “meeting‐events” – each friend is available at a fixed location during a given time window and you must spend a minimum amount of time with that friend. In addition, there is a travel time associated with going from one location to the next. In short, you need to choose an ordering and “start‐times” (or schedule times) for each meeting such that:

• The meeting at the first friend’s location cannot start before you can actually reach that location (starting from Pacific Heights at 9:00AM and adding the travel time).
• For each friend the meeting “start time” and “end time” (start time plus the required meeting duration) must lie within that friend’s availability window.
• When you travel from the location for one meeting to the next friend’s location, the start time for the next meeting must be at least the previous meeting’s end time plus the travel time between those locations.
• If you arrive earlier than the friend’s availability time, you have to “wait” (this is modeled by the constraint that the meeting cannot begin until the friend is available).
• Finally, your goal is to “meet as many friends as possible” – that is, choose a schedule (and implicitly an ordering, here chosen according to the feasibility windows) that maximizes the number of friends where all constraints are satisfied.

In our solution we assume the “natural” order given by the time‐windows:
  1. Kenneth (Chinatown, available until 12:45PM, meeting required 105 minutes)
  2. Lisa (Financial District, available 10:00AM–6:15PM, 105 minutes)
  3. Joseph (Union Square, available 2:30PM–5:00PM, 105 minutes)
  4. Michelle (North Beach, available 7:45PM–9:30PM, 45 minutes)
  5. Patricia (Golden Gate Park, available 8:45PM–9:45PM, 45 minutes)

We introduce an integer variable for each meeting’s start time (measured in minutes after midnight). The constraints (using the provided travel times) are then:
  • Kenneth’s meeting: must start no earlier than 9:00AM + travel from Pacific Heights to Chinatown (11 minutes) and end by 12:45PM.
  • Lisa’s meeting: must start at least after Kenneth’s meeting (including the 105‑minute meeting plus the 5‑minute travel from Chinatown to Financial District) and no earlier than 10:00AM.
  • Joseph’s meeting: must start after Lisa’s meeting (adding 105 plus 9 minutes travel from Financial District to Union Square) and obey his availability (2:30PM–5:00PM).
  • Michelle’s meeting: must start after Joseph’s meeting (adding 105 plus 10 minutes travel from Union Square to North Beach) and be within her available window (7:45PM–9:30PM).
  • Patricia’s meeting: must start after Michelle’s meeting (adding 45 plus 22 minutes travel from North Beach to Golden Gate Park) and be in her window (8:45PM–9:45PM).

This CSP is solved with the Z3 solver and then the script “simulates” the day by computing travel times, any waiting periods if the arrival time is earlier than the meeting’s scheduled start, and then outputs a narrative schedule as a list of strings.

SOLUTION:
Below is our reasoning followed by the complete Python code that uses Z3 to “solve” the schedule as a constraint‐satisfaction problem.

─────────────────────────────
1. Reasoning (Constraint Satisfaction Problem Explanation):

We must decide on a daily itinerary that starts at The Castro at 9:00AM and visits several districts where our friends are available during given time windows. For each friend (Patricia, Jeffrey, Ronald, Amanda, Joshua, Laura, Melissa) we must “schedule” a meeting that lasts at least a specified duration (75 minutes for most, 30 minutes for Amanda, and 15 minutes for Melissa) while staying within that friend’s availability window. In addition, traveling between districts takes a fixed number of minutes (given in the table). 

We model each meeting’s start time as a variable measured in minutes after 9:00AM. For instance, the meeting with Patricia (in Chinatown) must start no earlier than our arrival time to Chinatown (The Castro → Chinatown takes 20 minutes) and no later than (friend’s window end minus 75). For each subsequent meeting we add the previous meeting’s duration plus the corresponding travel time to get the “earliest‐possible arrival” at the next location. Then the meeting with that friend cannot start before both this arrival time and the friend’s availability–start time. (If you arrive too early you simply wait.) Finally the meeting must finish before that friend’s window closes.

By “chaining” these constraints one after the other – with the order determined by the time windows (for example, Jeffrey’s 10:45–12:15 window forces his meeting to occur early, and Melissa’s extremely brief window near the end fixes her meeting last) – we get one long chain of constraints. A solution satisfying all these constraints gives us a feasible schedule that meets every friend. (Since our goal is “to meet as many friends as possible” the optimum solution is one that schedules all meetings.)

─────────────────────────────
2. Python Code:

Below is the complete Python script. Save and run it (with Z3 installed) to see the schedule printed out step‐by‐step.

# Patricia (Chinatown): 8:30AM to 1:30PM  -> [-30, 270]
# Jeffrey (Embarcadero): 10:45AM to 12:15PM -> [105, 195]
# Ronald (Richmond): 12:30PM to 2:00PM -> [210, 300]

# Laura (Mission District): 5:00PM to 8:00PM -> [480, 660]
# Melissa (Pacific Heights): 9:30PM to 9:45PM -> [750, 765]

travel_Sunset_NobHill = 27

r   = Int('r')    # Meeting start time with Ronald at Richmond

s.add(j >= p + dur_pat + travel_Chinatown_Embarcadero)  # j >= p + 75 + 5 = p + 80

s.add(r >= j + dur_jeff + travel_Embarcadero_Richmond)  # r >= j+75+21 = j+96

s.add(r >= 210)
s.add(r + dur_ron <= 300)                     # finish by 2:00PM (300)

# Amanda constraints:

s.add(a >= r + dur_ron + travel_Richmond_Sunset)  # a >= r+75+11 = r + 86
s.add(a >= 285)   # available from 1:45PM (285 minutes)

# Joshua constraints:
# Arrival at Nob Hill = finish Amanda + travel (a+30+27)
s.add(js >= a + dur_amand + travel_Sunset_NobHill) # js >= a+30+27 = a+57
s.add(js >= 30)    # available from 9:30AM (30 minutes)
s.add(js + dur_josh <= 645)                     # finish by 7:45PM (645)

# Laura constraints:
# Arrival at Mission District = finish Joshua + travel (js+75+13)
s.add(l >= js + dur_josh + travel_NobHill_Mission) # l >= js+75+13 = js+88
s.add(l >= 480)   # available from 5:00PM (480)
s.add(l + dur_laura <= 660)                     # finish by 8:00PM (660)

# Melissa constraints:
# Arrival at Pacific Heights = finish Laura + travel (l+75+16)
s.add(m >= l + dur_laura + travel_Mission_Pacific) # m >= l+75+16 = l+91
s.add(m >= 750)   # available from 9:30PM (750)
s.add(m + dur_mel <= 765)                       # finish by 9:45PM (765)

    a_end = a_val + dur_amand
    js_end = js_val + dur_josh
    l_end = l_val + dur_laura
    m_end = m_val + dur_mel

    # Helper function: Convert minutes after 9:00AM into an HH:MM AM/PM string.
    def minutes_to_time_str(mnts):
        total = 9 * 60 + mnts  # total minutes since midnight, starting at 9:00AM
        hour = total // 60
        minute = total % 60
        suffix = "AM"
        if hour >= 12:
            suffix = "PM"
            if hour > 12:
                hour = hour - 12
        return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"
    
    # Build schedule steps as a list of strings.

SOLUTION:
Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We can “encode” the day‐planning problem as a CSP with two kinds of decision variables for each friend:
 • A meeting start time S for that friend (in minutes from 9:00AM) – the meeting will then last exactly the required minimum duration.
 • An order (a “position” in the route) telling us when that friend is visited. Since there are seven friends the order value will be an integer in {0,…,6} and all order–values must be distinct.

Each friend “f” comes with its own constraints:
 – Its meeting cannot start before its available start time (Aₛ) and must finish (S + required duration) before its available end time (Aₑ).
 – If friend “f” is the very first visit then you must allow for travel from the starting location “Richmond District” (i.e. S[f] must be at least the travel time from Richmond District to friend f’s location). 
 – If friend “f” is scheduled immediately before friend “g” (i.e. order[f] + 1 = order[g]) then you must also allow travel from f’s location to g’s location. In other words, the constraint is:
   S[g] ≥ S[f] + (duration of meeting with f) + (travel time from f’s location to g’s location).

The travel durations between any two locations are given. (Note that the travel time from, say, “Richmond District” to “Financial District” is not necessarily the same as the time in the reverse direction.) 

Finally, since your overall aim is to “meet as many friends as possible” (and in fact all seven can be scheduled) you use these constraints in combination with an objective (for example to minimize the overall finishing time) so that the “best” route is chosen.

Below is a complete Python script that encodes the above CSP and then prints a sample route in the requested output format. The “evening problem” is trickier because you want to meet several friends—but the required meeting durations and very “tight” time windows force you to choose among two alternative sequences. Below is our reasoning and the corresponding Python/Z3 implementation.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We want to “meet as many friends as possible” in one day by planning a route among seven meeting locations. We start from Pacific Heights at 9:00AM and then travel to visit friends located at:
 • Paul at Fisherman’s Wharf (available 4:15–6:45PM; meet ≥105 minutes),
 • Helen at Chinatown (available 11:45AM–1:15PM; meet ≥45 minutes),
 • Sandra at Alamo Square (available 6:00–9:45PM; meet ≥120 minutes),
 • Andrew at Golden Gate Park (available 9:00AM–2:30PM; meet ≥75 minutes),
 • William at Presidio (available 7:15AM–7:00PM; meet ≥120 minutes),
 • Brian at Embarcadero (available 11:30AM–8:00PM; meet ≥15 minutes),
 • Rebecca at Marina District (available 7:30AM–8:00PM; meet ≥15 minutes).

Our decision variables are:
 • The order in which to visit these friends – a permutation of 0…6 (each number representing one friend);
 • For each visit (in order) a meeting start time “s” (in minutes from midnight).

The constraints we need to satisfy are:

1. Permutation of visits:
 – Each friend is visited exactly once. (We model this by forcing each order variable to lie between 0 and 6 and using a “Distinct” constraint.)

2. Time-window constraints:
 For each friend we have an availability window [A, B] and a required meeting duration d. If a friend is visited in slot i then:
  • The meeting cannot start before both the friend’s available start time and the time you can arrive (given previous meetings and travel times).
  • You must spend at least the required duration d so that meeting start plus d does not exceed the friend’s available end time.
 For instance, if you start with friend i then its meeting “start time” s₀ must be at least:
  s₀ ≥ 9:00AM + travel_time(Pacific Heights, friend i’s location)
  s₀ ≥ A[i]
 and s₀ + d[i] ≤ B[i].

3. Travel-time constraints:
 For successive visits you must add the meeting duration of the previous friend and the travel time between their locations. That is, for visit i > 0, if the previous meeting ended at time e then:
  s[i] ≥ e + travel_time(location(previous friend), location(current friend))
 Travel times between any two locations are given (and are not symmetric in general).

By writing every one of these constraints, our CSP becomes: “find a permutation (route) and a set of scheduling times {s[i]} such that you satisfy the travel‐and‐meeting constraints for each friend; and ideally, you include all friends (thus meeting the goal of maximizing the number met).” We even use an optimization objective (minimizing overall finishing time) so that among many feasible routes our schedule is ‘good.’

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Python Script Using Z3

Below is the complete Python script (enclosed in ```python ...```) that uses Z3 to model the problem, enforce the constraints, optimize the finishing time, and then print out a “narrative” schedule similar to the example output.

from z3 import *

# -------------------------------
# Data definitions
# -------------------------------
# We represent time in minutes from midnight.
# Starting time is 9:00AM = 540 minutes.
start_time = 540

# Convert times to minutes from midnight:
# Paul: 4:15PM (975) to 6:45PM (1125) --> duration needed 105
# Helen: 11:45AM (705) to 1:15PM (795)   --> duration needed 45
# Sandra: 6:00PM (1080) to 9:45PM (1305)   --> duration needed 120
# Andrew: 9:00AM (540) to 2:30PM (870)     --> duration needed 75
# William: 7:15AM (435) to 7:00PM (1140)    --> duration needed 120
# Brian: 11:30AM (690) to 8:00PM (1200)     --> duration needed 15
# Rebecca: 7:30AM (450) to 8:00PM (1200)    --> duration needed 15

# For friend indices 0-6 we define:
# 0: Paul, 1: Helen, 2: Sandra, 3: Andrew, 4: William, 5: Brian, 6: Rebecca
friend_names = ['Paul', 'Helen', 'Sandra', 'Andrew', 'William', 'Brian', 'Rebecca']
# Their meeting locations:
friend_locations = ['Fisherman’s Wharf', 'Chinatown', 'Alamo Square', 'Golden Gate Park', 'Presidio', 'Embarcadero', 'Marina District']
# Availability start times
avail_start = [975, 705, 1080, 540, 435, 690, 450]
# Availability end times
avail_end   = [1125, 795, 1305, 870, 1140, 1200, 1200]
# Required meeting durations
durations   = [105, 45, 120, 75, 120, 15, 15]

# Starting location is Pacific Heights.
start_location = "Pacific Heights"

# To make our modeling easier we also assign a unique location index (0..7) to every place.
# We have:
# 0: Pacific Heights (starting point)
# 1: Fisherman’s Wharf, 2: Chinatown, 3: Alamo Square, 4: Golden Gate Park,
# 5: Presidio, 6: Embarcadero, 7: Marina District.
# For each friend the location is given by:
location_mapping = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]

# Travel time matrix for locations 0..7 (in minutes)
# Rows: from location, Columns: to location
# Row 0: Pacific Heights, Row 1: Fisherman’s Wharf, etc.
travel_matrix = [
    [0, 13, 11, 10, 15, 11, 10, 6],   # From Pacific Heights (0)
    [12, 0, 12, 20, 25, 17, 8, 9],     # From Fisherman’s Wharf (1)
    [10, 8, 0, 17, 23, 19, 5, 12],      # From Chinatown (2)
    [10, 19, 16, 0, 9, 18, 17, 15],     # From Alamo Square (3)
    [16, 24, 23, 10, 0, 11, 25, 16],    # From Golden Gate Park (4)
    [11, 19, 21, 18, 12, 0, 20, 10],    # From Presidio (5)
    [11, 6, 7, 19, 25, 20, 0, 12],      # From Embarcadero (6)
    [7, 10, 16, 15, 18, 10, 14, 0]       # From Marina District (7)
]

# -------------------------------
# Helper functions to return friend properties.
# Because the friend in each position is given by a Z3 Int variable (0..6),
# we must use If() expressions to “select” the appropriate value.
# -------------------------------
def friend_avail_start(f):
    return If(f == 0, avail_start[0],
           If(f == 1, avail_start[1],
           If(f == 2, avail_start[2],
           If(f == 3, avail_start[3],
           If(f == 4, avail_start[4],
           If(f == 5, avail_start[5],
           If(f == 6, avail_start[6], 0)))))))

def friend_avail_end(f):
    return If(f == 0, avail_end[0],
           If(f == 1, avail_end[1],
           If(f == 2, avail_end[2],
           If(f == 3, avail_end[3],
           If(f == 4, avail_end[4],
           If(f == 5, avail_end[5],
           If(f == 6, avail_end[6], 0)))))))

def friend_duration(f):
    return If(f == 0, durations[0],
           If(f == 1, durations[1],
           If(f == 2, durations[2],
           If(f == 3, durations[3],
           If(f == 4, durations[4],
           If(f == 5, durations[5],
           If(f == 6, durations[6], 0)))))))

def friend_location_index(f):
    # Returns the location index (1..7) for friend f.
    return If(f == 0, location_mapping[0],
           If(f == 1, location_mapping[1],
           If(f == 2, location_mapping[2],
           If(f == 3, location_mapping[3],
           If(f == 4, location_mapping[4],
           If(f == 5, location_mapping[5],
           If(f == 6, location_mapping[6], 0)))))))

# Function to return travel time given two location indices.
def travel_time_expr(from_loc, to_loc):
    expr = None
    # Loop over possible indices since from_loc and to_loc are Z3 expressions.
    for i in range(8):
        for j in range(8):
            cond = And(from_loc == i, to_loc == j)
            val = travel_matrix[i][j]
            if expr is None:
                expr = If(cond, val, 0)
            else:
                expr = If(cond, val, expr)
    return expr

# -------------------------------
# Z3 Model: Decision variables and constraints.
# -------------------------------
solver = Optimize()

# There are 7 meeting visits. For each, create a variable indicating which friend is visited at that slot.
route = [Int(f"r{i}") for i in range(7)]
# Create variables for meeting start times (in minutes).
s = [Int(f"s{i}") for i in range(7)]

# Permutation constraints: each route variable must be between 0 and 6 and all must be distinct.
for i in range(7):
    solver.add(route[i] >= 0, route[i] <= 6)
solver.add(Distinct(route))

# For each meeting in the route, add timing constraints.
for i in range(7):
    # For the friend in route slot i, get its parameters.
    # Use the helper functions (they depend on route[i])
    availS = friend_avail_start(route[i])
    availE = friend_avail_end(route[i])
    dur = friend_duration(route[i])
    friendLoc = friend_location_index(route[i])
    
    # Constraint: meeting must finish before availability end.
    solver.add(s[i] + dur <= availE)
    # Constraint: meeting cannot start earlier than the friend’s available starting time.
    solver.add(s[i] >= availS)
    
    if i == 0:
        # For the first meeting, we travel from Pacific Heights (location 0) to the friend’s location.
        travel_time_first = travel_time_expr(IntVal(0), friendLoc)
        arrival_time = start_time + travel_time_first
        # The meeting cannot start before the actual arrival.
        solver.add(s[i] >= arrival_time)
    else:
        # For subsequent meetings, we must account for previous meeting’s finish time and travel time.
        prev_dur = friend_duration(route[i-1])
        prev_friendLoc = friend_location_index(route[i-1])
        travel_t = travel_time_expr(prev_friendLoc, friendLoc)
        # The arrival time at the current meeting is the finish time of the previous meeting plus travel time.
        solver.add(s[i] >= s[i-1] + prev_dur + travel_t)

# We add an optimization objective:
# For example, minimizing the finishing time (end time of last meeting)
last_meeting_end = s[6] + friend_duration(route[6])
solver.minimize(last_meeting_end)

# -------------------------------
# Solve and extract the model
# -------------------------------
if solver.check() == sat:
    m = solver.model()

    # Build the schedule narrative
    schedule = []
    
    # Helper function: convert minutes to HH:MMAM/PM string.
    def minutes_to_time(t):
        total = int(t)
        hour = total // 60
        minute = total % 60
        ampm = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
        hour_disp = hour if 1 <= hour <= 12 else (hour-12 if hour>12 else 12)
        return f"{hour_disp}:{minute:02d}{ampm}"
    
    schedule.append(f"You start at {start_location} at {minutes_to_time(start_time)}.")
    
    # For each leg i, compute arrival time and meeting details.
    current_time = start_time
    current_loc = 0  # Pacific Heights location index is 0
    for i in range(7):
        # Determine friend for this slot.
        friend_idx = m.evaluate(route[i]).as_long()
        friend_name = friend_names[friend_idx]
        meeting_loc = friend_locations[friend_idx]
        # Get meeting parameters:
        dur = m.evaluate(friend_duration(route[i])).as_long()
        meeting_start = m.evaluate(s[i]).as_long()
        meeting_end = meeting_start + dur
        
        # Compute travel time from current location to next friend's location.
        travel_t = travel_matrix[current_loc][ location_mapping[friend_idx] ]
        arrival = current_time + travel_t
        
        # Output travel leg.
        if i == 0:
            schedule.append(f"You travel from {start_location} to {meeting_loc} in {travel_t} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival)}.")
        else:
            # previous meeting location is already printed.
            prev_loc_name = current_meeting_loc  # from previous iteration
            schedule.append(f"You travel from {prev_loc_name} to {meeting_loc} in {travel_t} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival)}.")
        
        # If arrival is earlier than the scheduled meeting start time, include a waiting message.
        if arrival < meeting_start:
            schedule.append(f"You wait until {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)}.")
        
        schedule.append(f"You meet {friend_name} for {dur} minutes from {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)} to {minutes_to_time(meeting_end)}.")
        
        # Update current time and current location for next leg.
        current_time = meeting_end
        current_loc = location_mapping[friend_idx]
        current_meeting_loc = meeting_loc  # store for narrative
        
    # Print the schedule (as a list of steps)
    print(schedule)
else:
    print("No solution found.")
```

1. We model the meeting order with 7 integer variables (route) that must be all different (i.e. a permutation over friends). For each meeting slot a start time variable is defined.
2. For the first meeting, we require that the meeting start is no earlier than the time it takes to travel from Pacific Heights (starting at 9:00AM) to the friend’s location and is within that friend’s available window.
3. For every subsequent meeting, we require that the meeting start is not before the previous meeting’s finish time plus the travel time from the previous friend’s location to the current one.
4. We use Z3’s Optimize() to minimize the finishing time of the last meeting.
5. Finally, the script constructs a narrative schedule with messages that detail when and where you travel, wait (if needed), and meet each friend.

Running this script will display a schedule narrative similar to the sample output format:

This problem can be modeled as a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) with an optimization objective.

Our decision variables include:
• A Boolean variable for each friend (x[i]) that is true if we decide to meet friend i and false otherwise.
• An integer variable for each friend (start_vars[i]) that represents the meeting’s start time (in minutes after midnight) if the meeting is scheduled.
• An integer variable (order_vars[i]) representing the order in which the meetings occur (if a friend is not visited, its order is 0; otherwise it must be between 1 and the total number of friends).

The constraints are:
1. If we meet a friend, the meeting start time must lie within the friend’s available interval – and the meeting must be long enough so that it finishes before the friend’s availability ends.
2. If we do not plan to meet a friend, then we force the start time and the order number to be 0.
3. If two friends are scheduled (both x[i] and x[j] are true), then they must have different order numbers.
4. For any two meetings scheduled in order (say friend i before friend j), the start time for friend j must be at least as late as friend i’s meeting start time plus meeting duration and the travel time from friend i’s location to friend j’s location.
5. For the first scheduled meeting (order variable equals 1) we also must consider the travel time from our starting point (Sunset District at 9:00AM) to that friend’s location.
6. Our objective is to maximize the number of friends we visit.

We can “translate” our friends‐meeting problem into a constraint–satisfaction scheduling problem. In our formulation we have a set of candidate “appointments” – one for each friend. Each appointment i is defined by:
 • a location (the place where your friend will be),
 • an “available time window” [avail_start, avail_end] during which the meeting can take place,
 • a required (contiguous) meeting duration.
You begin your day at 9:00AM in the Sunset District. For each friend you would “choose” to visit (or not) with a Boolean decision variable. If you decide to visit friend i then you must schedule a start time (an integer variable, measured in minutes since midnight) that lies no earlier than both the friend’s available‐time start and the time you can actually get there from your previous meeting (including the required travel time). Finally, to “chain” several meetings you introduce an ordering variable for each friend (if visited) so that if friend i comes before friend j then the start time for j must occur at least after i’s start time plus its required meeting duration plus the travel time from friend i’s location to friend j’s location. (For the very first meeting the constraint is that the arrival time from the Sunset District “departs” at 9:00AM plus the travel time.)

Thus the decision variables are:
 – For each friend i, a Boolean x[i] indicating whether to meet that friend.
 – A start time variable start[i] (if x[i] is true) that must obey  
    avail_start[i] ≤ start[i]  
    start[i] + duration[i] ≤ avail_end[i]

1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We model the day’s meeting plan as a scheduling problem where each “meeting” is a task that can be either scheduled (“selected”) or skipped. For every friend we have:
 • A fixed meeting location.
 • A fixed time‐window (availability) within which the meeting must occur.
 • A minimum meeting duration.
 • A travel “cost” (in minutes) needed to get from one location to the next.

Our decision variables include:
 – A Boolean variable for each friend (e.g. sel_friend) indicating whether we include that meeting.
 – An integer variable T_friend representing the start time (in minutes after midnight) at which the meeting starts if selected.

The constraints we impose are:

A. Time‐window constraints. For each friend “f” available between time A and B and with meeting duration D,
  if we choose to meet “f” then:
   T_f ≥ max(friend’s available start, (start time + travel time from “Chinatown”))
   and T_f + D ≤ friend’s available end.

B. Travel and ordering constraints among meetings. If you schedule two meetings f and g (with both sel_f and sel_g true) then one must come before the other. In other words, either
   T_f + (D_f + travel_time(from f.location to g.location)) ≤ T_g
or   T_g + (D_g + travel_time(from g.location to f.location)) ≤ T_f.
These disjunctive constraints “sequence” the selected meetings; note that travel times differ depending on the direction.

C. Initial condition. You start at Chinatown at 9:00AM (540 minutes) so for every meeting “f” the meeting’s start must be at least
  540 + travel_time(Chinatown, f.location).

We have a set of “meetings” each with a minimum duration (for example, Mark must be met for 105 minutes) and a friend-specific time window (e.g. Mark is available from 9:30AM to 11:45AM).   A ≤ t_F and t_F + D ≤ B.
For consecutive meetings in the schedule the travel time between the previous location and the next location must be added.   t_Elizabeth ≥ t_M + 105 + 20.
Similar travel–waiting constraints are enforced between every consecutive visit.

SOLUTION:
We can view this “day‐in–SF” scheduling as a constraint satisfaction and optimization problem. In our formulation we must decide, for each friend, whether or not to meet them (a Boolean decision), and if so, exactly when to start and finish the meeting. Each friend has a fixed meeting location, an available time window, and a minimum meeting duration. In addition, we start at the Financial District at 9:00AM and – because travel between locations takes time – if we plan to meet friend A and then friend B the schedule must satisfy that A’s meeting “ends” and, after the travel time from A’s location to B’s location, B’s meeting “starts.” (In other words, for any two meetings that are both scheduled, one must come before the other with enough time in between for travel.) 

Thus our decision variables are:
 • For each friend i, a Boolean (meet[i]) indicating whether we include that meeting.
 • For each friend i, an integer start time S[i] (in minutes from midnight) and an integer end time E[i] representing the meeting’s scheduled time.
The constraints are:
 1. If a friend is met then the meeting must lie entirely within that friend’s available window (for example, Mark’s meeting must be between 9:30AM and 10:30AM) and last at least the required duration.
 2. Even if a meeting is not first, the meeting’s start time must be “no earlier than” what you would have if you traveled directly from the Financial District. (This lower–bound is safe because any meeting after another will occur later anyway.)
 3. For any two friends i and j that are met the schedule must “order” them – either friend i’s meeting finishes and after the travel time from i’s location to j’s location friend j’s meeting can start, or vice‐versa.
The objective is to maximize the total number of friends met. (That is, we let the solver choose the “best” subset and order of meetings that satisfy all constraints while visiting as many friends as possible.)

In our formulation we must decide, for each friend, whether or not to meet them (a Boolean decision), and if so, exactly when to start and finish the meeting. Each friend has a fixed meeting location, an available time window, and a minimum meeting duration. In addition, we start at the Financial District at 9:00AM and – because travel between locations takes time – if we plan to meet friend A and then friend B the schedule must satisfy that A’s meeting “ends” and, after the travel time from A’s location to B’s location, B’s meeting “starts.” (In other words, for any two meetings that are both scheduled, one must come before the other with enough time in between for travel.) 

Thus our decision variables are:
 • For each friend i, a Boolean (meet[i]) indicating whether we include that meeting.
 • For each friend i, an integer start time S[i] (in minutes from midnight) and an integer end time E[i] representing the meeting’s scheduled time.

 1. If a friend is met then the meeting must lie entirely within that friend’s available window (for example, Mark’s meeting must be between 9:30AM and 10:30AM) and last at least the required duration.

Step 1 – Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem:
----------------------------------------------------------------
We model the schedule as a routing and scheduling problem with travel‐time and time‐window constraints. Think of the “nodes” as the starting point (Mission District at 9:00AM) and each friend’s location (with their availability window and required meeting duration). Our decision variables are:

• T[i]: the time at which you begin meeting at node i. For friend nodes, T[i] is bounded by the friend’s available start and end times (minus the service/meeting duration).
• y[i]: a Boolean flag for each friend node (i ≠ depot) indicating whether you meet that friend (y[i] = True) or skip that node.
• x[i,j]: a Boolean decision variable that is True if you travel directly from node i to node j. (We allow arcs from the depot (node 0) to friend nodes and between friend nodes—but to avoid returning to the depot, we disallow arcs that have the depot as the destination.)
• u[i]: an ordering variable used when friend i is visited, ensuring that if you travel from friend i to friend j then u[i] < u[j] (this helps eliminate subtours).

The constraints are:
1. Routing constraints – each visited friend must have exactly one incoming arc (the trip from another node arriving at the friend node) and, if visited, at most one outgoing arc. The depot is only allowed to have an outgoing arc (to start the route) and no arcs are allowed to point back to the depot.
2. Linking constraints – if an arc (i,j) is used then j must be “visited” (and, for non‐depot i, i must be “visited” too).
3. Time propagation – if you travel from i to j then the meeting at j can only start after you finish meeting at i and travel (i→j) the required number of minutes.
4. Time windows – if friend i is visited then the meeting time T[i] must lie within the friend’s available window (taking into account the meeting/service duration).
5. Subtour elimination constraints – these are additional ordering constraints on the friend nodes (using variables u[i]) so that the selected friend visits form one consistent route.
6. Objective – maximize the total number of friends visited.

Step 1. Reasoning as a constraint‐satisfaction problem

We are given a list of eight friends – each “located” in a different San Francisco neighborhood–and each friend is available during a specific time‐window and must be “met” for at least a specified number of minutes. In addition, we must account for travel times between districts (and from the starting point, Mission District, at 9:00AM) as given by the table. For each friend f we know:
 • f’s “service” (meeting) time d₍f₎ (eg. Jason requires 90 minutes),
 • a time window [A₍f₎, B₍f₎] (eg. Jason is available from 12:00PM to 7:00PM),
 • and his/her district (eg. Jason is in Chinatown).

We “rebase” time in minutes with 9:00AM as zero. For example, Jason’s window becomes [180,600] because 12:00PM is 180 minutes after 9:00AM and 7:00PM is 600 minutes later. (Also note that if a friend is “available” before 9:00AM [eg. Joseph from 8:00AM], we only can start at 9:00 so the lower‐bound is raised to 0.)

A decision variable is needed for every candidate meeting:
 • visited[f] (a Boolean) says whether or not we include friend f.
 • start[f] (an integer) gives the meeting starting minute (relative to 9:00AM). If friend f is visited then we must have
  A₍f₎ ≤ start[f] ≤ B₍f₎ – d₍f₎.
 • order[f] (an integer) indicates the visit “rank” in our route (with “0” meaning “not visited”). If friend f is visited then order[f] must be a positive integer (and distinct among visited friends).

There are also ordering “travel” constraints. If friend i is visited before friend j the meeting at i will finish at start[i] + d₍i₎ and we must add the travel time T(i,j) (which is not necessarily symmetric) from i’s district to j’s district. In that case the constraint is:
  start[i] + d₍i₎ + T(i,j) ≤ start[j].
For the very first meeting (say friend i with order = 1) we have to “come from” the Mission District. (For simplicity we add
  start[i] ≥ T(Mission, f))
since T(Mission,f) is a lower‐bound on the time it takes to reach any friend f from Mission District. 

Finally, the overall objective is to “meet as many friends as possible” – that is, we maximize the sum over f of the indicator for visited[f]. (Notice that some friends’ time windows conflict so it is not possible to schedule them all; for example, John (meeting for 105 minutes in Pacific Heights between 4:15PM and 6:45PM) and Jeffrey (only available 5:30PM–5:45PM in Haight‐Ashbury for a 15–minute meeting) cannot both be scheduled contiguously when their travel times are taken into account.)

We model the schedule as a routing and scheduling problem with travel‐time and time‐window constraints. Think of the “nodes” as the starting point (Mission District at 9:00AM) and each friend’s location (with their availability window and required meeting duration). Our decision variables are:

• u[i]: an ordering variable used when friend i is visited, ensuring that if you travel from friend i to friend j then u[i] < u[j] (this helps eliminate subtours).

Step 1 – Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem:
• We have a set of activities (meeting each friend) with individual time‐windows (their available times) and minimum meeting durations.
• Our decision variables are the meeting start times (in minutes after midnight) for each friend.
• In addition, travelling between neighborhoods (with given travel times) creates extra constraints. For any two consecutive meetings, the meeting start time of the later friend must be at least as late as the previous friend’s “departure time” (i.e. the previous meeting’s start time plus its minimum meeting duration) plus the travel time between the two locations.
• We also require that the meeting start time for each friend is no earlier than both the arrival time at that location (from our previous stops) and the start of that friend’s availability window, and that the meeting finishes within the available window.
• Our goal is to “meet as many friends as possible” by finding a schedule (i.e. an ordering and start times for each meeting) that satisfies all these hard constraints.
• The Z3 solver will “choose” meeting start times that satisfy all these constraints. In our implementation we fix a particular order (which in our case turns out to permit meeting every friend) and add the corresponding travel/wait constraints.

 • Our “variables” are defined for each friend:

SOLUTION:
Step 1 – Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem:
• Variables:
  – We create a fixed number (8) of “slots” representing potential meetings. For each slot k we have two decision variables:
  • slot[k]: an integer representing which friend (0 to 7) is scheduled (or –1 if unused).
  • T[k]: an integer representing the meeting’s start time (in minutes from midnight).
• Domains:
  – For slot[k]: either –1 (unused) or one of the friend indices 0 to 7.
  – For T[k]: any integer in a wide enough range, but will be constrained by each friend’s available window.
• Constraints:
  – Ordering and Uniqueness: If a slot is unused then all later slots must be unused and all used slots must have distinct friend assignments.
  – Availability: For each slot k if a friend f is assigned then the meeting must start no earlier than f’s available start time and finish by f’s available end (i.e. T[k] + (required meeting duration) ≤ avail_end).
  – Travel: You begin from The Castro at 9:00AM (540 minutes) and must allow enough travel time between locations. For example, the start time of slot 0 must be at least 540 plus the travel time from The Castro (location 0) to the friend’s location. For subsequent slots the start time must be after the end of the previous meeting plus the travel time between the two friends’ locations.
    (Note: To avoid errors when the same location appears in sequential iterations—even though distinct meetings prevent the same friend from being scheduled twice—we explicitly set the travel time from any location to itself as 0.)
• Objective:
  – Maximize the number of meetings (i.e. maximize the sum of slots that are used).

Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP):

We have a scheduling problem where you start at “The Castro” at 9:00AM (i.e. 540 minutes from midnight) and wish to “meet” several friends, each located at a fixed neighborhood in San Francisco. Each friend f has:
  • a fixed location (for example, Ronald is at Union Square),
  • an availability window [start, end] (expressed in minutes from midnight) and 
  • a desired “meeting” duration (a minimum number of minutes you must spend with that friend).

In addition, travel times (in minutes) are given between every pair of locations (including from “The Castro” to each location). When you travel from a previous meeting to the next one your arrival must be early enough so that you can (if needed) wait until the friend’s available time; once the meeting starts it must last at least the required duration and finish by the friend’s “end‐time”. Also, consecutive visits must account for the travel time between the two meeting locations.

To model this as a constraint satisfaction problem we define for each friend f (f = 0…7 corresponding to Ronald, Amanda, Kevin, Betty, Michelle, George, Steven, Mark):
  • a Boolean variable visited[f] that indicates whether you actually meet friend f,
  • two integer variables s[f] and e[f] representing the start and end time (in minutes) of meeting f (if met),
  • an integer variable order[f] indicating the position in your itinerary (with the convention that if visited then order ≥ 0 and if not visited, the order is forced to –1).

We impose the following constraints:
1. For each friend f (if visited):
  a. The meeting start time must be at or after the friend’s available start time.
  b. The meeting must end by the friend’s available end time and last at least the required meeting duration:
    e[f] – s[f] ≥ (required duration).
2. The “chain” constraints on travel:
  a. For the first visited friend (order = 0) the meeting start time must be at or after the time it takes to travel from “The Castro” at 9:00AM to that friend’s location.
  b. For any two friends f and g that are consecutive in the itinerary (i.e. order[g] = order[f] + 1) we require:
    s[g] ≥ e[f] + (travel time from f’s location to g’s location).
3. Ordering constraints:
  a. For any two visited friends the orders must be distinct.
  b. To “chain” the meetings correctly, if a friend f is visited with order > 0 then there must exist some friend with order f–1.
4. The objective is to maximize the number of friends met (i.e. maximize the sum over f of 1 if visited[f] is true).

Thus the CSP decides, among all possible orders and start/end times (subject to travel‐time lags and the availability windows) which meetings can be “fitted” into one valid schedule and picks the solution that meets as many friends as possible.

SOLUTION:

Below is one way to “think‐through” the problem and then solve it with Z3. In our formulation we view the day’s schedule as a constraint satisfaction (and optimization) problem, where you must decide:

1. For each friend (with a known location, available time window and a “service–time” requirement that is the minimum meeting duration) whether to visit them (a Boolean decision variable) and, if so, at what time to begin the meeting. (We express time in “minutes after 9:00AM”, so 9:00AM = 0, 1:45PM = 285, 3:15PM = 375, etc.)

2. In what order to visit the friends. We introduce an “order” integer variable for each friend (with value 0 meaning “not visited” and a positive order number if visited) so that if friend i is scheduled before friend j then the meeting time for friend j must be at least the sum of the meeting time at friend i plus the travel time from friend i’s location to friend j’s.

3. Travel times are “hard” constraints. For example, if you start at Chinatown at 9:00AM and you decide to go to Golden Gate Park (Melissa’s location) then you must allow the travel time of 23 minutes. Likewise, between any two visited friends the required travel minutes (taken from our table of distances) are added. Also, if a friend is the first meeting then you must “travel” from Chinatown (the starting point) to that friend’s location.

4. In addition, the meeting with each friend must occur entirely in the friend’s available time window. That is, if friend X is available from time a to b minutes then the scheduled meeting start Sₓ must obey Sₓ ≥ a and Sₓ + (minimum meeting duration) ≤ b.

5. Finally, we “optimize” by maximizing the total number of friends met (i.e. the sum of the binary variables for each friend). In our “example solution” the optimum turns out to be a schedule that meets five friends – one possible chain (that meets the time‐ and travel–constraints) is to visit Melissa (Golden Gate Park), then Mark (Pacific Heights), then Richard (Embarcadero), then Margaret (Fisherman’s Wharf) and finally Matthew (Russian Hill).

Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have a set of friends F (Kimberly, Sandra, Elizabeth, Lisa, Thomas, Jeffrey, Deborah, Ashley) where each friend f ∈ F has:
 • a fixed location,
 • an availability window [avail_start, avail_end] (measured in minutes after 9:00AM), and
 • a required meeting duration.
In addition, travel-times are given between any two locations (including the “start” location Embarcadero). We start at the Embarcadero at 9:00AM (time 0).

Our decision variables for each friend f are:
 • visited[f] ∈ {True, False} – whether we choose to meet friend f.
 • start_time[f] ∈ ℤ – the time (in minutes after 9:00AM) when we begin the meeting with friend f (if visited).
 • order[f] ∈ ℤ – an integer indicating the position in our itinerary (we set order 0 for friends we do NOT visit).

The constraints needed are:
1. For each friend f that is visited, the meeting must occur completely within the friend’s availability window:
  start_time[f] ≥ max(avail_start, (travel time from Embarcadero to f’s location)) and start_time[f] + duration(f) ≤ avail_end.
(The “travel time from Embarcadero” is used for the first meeting if friend f is visited first. For later meetings the ordering constraints will force a later start time.)
2. If a friend is visited then its order must be at least 1 (and different friends get distinct positive order numbers); if the friend is not visited then we fix order = 0.
3. For any two friends f and g that are both visited, assume without loss that order[f] < order[g]. Then we must have sufficient time to wrap up f’s meeting and travel from f’s location to g’s location. That is:
  start_time[g] ≥ start_time[f] + duration(f) + travel_time(f.location, g.location).
4. Our objective is to maximize the number of friends visited (i.e. maximize ∑_f If(visited[f] then 1 else 0)).

This forms a scheduling (and routing) constraint satisfaction model with “time” and “order” variables, plus extra travel–waiting constraints.

We can “model” the problem as a constraint‐satisfaction and optimization problem. In our formulation we have eight meetings – one for each friend – each happening at a fixed location with given “availability windows” (earliest and latest possible start/end times) and a minimum duration requirement. In addition we have fixed travel times between locations (and from the starting point, Embarcadero, at 9:00AM) so that if you visit friend A (say, at Union Square) and then friend B (say, at North Beach) the meeting start time for B must be later than the finish time of A plus the travel time from Union Square to North Beach.

We introduce for each friend i three decision “variables”:
 • a Boolean visited[i] that tells if you meet that friend,
 • an integer start[i] (in minutes from midnight) representing the meeting start time (if visited) – with the inequality
   start[i] ≥ friend’s available start and start[i] + (minimum duration) ≤ friend’s available end,
 • an integer order[i] that indicates the position in your overall route (with “0” meaning “not visited”). 

To “chain” the visits correctly we require that if friend i is followed immediately by friend j in your route then 
  start[j] ≥ start[i] + (minimum meeting duration for i) + (travel_time from i’s location to j’s location).
There is a similar constraint for the very first visited friend: its meeting start time must be at least the start time plus the travel time from Embarcadero (9:00AM). Moreover, to “line‐up” the sequence we force that the visited meeting orders are “contiguous” – that is, if one meeting is scheduled as “3” then meetings numbered 1 and 2 must exist (this is done by introducing, for each possible order number from 1 to 8, a constraint that if any friend is assigned an order ≥ that number then exactly one friend gets the next order number).

  start_time[f] ≥ max(avail_start, (travel time from Embarcadero to f’s location)) and start_time[f] + duration(f) ≤ avail_end.
(The “travel time from Embarcadero” is used for the first meeting if friend f is visited first. For later meetings the ordering constraints will force a later start time.)
2. If a friend is visited then its order must be at least 1 (and different friends get distinct positive order numbers); if the friend is not visited then we fix order = 0.
3. For any two friends f and g that are both visited, assume without loss that order[f] < order[g]. Then we must have sufficient time to wrap up f’s meeting and travel from f’s location to g’s location. That is:
  start_time[g] ≥ start_time[f] + duration(f) + travel_time(f.location, g.location).
4. Our objective is to maximize the number of friends visited (i.e. maximize ∑_f If(visited[f] then 1 else 0)).

This forms a scheduling (and routing) constraint satisfaction model with “time” and “order” variables, plus extra travel–waiting constraints.

SOLUTION:
Below is one way to “think‐in constraints” about the problem and then implement a solution with Z3. In our reasoning we view the day’s itinerary as a sequence of “visits” (or not) to friends. For each friend we introduce:
 • a binary decision variable (say x[i]) that is 1 if we choose to meet friend i and 0 otherwise,
 • an integer variable s[i] for the start time (in minutes counted from our 9:00AM arrival at Sunset District) when we begin the meeting, and
 • an order variable order[i] (if friend i is visited, order[i] is its “position” in the itinerary; if not, we set order[i] = 0).

Then we add these types of constraints:
 1. “Window constraints”: If we visit friend i (x[i] = 1) then the meeting must start no earlier than friend i’s availability start and finish (start + required meeting duration) by friend i’s available end.
 2. “Sequence constraints”: The very first visited friend must be reached from the starting district “Sunset District” (i.e. the travel time from Sunset to that friend’s location is added to the fixed start time 9:00AM). Furthermore, if friend i is visited immediately before friend j (i.e. order[i] < order[j]), then the travel time from friend i’s district to friend j’s district must be accommodated. In other words, the finish time of i plus the travel time must be ≤ the start time of j.
 3. “Ordering constraints”: For every pair of visited friends the “order” variables are forced to be all‐different and positive.
 4. Finally, we maximize the sum of the binary variables x[i] so as to “meet as many friends as possible.”

The Python code below builds the Z3 model with these constraints. (For simplicity we assume that if a friend is visited then we meet them exactly for the minimum required duration.) After solving the optimization model the code “simulates” the itinerary step–by–step, producing an output schedule (as a list of strings) that resembles:

 ["You start at Sunset District at 9:00AM.",
  "You travel to Alamo Square in 17 minutes and arrive at 9:17AM.",
  "You wait until 9:30AM.",
  "You meet Carol for 30 minutes from 9:30AM to 10:00AM.",
  …]

    period = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
    hour_display = hour if hour <= 12 else hour - 12
    # if hour==0 then display as 12; however here we never get hour==0
    return f"{hour_display}:{minute:02d}{period}"

# Friend data. Times are expressed in minutes after 9:00AM.

For example, if you meet friend A at one district and then friend B at another district, the start time for friend B must be no earlier than (A’s start time + A’s meeting duration + the travel time from A’s district to B’s district). Also, each meeting time must “fit” within the friend’s availability window – that is, the meeting must start no earlier than the friend’s available start and finish no later than the available end.

 • can only begin once you have finished the previous meeting and traveled from its location.
For instance, if “George” is met at The Castro then “Patricia” at North Beach, we enforce:

and similarly for the subsequent legs. Finally, we add the constraint for the very first meeting that you must have sufficient time to travel from Sunset District (your starting point at 9:00AM) to that friend’s location.

Step 1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We can “think‐in” this day‐planning problem as follows. You have a set of friend meetings. For each friend you decide whether to “schedule” a meeting or not (a Boolean decision) and, if scheduled, you must pick a start time for the meeting. Each friend’s meeting must happen entirely within the friend’s available time‐window and last at least the required minutes. In addition, because you travel from one district to the next (with “setup” times given by the travel minutes between the originating district and the destination), if you schedule two meetings then one must come completely before the other – that is, if you meet friend A and then later friend B, the start time for B must be at least “(A’s start time + meeting duration of A + travel time from A’s district to B’s district)”. (For the very first meeting you start at “Sunset District” at 9:00AM so you must “leave” Sunset and still obey the travel time from Sunset District to that meeting’s location.) 

Thus, the decision variables are:

  • For each friend i:
   – A Boolean “selected[i]” that indicates whether friend i is met.
   – An integer start time s[i] (minutes after 9:00AM) for the meeting.
  • For each friend, we have fixed constants:
   – Friend i’s available window [avail_start[i], avail_end[i]] (converted into minutes),
   – Friend i’s required meeting duration, and
   – Friend i’s district.
  • Travel times between every pair of districts (and from the starting “Sunset District”).
  
Then the constraints are:
  1. If friend i is scheduled then 
   s[i] must be no earlier than both the friend’s avail_start[i] and the time needed to get there from “Sunset District” (this guarantees that if i is first then you leave Sunset District at 9:00AM).
  2. If friend i is scheduled then s[i] + duration[i] ≤ avail_end[i].
  3. For every pair (i, j) of scheduled meetings (i ≠ j) the meetings cannot “overlap” taking travel into account. In other words, either
    s[i] + duration[i] + travel_time(from i’s district to j’s district) ≤ s[j]
  or
    s[j] + duration[j] + travel_time(from j’s district to i’s district) ≤ s[i].
  
Our objective is simply to maximize the number of friends seen, namely to maximize the sum of “selected” friends.
This “disjunctive‐” formulation (each pair of scheduled tasks is forced into one time–ordering or the other) is classical in scheduling with time‐windows and sequence–dependent “setup” (here, travel) times.

We can view the “day‐plan” as a scheduling problem where our decision variables are the start times (in minutes after 9:00AM) for each meeting with a friend. For example, if you meet friend A at one district and then friend B at another district, the start time for friend B must be no earlier than (A’s start time + A’s meeting duration + the travel time from A’s district to B’s district). Also, each meeting time must “fit” within the friend’s availability window – that is, the meeting must start no earlier than the friend’s available start and finish no later than the available end.

In our Z3 formulation we define integer variables (in minutes after 9:00AM) for the start time of each meeting (e.g. sGeorge, sPatricia, etc.). We add constraints that each meeting:

––––– REASONING –––––
We model the “day of meeting friends” as a constraint‐satisfaction problem with time‐windows and travel time constraints. For each friend we introduce:
 • A Boolean variable (visited_i) which is true if we schedule a meeting with friend i.
 • Two integer variables (start_i and end_i) representing the meeting’s start and end times (in minutes after midnight). When a friend is scheduled the meeting must last at least the given minimum duration.
 • A constraint that the meeting’s start and end must lie within the friend’s available time window.
 • A constraint that if friend i is scheduled then its meeting end time is exactly start_i + (minimum meeting minutes) (we choose the minimum necessary duration to keep the schedule “tight”).
Before the first meeting we start at Alamo Square at 9:00AM (540 minutes). Thus, if a friend meeting is scheduled first the meeting’s start time must be no earlier than 9:00AM plus the travel time from Alamo Square to that friend’s location.
Since we visit friends sequentially, for any two scheduled friend meetings (say i and j) we must have enough time to travel from one location to the other. This is modeled by a disjunction stating that either i comes before j:
   start_j ≥ (end_i + travel_time(from location_i to location_j))
or j comes before i:
   start_i ≥ (end_j + travel_time(from location_j to location_i)).
Our overall objective is to maximize the total number of friends visited (i.e. maximize the sum of all visited booleans).

We can “think‐in constraints” about the problem as follows. We have eight potential meetings (one per friend with a prescribed location, available time window and a minimum meeting duration) as well as a “starting” location (Embarcadero at 9:00AM). For each friend f we want to decide whether to “include” the meeting (a Boolean decision variable) and, if so, we assign a start‐time s[f] (an integer, in minutes since midnight) and a “position” (or order) in our itinerary. The meeting for friend f is “feasible” if:
 • s[f] lies within f’s available window (s[f] ≥ available_start[f] and s[f] + duration[f] ≤ available_end[f]); 
 • if f is the first meeting then s[f] is after the travel time from Embarcadero to f’s district; and 
 • if two meetings f and g are both scheduled and f comes immediately before g in our “order” then we must allow enough time: that is, f finishes at s[f] + duration[f] and after traveling from f’s location to g’s location (using the provided travel time) we have reached g’s meeting start time (s[g]).
Also, we add “distinct‐order” constraints so that (if scheduled) every friend has a unique order in the itinerary.
Finally, we “optimize” by maximizing the total number of meetings scheduled. (It turns out that because of the early time–window for Andrew, his meeting cannot “fit” into the schedule so the best itinerary includes the seven other meetings.)

1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have eight meetings (one per friend) that must happen in a fixed order. For each friend we know:

 • A minimum meeting duration.

We begin at 9:00AM at the Marina District. Thus the meeting with the first friend must start no earlier than our arrival at that friend’s location (Marina → friend’s location takes a fixed number of minutes). Then for every consecutive pair of meetings the following must hold:

  ◦ In addition, the meeting’s start and finish must lie inside the friend’s available time window.
  ◦ If you arrive earlier than the available start time you “wait” until the meeting can begin.
By “choosing” an order and suitable start times that satisfy the availability and transit–time constraints, the problem becomes a constraint satisfaction problem. (In our model we “hard–wired” an order that “visits” every friend. If no order had allowed all eight meetings then one might maximize the number of meetings met; here a feasible schedule meeting every constraint exists.)

We now model your “day in San Francisco” as a scheduling problem with spatial–temporal constraints. We must choose, order, and time a (possibly non‐empty) sequence of friend meetings so that:

We have a “time–window vehicle‐routing” (or “traveling salesman with time windows and service durations”) problem. You begin at a fixed location (“Presidio”) at 9:00AM. There are eight potential meetings (with Nancy, Joshua, Joseph, David, John, Daniel, Jessica and Paul) to “visit” at fixed places around the city. Each friend i is only available during a time window [available_start[i], available_end[i]] (converted into minutes – here we use 9:00AM as time‐0) and if you meet friend i you must spend at least a “service time” equal to the required meeting duration.

In addition the travel times between locations (and from the start “Presidio”) are given. The ordering of visits is not fixed. For any two meetings that you decide to “take,” the meeting times must not only fall inside the friend’s available window but must also be “sequenced” in time with enough “gap” (the service time plus the travel time from the earlier friend’s location to the later friend’s location) so that you can physically get from one meeting to the next.

We introduce for each friend i:
 • A Boolean variable visited[i] telling whether the meeting is scheduled.
 • An integer variable start[i] giving the meeting’s start (in minutes after 9:00AM).
The following constraints hold for each friend i if visited:
  – The meeting start must be at (or after) the friend’s available start (and, in practice, also after any travel time if friend i is the first meeting).
  – The meeting must be completed by friend i’s availability end. (That is, start[i] + duration[i] ≤ available_end[i].)
For any two different friends i and j that are both “visited” the order must be decided so that either:
  – Friend i’s meeting (plus travel time from i’s location to j’s location) finishes before friend j’s meeting starts, or 
  – j’s meeting (plus travel time from j’s location to i’s location) finishes before friend i’s meeting starts.
Finally, we “connect” the chain by ensuring that the “first” visited friend in our schedule is reached from the Presidio. (That is, if friend i is the earliest meeting then start[i] must be no earlier than the travel time from Presidio to friend i’s location.)

Our goal is to “maximize” the number of meetings scheduled (that is, maximize the number of visited[i] set to true) because you want to meet as many friends as possible.

─────────────────────────────

 We have a set of nine friends, each with a fixed location, an availability window (start and end times in minutes after midnight), and a required minimum meeting duration. In addition, we start at a fixed location (Golden Gate Park) at 9:00AM. There is a full matrix of travel times between all locations, and if you plan to meet two friends one after the other then you must allow time to travel between the locations.
 We model the decision of whether to “visit” a friend with a Boolean variable. For each friend we introduce integer decision variables for the meeting’s start time (S) and end time (E) – with the constraint that if the friend is visited then the meeting time must fall entirely within the friend’s availability and last at least the required duration. We also assign an “order” variable (an integer) so that if friends i and j are both visited and one follows the other in the tour then we require that the second’s start time is no earlier than the first’s end time plus the travel time between their locations.

 This is a typical constraint satisfaction (and scheduling) problem with both time‐window constraints and “routing/travel” constraints.

Below is one way to “think‐out” the problem as a constraint satisfaction problem and a revised Z3 model in Python.

1. Explanation as a CSP

• Our “variables” are the slots in our day that might contain a meeting. In our revised formulation we create M slots (with M = number of friends) that are arranged in order. For each slot i we introduce:
  – A Boolean variable used[i] that is True if this slot is “filled” with a meeting.
  – An integer variable friend_idx[i] that (when used[i] is True) tells which friend (by its index in our list) is met in that slot. If the slot is not used, we set friend_idx[i] to –1.
  – An integer variable start[i] giving the meeting’s start time (in minutes from midnight) for that slot.

• The “constraints” are:
  – If a slot is used then the meeting must occur within that friend’s available window. In other words, for a friend m that might be assigned to slot i we require
   start[i] ≥ avail_start[m] and start[i] + min_meeting[m] ≤ avail_end[m].
  – The travel constraints are enforced across consecutive slots. For the very first slot (i = 0) the meeting’s start time must be at least the arrival time from Union Square (the start location) plus the travel time from Union Square to the friend’s meeting location. For subsequent slots i > 0 we require that the start time in slot i is at least the previous slot’s meeting finish time plus the travel time from that previous meeting’s location to the new meeting’s location.
  – We add “contiguity” by requiring that if slot i is used then slot i–1 is also used (so the used slots form a contiguous block from the beginning).
  – We also add a distinctness constraint so that each friend appears at most once.

• Our “objective” is to maximize the total number of scheduled meetings (i.e. the sum over used[i]). The resulting “plan” then tells us in order which friend to meet, when to leave from each location, whether to wait until the meeting’s start time, and when each meeting ends.

SOLUTION:
We can “model” our day‐planning problem as a scheduling (constraint satisfaction) problem with routing. In our formulation we have a set of candidates (one per friend) and for each friend we decide:
 • Whether to “visit” that friend (a Boolean decision variable).
 • If visited, at what time (an integer variable representing minutes after 9:00AM) the meeting begins.
Each friend comes with an availability window and a minimum meeting‐duration requirement. In addition, we know the travel times between locations (including from the starting location, Golden Gate Park, to each friend’s spot).

The constraints we add are as follows:
 1. For any friend “i” that is visited the meeting must start no earlier than both the beginning of that friend’s availability and the travel time required from Golden Gate Park to get there. Also the meeting must finish (start time + required minutes) before the friend’s availability window closes.
 2. For every pair of friends i and j that are both visited, the meetings cannot “overlap” in time. In fact, if you meet friend i before friend j then the meeting i’s finish time plus the travel time from friend i’s location to friend j’s location must be no later than friend j’s start time. (Since the order is not predetermined, we add a disjunctive constraint saying that either i comes before j or vice‐versa.)
 3. All meeting “start” times are naturally non‐negative.

Finally, our objective is to “optimize” (i.e. maximize) the number of friends met. In other words, we choose among many potential itineraries the one that visits as many friends as possible while satisfying all time–window and travel–time constraints.
The z3 optimization engine is well suited for this kind of “scheduling with time windows and routing” problem.

We can “model” our day‐planning problem as a scheduling (constraint satisfaction) problem with routing. In our formulation we have a set of candidates (one per friend) and for each friend we decide:
 • Whether to “visit” that friend (a Boolean decision variable).
 • If visited, at what time (an integer variable representing minutes after 9:00AM) the meeting begins.
Each friend comes with an availability window and a minimum meeting‐duration requirement. In addition, we know the travel times between locations (including from the starting location, Golden Gate Park, to each friend’s spot).

The constraints we add are as follows:
 1. For any friend “i” that is visited the meeting must start no earlier than both the beginning of that friend’s availability and the travel time required from Golden Gate Park to get there. Also the meeting must finish (start time + required minutes) before the friend’s availability window closes.
 2. For every pair of friends i and j that are both visited, the meetings cannot “overlap” in time. In fact, if you meet friend i before friend j then the meeting i’s finish time plus the travel time from friend i’s location to friend j’s location must be no later than friend j’s start time. (Since the order is not predetermined, we add a disjunctive constraint saying that either i comes before j or vice‐versa.)
 3. All meeting “start” times are naturally non‐negative.

Finally, our objective is to “optimize” (i.e. maximize) the number of friends met. In other words, we choose among many potential itineraries the one that visits as many friends as possible while satisfying all time–window and travel–time constraints.
The z3 optimization engine is well suited for this kind of “scheduling with time windows and routing” problem.

1. Explanation as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have a “route‐meeting” problem where you (the “agent”) start at Nob Hill at 9:00AM (time = 540 in minutes since midnight) and want to meet as many friends as possible. Each friend is located in a different district and is available only during their own time window. Moreover, for each friend there is a minimum meeting duration required. Travel times between any two districts (including leaving from “Nob Hill”) are given.

The decision variables include, for each friend:
 • A Boolean (or 0/1) variable “visited” telling whether you schedule a meeting with that friend.
 • A meeting start time and meeting end time (both integer variables in minutes) which must lie inside the friend’s available window and be separated by at least the minimum meeting duration.
 • An “order” integer (if visited) representing the position in your itinerary. (We force the order to be unique among the visited friends; if not visited, we set the order to 0.)

The main constraints are:
 – For each friend i that is visited:
  • meeting_start[i] must be no earlier than the friend’s availability start and meeting_end[i] must be no later than the friend’s availability end.
  • The meeting duration (meeting_end[i] − meeting_start[i]) must be at least the required minimum.
 – For the friend that is scheduled first (that is, order = 1) the travel time from Nob Hill must be taken into account. Specifically, you must have: 9:00AM + travel_time(Nob Hill, friend_location) ≤ meeting_start.
 – For any two friends i and j that are both visited and are consecutive in your itinerary (i.e. order[j] = order[i] + 1) the travel time between their districts forces: meeting_end[i] + travel_time(location_i, location_j) ≤ meeting_start[j].
 – If a friend is not visited then the “order” can be set to 0.
 – Finally, we add a goal (objective) to “maximize” the number of friends visited.
 
Thus the overall formulation is similar to a traveling salesman problem with time windows and service durations, where the “service” to be performed is the meeting (of minimum length). The Z3 Optimize API is used so that many “schedules” are tried and the one that meets the most friends (our objective) is chosen.

• “Pair‐wise” (disjunctive) ordering constraints for any two friends whom you decide to meet. In effect, if you plan to meet friends i and j then one of them must come before the other. More precisely, for each unordered pair (i,j) we introduce a binary (Boolean) decision variable (defined only once for each unordered pair) that indicates the “logical order”–that is, if the Boolean is True then we decide that meeting i comes before meeting j. Once that decision is made the model forces the “next‐meeting” constraint:

If, on the other hand, the Boolean is False (so that j comes “before” i) then

1. A set of “meeting” tasks – one for each friend. For each friend we know:
 • the location (for which we have travel times from every other location),
 • an availability window (start time and end time) during which that friend is “on‐site,” and
 • a minimum meeting duration that we must “spend” with that friend.

2. We also have a “starting point” (The Castro at 9:00AM) from which we set off.

3. We add decision variables:
 – A Boolean variable for each friend indicating whether you will actually meet that friend.
 – A (integer) start‐time variable for each friend’s meeting (if it occurs) and a “finish time” defined as start time plus the required meeting duration.
 – An ordering variable (an integer rank) for every friend that you choose to visit so that you “chain” your visits. For the first visited friend (order 0) you must have traveled from The Castro and arrived early enough to wait if necessary. For any friend that is not the first in the schedule, its start time must be at least the finish time of its immediate predecessor plus the travel time between the two locations.

 • If you decide to meet friend i (visited[i] is true) then the meeting must occur inside the friend’s available time window:

Explanation:

• For each friend that we choose to visit (visited[i] true) we enforce that:
 – The meeting starts after the friend’s available start time and finishes (start + required meeting minutes) before the available end.
 – If it is the first meeting (order == 0) then we must have at least traveled from The Castro.

One way to think about this “meet‐all‐your‐friends” problem is to see it as a scheduling (or “traveling salesman with time windows”) constraint satisfaction problem. In our formulation we have:

1. A set of “meeting” tasks – one for each friend. For each friend we know:
 • the location (for which we have travel times from every other location),
 • an availability window (start time and end time) during which that friend is “on‐site,” and
 • a minimum meeting duration that we must “spend” with that friend.

2. We also have a “starting point” (The Castro at 9:00AM) from which we set off.

3. We add decision variables:
 – A Boolean variable for each friend indicating whether you will actually meet that friend.
 – A (integer) start‐time variable for each friend’s meeting (if it occurs) and a “finish time” defined as start time plus the required meeting duration.
 – An ordering variable (an integer rank) for every friend that you choose to visit so that you “chain” your visits. For the first visited friend (order 0) you must have traveled from The Castro and arrived early enough to wait if necessary. For any friend that is not the first in the schedule, its start time must be at least the finish time of its immediate predecessor plus the travel time between the two locations.

4. The constraints are then as follows:
 • If you decide to meet friend i (visited[i] is true) then the meeting must occur inside the friend’s available time window:
   s_i ≥ availability_start(i) and s_i + meeting_duration(i) ≤ availability_end(i).
