Below is one way to “think‐about” the problem as a constraint–satisfaction (and optimization) problem and then a complete Python script that uses Z3 to solve it.

──────────────────────────────
1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have a set F of 10 friends. For each friend we know:
 • The district (location) where the friend may be met.
 • A time window [A, B] (converted here into “minutes after 9:00AM”) during which the friend is available.
 • A minimum meeting (service) duration d.

We start our day at the “Presidio” at 9:00AM (time = 0 minutes). Also given is a travel–time matrix: for any pair (L1, L2) of districts (including the Presidio) the travel time T(L1,L2) is given.

Our “decision” is to choose a subset of friends to “meet” (each meeting is a service, and we want to maximize the number of friends we see) and decide on a “schedule” (that is, the order in which the meetings are held, and when we start each meeting). For each friend i we define:
  • A Boolean decision variable visit[i] indicating whether we actually meet friend i.
  • An integer variable start[i] – the scheduled meeting‐start time (in minutes after 9:00AM). (We assume the meeting is exactly the minimum required duration.)
  
The constraints are:
 – (Time Windows) For each friend i that is “visited” we must have 
      start[i] ≥ avail_start[i] and start[i] + d[i] ≤ avail_end[i].
 – (Initial “arrival” from Presidio) Even the first meeting must occur no earlier than the travel time from the Presidio to that friend’s location:
      start[i] ≥ T(“Presidio”, location[i]).
 – (Nonoverlap and ordering with travel times) For any two friends i and j that are both visited, the meetings (including travel time from i to j) must not “overlap.” In other words, one of the two must occur before the other. We can state this with a disjunction:
      If (visit[i] ∧ visit[j]) then
            (start[i] + d[i] + T(location[i], location[j]) ≤ start[j])
         ∨ (start[j] + d[j] + T(location[j], location[i]) ≤ start[i]). 
This “disjunctive” constraint ensures that if both meetings are scheduled, they will be carried out in some order such that enough time is allocated to travel from one meeting’s district to the next.
 – (Objective) Our overall goal is to “meet as many friends as possible.” In other words we maximize
      Sum( if visit[i] then 1 else 0 ).
      
Once an optimal solution is found we can “simulate” the route. In the final schedule the visited friends will have assigned meeting start–times. Sorting the visited friends in ascending order of start time yields the order in which you will visit the districts. Then, starting from the Presidio at 9:00AM, we simulate travel (adding the travel time T from the current district to the next) and, if you arrive early relative to the scheduled meeting start time, a “wait” is inserted. Finally, we output a list of strings (one for each “step”) that describe your journey.

1. Reasoning as a Constraint Satisfaction Problem

We have a set F of 10 friends. For each friend we know:
 • The district (location) where the friend may be met.
 • A time window [A, B] (converted here into “minutes after 9:00AM”) during which the friend is available.
 • A minimum meeting (service) duration d.

We start our day at the “Presidio” at 9:00AM (time = 0 minutes). Also given is a travel–time matrix: for any pair (L1, L2) of districts (including the Presidio) the travel time T(L1,L2) is given.

Our “decision” is to choose a subset of friends to “meet” (each meeting is a service, and we want to maximize the number of friends we see) and decide on a “schedule” (that is, the order in which the meetings are held, and when we start each meeting). For each friend i we define:
  • A Boolean decision variable visit[i] indicating whether we actually meet friend i.
  • An integer variable start[i] – the scheduled meeting‐start time (in minutes after 9:00AM). (We assume the meeting is exactly the minimum required duration.)
  
The constraints are:
 – (Time Windows) For each friend i that is “visited” we must have 
      start[i] ≥ avail_start[i] and start[i] + d[i] ≤ avail_end[i].
 – (Initial “arrival” from Presidio) Even the first meeting must occur no earlier than the travel time from the Presidio to that friend’s location:
      start[i] ≥ T(“Presidio”, location[i]).
 – (Nonoverlap and ordering with travel times) For any two friends i and j that are both visited, the meetings (including travel time from i to j) must not “overlap.” In other words, one of the two must occur before the other. We can state this with a disjunction:

            (start[i] + d[i] + T(location[i], location[j]) ≤ start[j])

This “disjunctive” constraint ensures that if both meetings are scheduled, they will be carried out in some order such that enough time is allocated to travel from one meeting’s district to the next.

      Sum( if visit[i] then 1 else 0 ).

Below is one way to “think‐out” the problem. In our setting we have a set of friends (each with a fixed location, an available (time window) interval, and a required “meeting‐duration”). In addition we know the travel times between any two locations (including from the start at Union Square). We introduce for each friend a Boolean decision variable x indicating whether we “visit” that friend, an integer variable s (in minutes after 9:00AM) for the friend’s meeting‐start time, and an integer “order” variable representing that friend’s position in our overall schedule (with –1 meaning “not scheduled”). Then we impose the following constraints:
 
1. For each friend f that we choose to visit (x[f] true) the meeting “must” take place during the friend’s visiting interval – namely,
    s[f] ≥ (friend f’s available‐start)
    s[f] + (meeting duration) ≤ (friend f’s available‐end)
2. If f is not visited, we “fix” the order (for example, −1).
3. In any “sequence” of visited friends, the travel time must be “accounted for.” In particular, if friend f is visited before friend g then we require that
    s[f] + (duration of f) + [travel time from f’s location to g’s location] ≤ s[g].
4. For the very first meeting (the friend scheduled in “position 0”) we must depart from Union Square at 9:00 and therefore 
    s[f] ≥ (travel time from Union Square to f’s location).
5. Finally the objective is to maximize the number of friends visited (maximize the sum of the Boolean x variables).

A solution (found by the z3 optimizer) then “chooses” a sequence (an ordering, with each friend’s start time suitably delayed to allow travel and even possible waiting in between) so that all the time‐window and travel constraints are obeyed. We can cast the “meeting friends” problem as a scheduling/constraint satisfaction problem with time‐windows and travel times. In our formulation we have a set of “tasks” (meeting with a friend) that each must be scheduled within a “time window” (the friend’s available hours) and must last at least a given duration. In addition, there is a travel time between the locations where the meetings occur. Our decision variables are:
 • Which friends to meet and in what order (i.e. a permutation of a subset of friends), and
 • The meeting start and end times for each scheduled friend.
For each friend meeting we must ensure that:
 – The meeting starts no earlier than the friend’s available start time.
 – The meeting lasts at least the minimum required duration (in our optimal solution we actually set the meeting duration exactly equal to the minimum so that the schedule is as “tight” as possible).
 – The meeting ends before or at the friend’s available end time.
Also, the meeting schedule must “chain” properly. In other words, if you meet one friend then travel to the next friend’s location, the start time of the next meeting must be at least the previous meeting’s ending time plus the travel time from the previous friend’s location to the next friend’s location. (For the very first meeting the travel originates from Union Square at 9:00AM.)
Finally, our objective is to maximize the number of friends met. One way to model this is to assume a fixed sequence of “schedule slots” (here we use 10 slots – one per friend) where each slot can either be unused (denoted by –1) or assigned a friend index. We enforce that the used slots appear contiguously and that any two used slots host different friends. Then, using “if–then” constraints we link a slot value (which friend is scheduled there) to its meeting window, the travel constraint (from either Union Square or the previous meeting’s location), and the meeting duration.

1. We first “translate” the city‐meeting problem into a constraint satisfaction scheduling problem. Each friend is seen as a “task” that must be scheduled if you choose to meet them. Every task has:
 • A fixed location and an associated availability interval (for example, Jeffrey is in Chinatown from 7:45PM to 9:45PM).
 • A required (minimum) meeting duration.
 • A “release” condition coming from your starting time and travel time (for instance, if you are to meet a friend at “Financial District,” you must allow for the travel time from your starting point, North Beach, at 9:00AM).
In addition, travel times between every pair of locations are provided. If you decide to “visit” two friends, the meetings must be “non‐overlapping” in the sense that whichever meeting comes first must finish (after its required duration) and then you must be able to travel from that friend’s location to the next friend’s location before that meeting begins.
This naturally leads to defining, for each friend i:
  – a Boolean variable visited[i] (indicating whether you include that meeting in your itinerary),
  – an integer variable start[i] (representing the meeting’s start time in minutes after midnight) if you do visit them.
The constraints we add are:
 • If visited, the meeting must start no earlier than the friend’s availability start, and no earlier than your arrival time from North Beach.
 • The meeting’s end time (start time plus required duration) must occur before the friend’s availability ends.
 • For every pair of friends i and j that are both visited, one must “come before” the other – that is, either i’s finish time plus the travel time from i’s location to j’s location is less than or equal to j’s start time, or vice‐versa.
Our objective is simply to maximize the total number of friends visited (i.e. maximize Σ visited[i]). Once a satisfying (optimal) assignment is found, we can “reconstruct” the itinerary by sorting the visited friends by their meeting start times and then “simulating” the travel (including any waiting time) from the starting location (North Beach) to the first meeting and then sequentially between the meetings.

If you decide to “visit” two friends, the meetings must be “non‐overlapping” in the sense that whichever meeting comes first must finish (after its required duration) and then you must be able to travel from that friend’s location to the next friend’s location before that meeting begins.
